Chapter 1 Preliminary

Question 1. MNP Private Ltd. is a company registered under the Companies Act, 2013 with a paid-up share capital of Rs 2 crore and turnover of Rs 60 crore. Explain the meaning of the “Small Company” and examine the following in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013: (i) Whether MNP Private Ltd. can avail the status of a small company? (ii) What will be your answer if the turnover of the company is Rs 30 crore?

(5 marks|5minutes) (Study Material) (Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 1. Small Company Definition: According to Section 2(85) of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 2(1)(t) of the Companies (Specification of Definition Details) Rules, 2014 [as amended by Notification dated 01-12- 2025], "Small Company" means a company, other than a public company, which satisfies both the following conditions:

1. Paid-up share capital of waahich does not exceed Rs. 10 crore (Ten Crore Rupees); AND
2. Turnover of which as per its profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year does not exceed Rs. 100 crores (One Hundred Crore Rupees).

Exceptions: Nothing in this clause shall apply to: (A) A holding company or a subsidiary company; (B) A company registered under section 8; or (C) A company or body corporate governed by any special Act. (2.5marks)

Analysis of the Case: (i) Case 1: Capital Rs. 2 Crore & Turnover Rs. 60 Crore:  Paid-up Capital: Rs. 2 Crore (which is ≤ Rs. 10 Crore) → Condition Met.  Turnover: Rs. 60 Crore (which is ≤ Rs. 100 Crore) → Condition Met.  Company Type: MNP Private Ltd. is a private company.

Conclusion: Since MNP Private Ltd. satisfies both the revised criteria (Capital ≤ 10 Cr and Turnover ≤ 100 Cr), it can avail the status of a Small Company. (Note: Under the old limits of 4Cr/40Cr, this company would NOT have been a small company because turnover exceeded 40Cr. Under the new 2026 limits, it IS a small company).

(ii) Case 2: Capital Rs. 2 Crore & Turnover Rs. 30 Crore:

 Paid-up Capital: Rs. 2 Crore (which is ≤Rs. 10 Crore) → Condition Met.  Turnover: Rs. 30 Crore (which is ≤ Rs. 100 Crore) → Condition Met.

Conclusion: In this case as well, MNP Private Ltd. can avail the status of a Small Company. (2.5 marks)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 2

1. First write the definition of “Small Company” under Section 2(85) with both limits: paid-up capital and

turnover.

2. Check both conditions one by one using a simple comparison table.
3. Mention exceptions only briefly to save time and directly conclude whether the company qualifies or not.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often forget that both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.
2. Many write old limits instead of revised limits and lose marks in practical questions.

Answer 2. 1. Paid-up share capital of which does not exceed Rs. 10 Crores (Ten Crore Rupees); AND
2. Turnover of which as per its profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year does not 1 exceed Rs. 100 Crores (One Hundred Crore Rupees).

Exceptions: Nothing in this clause shall apply to: (A) A holding company or a subsidiary company; (B) A company registered under section 8; or (C) A company or body corporate governed by any special Act.

Analysis of the Case: (i) Case 1: Capital Rs. 70 Lakhs & Turnover Rs. 30 Crores

Conclusion: Since New Private Ltd. satisfies both the revised criteria (Capital ≤ 10 Cr and Turnover ≤ 100 Cr), it can

4 avail the status of a Small Company.

Question 3. The paid-up share capital of Altar Private Limited is Rs 1 crore, consisting of 8 lacs Equity Shares of Rs 10 each, fully paid-up and 2 lacs Cumulative Preference Shares of Rs10 each, fully paid-up. New Private Limited and Ultra Private Limited are holding 3 lacs Equity Shares and 50,000 Equity Shares respectively in Altar Private Limited. New Private Limited and Ultra Private Limited are the subsidiaries of PQR Private Limited. With reference to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 examine whether Altar Private Limited is a subsidiary of PQR Private Limited? Would your answer be different if PQR Private Limited has 8 out of 9 Directors on the Board of Altar Private Limited?

(5 marks|5 minutes) (RTP May’19 & May’18) (Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 3. In terms of section 2 (87) of the Companies Act 2013 "subsidiary company" or "subsidiary", in relation to any other company (that is to say the holding company), means a company in which the holding company— (i) Controls the composition of the Board of Directors; or (ii) Exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power either at its own or together with one or more of its subsidiary companies:

Explanation: - For the purposes of this clause (2 marks) (a) A company shall be deemed to be a subsidiary company of the holding company even if the control referred to in sub- clause (i) or sub-clause (ii) is of another subsidiary company of the holding company; (b) The composition of a company's Board of Directors shall be deemed to be controlled by another company if that other company by exercise of some power exercisable by it at its discretion can appoint or remove all or a majority of the directors.

In the present case, New Pvt. Ltd. and Ultra Pvt. Ltd. together hold less than one half of the total share capital i.e. less than one-half of total voting power. Hence, PQR Private Ltd. (holding of New Pvt. Ltd. and Ultra Pvt. Ltd) will not be a holding company of Altar Pvt. Ltd. However, if PQR Pvt. Ltd. has 8 out of 9 Directors on the Board of Altar Pvt. Ltd. i.e. controls the composition of the Board of Directors; it (PQR Pvt. Ltd.) will be treated as the holding company of Altar Pvt. Ltd. (3 marks)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. First state Section 2(87) and the two tests: control of Board or control of voting power.
2. Calculate total voting power properly and compare whether it exceeds 50%.
3. In the second part, directly apply “control of Board composition” without unnecessary calculations.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 4

Examiner Observations:

1. Students confuse total share capital with voting power.
2. Many fail to discuss the second condition relating to Board control.

Question 4. Referring the relevant provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, examine, whether following companies will be considered as listed company or unlisted company: I. ABC Limited, a public company, has listed its non-convertible Debt securities issued on private placement basis in terms of SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations, 2008. II. CHG Limited, a public company, has listed its non-convertible redeemable preference shares issued on private placement basis in terms of SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non- Convertible Redeemable Preference Shares) Regulations, 2013. III. PRS Limited, a public company, which has not listed its equity shares on a recognized stock exchange but whose equity shares are listed on a stock exchange in a jurisdiction as specified in sub-section (3) of section 23 of the Companies Act, 2013.

(5 marks|5 minutes) (PYP Nov ‘22)(Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 4. According to Section 2(52) of the Companies Act, 2013, listed company means a company which has any of its securities listed on any recognized stock exchange. RULE 2A: According to Rule 2A of the Companies (Specification of definitions details) Rules, 2014, the following classes of companies shall not be considered as listed companies, namely: -(a) Public companies which have not listed their equity shares on a recognized stock exchange but have listed there:-

 Non-convertible debt securities issued on private placement basis in terms of SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt

Securities) Regulations, 2008; or  non-convertible redeemable preference shares issued on private placement basis in terms of SEBI (Issue and

Listing of Non-Convertible Redeemable Preference Shares) Regulations, 2013; or  Both categories of (i) and (ii) above.

(b) Public companies which have not listed their equity shares on a recognized stock exchange but whose equity shares are listed on a stock exchange in a jurisdiction as specified in subsection

(c) Of section 23 of the Act. In view of the above provisions of the Act:  ABC Limited is an unlisted company.  CHG Limited is an unlisted company.  PRS Limited is an unlisted company.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quote Section 2(52) and Rule 2A first.
2. Prepare answers in point-wise format for all three companies separately.
3. Remember that listing of debt securities or preference shares alone does not make the company listed.

Examiner Observations:

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 5

1. Students generally assume every company having listed securities is a listed company.
2. Many fail to mention Rule 2A exemptions.

Question 5. ABC Private Ltd. has two wholly owned subsidiary companies, D Private Limited and E Private Limited. Examine, whether, D Private Limited and E Private Limited will be treated as related party as per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013?

(3 marks|3 minutes) (PYP May ’22) (Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 5. According to section 2(76) (viii) of the Companies Act, 2013, Related party, with reference to a company, means anybody corporate which is - (A) A holding, subsidiary or an associate company of such company; (B) A subsidiary of a holding company to which it is also a subsidiary; or (C) An investing company or the venture of the company;

In the given Question, D Private Limited and E Private Limited are wholly owned subsidiary companies of ABC Private Ltd. According to stated clause (B), above, D Private Limited and E Private Limited are related parties. However, as per the Notification No. G.S.R. 464(E) dated 5th June, 2015, clause (viii) shall not apply with respect to section 188 to a private company, though being a related party.

Alternate Answer: According to section 2(76) (viii)(B) of the Companies Act, 2013, Related party, with reference to a company, means anybody corporate which is a subsidiary of a holding company to which it is also a subsidiary. However, Clause (viii) shall not apply with respect to section 188 (Related Party transactions) to a private company vide Notification No. G.S.R. 464(E) dated 5th June, 2015.

In the given Question, D Private Limited and E Private Limited are wholly owned subsidiary companies of ABC Private Ltd. According to stated clause (B), above, D Private Limited and E Private Limited are related parties. However, as per the mentioned Notification, clause (viii) shall not apply with respect to section 188 to a private company. Therefore, D Private Limited and E Private Limited are not related parties for the purpose of section 188\.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Write the exact cause of Section 2(76)(viii).
2. Apply the concept of fellow subsidiaries carefully.
3. Mention the private company exemption under Section 188 separately.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often stop after proving related party status and forget the notification exemption..
2. Many confuse holding-subsidiary relationship with associate relationship.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 6

Question 6. Teresa Ltd. is a company registered in New York (U.S.A.). The company has no place of business established in India, but it is doing online business through data interchange in India. Explain with reference to relevant provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 whether Teresa Ltd. will be treated as Foreign Company.

(6 marks|5 minutes) (PYP Nov’18) (Same concept different figures PYP Nov’19) (Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 6. According to section 2(42) of the Companies Act, 2013, foreign company means any company or body corporate incorporated outside India which,- (a) Has a place of business in India whether by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode; and

(b) Conducts any business activity in India in any other manner.

As per the Rule given in the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014, the term “electronic mode”, means carrying out electronically based, whether main server is installed in India or not, including, but not limited to:-  Business to business and business to consumer transactions, data interchange and other digital supply

transactions;  Offering to accept deposits or inviting deposits or accepting deposits or subscriptions in securities, in India or

from citizens of India;  Financial settlements, web based marketing, advisory and transactional services, database services and

products, supply chain management;  Online services such as telemarketing, telecommuting, telemedicine, education and information research;

and  All related data communication services, whether conducted by e-mail, mobile devices, social media, cloud

computing, document management, voice or data transmission or otherwise;

In the given question, Teresa Ltd. will be treated as a foreign company within the meaning of section 2(42) of the Companies Act, 2013 since it is doing online business through data interchange in India even though the company has no place of business established in India.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Focus on two essentials: place of business in India and business activity in India.
2. Highlight “electronic mode” and “data interchange” since these are keywords in the question.
3. Avoid writing all modes in detail unless required.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students incorrectly assume physical presence in India is compulsory.
2. Many ignore the electronic mode provision.

Question 7. Flora Fauna Limited was registered as a public company. There are 230 members in the company as noted below:

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 7

(a) Directors and their relatives 50 (b) Employees 15 (c) Ex-Employees (Shares were allotted when they were employees) 10 (d) 5 couples holding shares jointly in the name of husband and wife (5\*2) 10 (e) Others 145

The Board of Directors of the company propose to convert it into a private company. Also advise whether reduction in the number of members is necessary.

(5 marks|5 minutes) (Study Material) (Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 7. According to section 2(68) of the Companies Act, 2013, "Private company" means a company having a minimum paid-up share capital as may be prescribed, and which by its articles, except in case of One Person Company, limits the number of its members to two hundred. However, where two or more persons hold one or more shares in a company jointly, they shall, for the purposes of this clause, be treated as a single member. It is further provided that -

(A) Persons who are in the employment of the company; and (B) Persons who, having been formerly in the employment of the company, were members of the company while in that employment and have continued to be members after the employment ceased, (3 marks)

(i) Directors and their relatives 50 (ii) Directors and their relatives 5 (iii) Others 145

Total 200

Therefore, there is no need for reduction in the number of members since existing number of members are 200 which does not exceed maximum limit of 200. \*The provisions relating to conversion of public company to private company is covered in the Chapter 2 – Incorporation of Company and Matters incidental thereto. (2 marks)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. First explain the 200-member limit under Section 2(68).
2. Exclude employees, ex-employees, and joint holders while counting members.
3. Present the adjusted calculation in tabular form for easy marks.

Examiner Observations:

1. Wrong member counting is the most common error.
2. Students forget that joint holders are treated as a single member.

Question 8. Hastprat Ltd. is an unlisted public company, having five directors in its board which includes two independent directors. Sankul (P) Ltd., is subsidiary company of Hastprat Ltd., actively carrying on its business, having paid up capital of Rs 1.5 crore with 40 members and turnover of Rs 18 crore, respectively and the said company is not a start-up company. In the context of aforesaid case-scenario, please answer to the following question(s): - hether Sankul (P) Ltd. is mandatorily required to prepare cash flow statement for the financial year as a part of its financial statements? Provide your answer by analyzing Sankul (P) Ltd. into following category of companies: - (i) One Person Company, (ii) Small Company, (iii) Dormant Company and (iv) Private Company, respectively.

(8 marks|7 minutes) (RTP May ‘23) (Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 8. According to section 2(10) of the Companies Act, 2013, Financial statement in relation to a company, includes— (i) A balance sheet as at the end of the financial year;

(ii) A profit and loss account, or in the case of a company carrying on any activity not for profit, an income and expenditure account for the financial year;

(iii) cash flow statement for the financial year;

(iv) A statement of changes in equity, if applicable; and

(v) Any explanatory note annexed to, or forming part of, any document referred to in sub- clause (i) to sub-clause

(iv):Provided that the financial statement, with respect to one-person company, small company, dormant company and private company (if such private company is a start-up) may not include the cash flow statement.

For considering the applicability of preparation cash flow statement in case of Sankul (P) Ltd., it is required first to be analyzed that Sankul (P) Ltd. does not fall in any of the categories of companies mentioned under provision to section 2(10) of the Companies Act, 2013:

(i) One-person company – It is given that the company is having 40 members and also its name does not contain the words ‘OPC’, so it is not a one-person company.

(ii) Small company – A company which is a subsidiary company cannot be categorized as a small company as per provision to section 2(85) even though its paid up capital and turnover are within the prescribed limits and accordingly, as Sankul (P) Ltd. is a subsidiary company of Hastprat Ltd., it cannot be considered as small company also. (iii) Dormant company – It is given that the company is actively carrying on its business, so it cannot be also categorized as a dormant company based upon the facts given.

(iv) Private company (which is a start-up) – It is given that Sankul (P) Ltd. is not a start- up company and also, as per provision to section 2(71) of the Act, a company which is a subsidiary of a company, not being a private

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 9

company, shall be deemed to be public company for the purposes of this Act even where such subsidiary company continues to be a private company in its articles.

So, Sankul (P) Ltd. shall be deemed to be a public company as it is subsidiary of Hastprat Ltd., an unlisted public company and so it will not fall into this category of exemption as well. Thus, it can be concluded that Sankul (P) Ltd. is mandatorily required to prepare cash flow statement for the financial year as a part of its financial statements as it does not fall in any of the categories of companies mentioned under provision to section 2(10) of the Companies Act, 2013.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Identify all exempt categories one by one: OPC, small company, dormant company, startup private company.
2. Eliminate each category based on facts given in the question.
3. Finish with a clear conclusion regarding mandatory preparation of cash flow statement.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students directly conclude without analysing each category separately.
2. Many forget that a subsidiary of a public company is deemed to be a public company.

(iii) cash flow statement for the financial year;

(iv) A statement of changes in equity, if applicable; and

(v) Any explanatory note annexed to, or forming part of, any document referred to in sub- clause

Question 11. Mr. Kaushal is a Chartered and an MBA by profession, has been appointed as an Executive Director on the Board of XYZ Limited. His job profile includes advising the Board of Directors of the company on various compliance matters, strategies, business plans, and risk matters relating to the company. Keeping in view of above position whether Mr. Kaushal can be classified as the Promoter of XYZ Limited? Examine the same under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.

(4 marks|3 minutes) (MTP Jan 2025) (Medium |ICAI Fav |High chance for exam)

Answer 11. According to section 2(69) of the Companies Act, 2013, Promoter means a person: -

(a) Who has been named as such in a prospectus or is identified by the company in the annual return; or

(b) Who has control over the affairs of the company, directly or indirectly whether as a shareholder, director or otherwise; or

(c) In accordance with whose advice, directions or instructions the Board of Directors of the Company is accustomed to act.

Provided that nothing in sub-clause (c) shall apply to a person who is acting merely in a professional capacity. As the job profile of Mr. Kaushal is only limited to advise the Board of Directors on various compliance matters, strategies, business plans and risk matters relating to business of the company and that to only in a professional capacity, he will not be classified as a Promoter of XYZ Limited.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Mention all three conditions under Section 2(69).
2. Focus on the proviso relating to “professional capacity”.
3. Avoid writing all modes in detail unless required.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students forget the professional capacity exception.
2. Many incorrectly treat every adviser/director as a promoter.

Question 12 Referring the relevant provisions of the audited Financial Statement of Smart Solutions Private Limited as at 31st March, 2025 is as below: (1) Paid-up equity share capital Rs. 50,00,000 divided into 5,00,000 equity shares (carrying voting rights) of Rs. 10 each. There is no change in the paid-up share capital thereafter. (2) The turnover is Rs. 2,00,00,000 (Rs. 2 Crores).

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 12

It is further understood that Nice Software Limited, which is a public limited company, is holding 2,00,000 equity shares, fully paid-up, of Smart Solutions Private Limited. Smart Solutions Private Limited has filed its Financial Statement for the said year with the Registrar of Companies (ROC) excluding the Cash Flow Statement within the prescribed timeline during the financial year 2025-26. The ROC has issued a notice to Smart Solutions Private Limited as it has failed to file the cash flow statement along with the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account. You are to advise on the following points explaining the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013: (i) Whether Smart Solutions Private Limited shall be deemed to be a small company whose significant equity shares are held by a public company? (ii) Whether the company has defaulted in filing its financial statements?

(8 marks|7 minutes) (PYP July ’21,) (MTP Oct ’23) (Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 12 (i) Status of Smart Solutions Private Limited Legal Provision (Small Company): According to Section 2(85) of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 2(1)(t) of the Companies (Specification of Definition Details) Rules, 2014 [amended w.e.f. 01-12-2025], a "Small Company" means a company, other than a public company, having:

1. Paid-up share capital not exceeding Rs. 10 crores; AND
2. Turnover as per profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year not exceeding Rs. 100 crore.

Exceptions: The status of a small company is not applicable to:  A holding company or a subsidiary company;  A company registered under Section 8; or  A company or body corporate governed by any special Act.

Legal Provision (Subsidiary Company): According to Section 2(87), a subsidiary company is one in which the holding company exercises or controls more than one-half (50%) of the total voting power.

Analysis: 1. Subsidiary Check: Nice Software Limited (Public Company) holds 2,00,000 equity shares out of 5,00,000 total equity shares of Smart Solutions Private Limited.

o Holding % = (2,00,000 / 5,00,000) x 100 = 40% o Since the holding is less than 50%, Smart Solutions Pvt Ltd is NOT a subsidiary of Nice Software Ltd.

Consequently, it is not deemed to be a public company and remains eligible for Small Company status.

2. Financial Limits Check:

o Paid-up Capital: Rs. 50 Lakhs (0.50 Cr) → This is within the limit of Rs. 10 Cr. o Turnover: Rs. 2 Crores →This is within the limit of Rs. 100 Cr.

Conclusion: Smart Solutions Private Limited satisfies the revised criteria for a Small Company and is not disqualified by the subsidiary relationship. Therefore, it is a Small Company.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 13

(ii) Validity of ROC Notice (Filing of Cash Flow Statement)

Legal Provision: According to Section 2(40) of the Companies Act, 2013, the term "Financial Statement" typically includes a Cash Flow Statement. However, the proviso to Section 2(40) explicitly states that the financial statement with respect to a Small Company, One Person Company (OPC), and Dormant Company, may not include the cash flow statement.

Analysis & Conclusion: Since Smart Solutions Private Limited is a Small Company (as established in part i), it is exempted from filing a Cash Flow Statement as part of its financial statements.

Therefore, Smart Solutions Private Limited has not defaulted in filing its financial statements. The notice issued by the ROC is not sustainable in law. (3 marks)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Solve in two parts separately: small company status and filing default.
2. Focus on the proviso relating to “professional capacity”.
3. Use voting power percentage calculation properly.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students assume shareholding by a public company automatically makes it a subsidiary.
2. Many forget thdat exemption from cash flow statement applies to small companies.

Question 13. The paid-up share capital of Saras Private Limited is Rs. 1 crore, consisting of 8 lacs Equity Shares of Rs. 10 each, fully paid-up and 2 lacs Cumulative Preference Shares of Rs. 10 each, fully paid-up. Jeevan (JVN) Private Limited and Sudhir Private Limited are holding 3 lacs Equity Shares and 50,000 Equity Shares respectively in Saras Private Limited. Jeevan Private Limited and Sudhir Private Limited are the subsidiaries of Piyush Private Limited. With reference to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 examine whether Saras Private Limited is a subsidiary of Piyush Private Limited? Would your answer be different if Piyush Private Limited has 8 out of 9 Directors on the Board of Saras Private Limited?

(RTP MAY 18, MAY 19)

Answer 13. Relevant Provisions: As per section 2(87) of the Companies Act, 2013, "subsidiary company" or "subsidiary", in relation to any other company (that is to say the holding company), means a company in which the holding company— (i) controls the composition of the Board of Directors; or (ii) exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power either at its own or together with one or more of its subsidiary companies.

Explanation: (a) A company shall be deemed to be a subsidiary company of the holding company even if the control referred to in sub-clause (i) or sub-clause (ii) is of another subsidiary company of the holding company. (b) The composition of a company’s Board of Directors shall be deemed to be controlled by another company if that

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 14

other company, by exercise of some power exercisable by it at its discretion, can appoint or remove all or a majority of the directors. (Note: The earlier reference to "total share capital" in the definition was amended by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017, and substituted with "total voting power" to align with the actual voting rights, excluding non-voting shares like most preference shares.)

Conclusion: In the present case, the total equity shares (which carry voting rights under section 47 of the Act) are 8,00,000. Jeevan Pvt. Ltd. holds 3,00,000 equity shares, and Sudhir Pvt. Ltd. holds 50,000 equity shares. Since both are subsidiaries of Piyush Pvt. Ltd., their combined holding is 3,50,000 equity shares. This amounts to 3,50,000 / 8,00,000 = 43.75% of the total voting power (less than one-half or 50%). The cumulative preference shares do not carry voting rights in general meetings (except in specific circumstances as per section 47(2), which are not applicable here).

Therefore, Piyush Private Limited does not exercise or control more than one-half of the total voting power in Saras Private Limited, nor is there any indication that it controls the composition of the Board. Hence, Saras Private Limited is not a subsidiary of Piyush Private Limited.

However, if Piyush Private Limited has 8 out of 9 Directors on the Board of Saras Private Limited, it clearly controls the composition of the Board of Directors (as it can appoint/remove the majority of directors). In such a scenario, Piyush Private Limited will be treated as the holding company of Saras Private Limited, irrespective of the shareholding/voting power percentage. Thus, the answer would be different in the second situation — Saras Private Limited would be a subsidiary of Piyush Private Limited

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Calculate voting power only from equity shares carrying voting rights.
2. Ignore preference shares unless voting rights are specifically applicable
3. In the second part, directly apply Board control provision.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students wrongly include preference shares in voting power calculation.
2. Many forget indirect control through subsidiary companies.

Question 14. The statutory auditors of a company were required to issue a certificate on the net worth of the company as on 30th September 2024 computed as per Section 2(57) of the Companies Act, 2013. The company had fair valued its property, plant and equipment in the current year which was mistakenly taken into retained earnings of the company. Advise whether this fair valuation would be covered in the net worth of the company.

(8 MARKS| 12 Minutes) (RTP NOV, 18 MAY 23)

Answer 14. Relevant Provisions: As per Section 2(57) of the Companies Act, 2013 (as amended), “net worth” means the aggregate value of the paid-up share capital and all reserves created out of the profits, securities premium account and debit or credit balance of profit and loss account, after deducting the aggregate value of the accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off, as per the audited

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 15

balance sheet, but does not include reserves created out of revaluation of assets, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation.

Analysis: The Company has fair valued its property, plant and equipment (PPE) in the current year. Under applicable accounting standards (Ind AS 16 or AS 10, depending on whether the company follows Ind AS or Indian Accounting Standards), fair valuation/revaluation of PPE typically results in a revaluation surplus (gain) which is recognized in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) and accumulated in equity as a revaluation reserve (not routed through profit or loss). However, in this case, the fair valuation surplus has been mistakenly taken directly into retained earnings instead of the proper revaluation reserve/OCI.

The exclusion in Section 2(57) is specifically for “reserves created out of revaluation of assets”. The substance of the adjustment is a revaluation gain (unrealized/notional gain arising from revaluation of assets), irrespective of the accounting head where it is parked due to the mistake. The nature of the credit remains a revaluation-related reserve/gain, which is explicitly excluded from the computation of net worth to prevent inclusion of unrealized gains.

Even if incorrectly classified under retained earnings (which otherwise forms part of net worth via the debit/credit balance of profit and loss account), the fair valuation surplus cannot be treated as a reserve “created out of profits” for the purpose of net worth. The statutory definition prioritizes substance over form in this context, and such notional/unrealized gains from revaluation are not to be included.

Conclusion: The fair valuation surplus on PPE, even though mistakenly credited to retained earnings, would not be covered/included in the net worth of the company as per Section 2(57). It should be excluded while computing net worth, as it falls under the category of reserves/amounts created out of revaluation of assets. The statutory auditors should:

 Point out the incorrect accounting treatment (misclassification of revaluation surplus).  Advise rectification in the books of account to reflect it as a revaluation reserve (in equity/OCI).  Compute and certify the net worth by excluding this amount, ensuring compliance with the statutory

definition.

This ensures the net worth reflects only realized profits and excludes unrealized revaluation gains, in line with the legislative intent of the Companies Act, 2013.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. First define net worth under Section 2(57).
2. Emphasize exclusion of revaluation reserves from net worth.
3. Apply “substance over form” even if the amount is wrongly shown in retained earnings.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students incorrectly include fair valuation gains in net worth.
2. Many ignore the specific statutory exclusion for revaluation reserves.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 16

Question 15. SKP Limited (Registered in India), a wholly owned subsidiary company of Herry Limited, decided to follow a different financial year for consolidation of its accounts outside India. State the procedure to be followed in this regard.

(7 MARKS | MINUTES 10) (RTP NOV 21)

Answer 15. Relevant Provisions: As per Section 2(41) of the Companies Act, 2013 (as amended), “financial year”, in relation to any company or body corporate, means the period ending on the 31st day of March every year, and where it has been incorporated on or after the 1st day of January of a year, the period ending on the 31st day of March of the following year, in respect whereof financial statement of the company or body corporate is made up.

Provided that where a company or body corporate, which is a holding company or a subsidiary or associate company of a company incorporated outside India and is required to follow a different financial year for consolidation of its accounts outside India, the Central Government may, on an application made by that company or body corporate in such form and manner as may be prescribed, allow any period as its financial year, whether or not that period is a year.

(Note: The powers of the Central Government under the first proviso to Section 2(41) have been delegated to the Regional Director concerned vide MCA Notification dated 18.12.2018. The application is to be filed in e-Form RD- 1 as per Rule 40 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014.)

Procedure to be followed: SKP Limited (being an Indian subsidiary of Herry Limited, assumed to be a foreign company) is eligible to apply for a different financial year to facilitate consolidation of accounts with its holding company outside India. The step-by-step procedure is as follows:

Step Particulars Detailed Action No. 1 Convene Pass a Board Resolution approving the proposal to alter/change the financial year of

Board the company. The resolution should mention the reason for change (i.e., consolidation Meeting of accounts with the foreign holding company), specify the proposed financial year

period, and authorize a Director/Company Secretary to file the application and complete related formalities. 2 Prepare Prepare and collect the necessary supporting documents, including:

Supporting  Justification letter explaining the requirement for alignment with the holding Documents company’s financial year.

 Copy of holding company’s financial year policy/Board Resolution/confirmation

from Herry Limited.  Certified True Copy (CTC) of the Board Resolution.  Latest audited financial statements, if applicable.  Memorandum & Articles of Association (if amendment in AoA is required).  Any additional documents as may be required by the Regional Director, such as

impact on taxation/FEMA compliances.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 17

3 File File e-Form RD-1 on the MCA Portal along with the prescribed fee before the concerned

Application Regional Director (RD) having jurisdiction over the registered office of SKP Limited. with Regional Attach all supporting documents with the application. Director 4 Obtain The Regional Director, after examining the application and being satisfied with the

Approval justification provided, may pass an order approving the change in the financial year. from RD The approval is generally granted within a reasonable period (normally around 30 days,

subject to processing time). 5 Give Effect to After receipt of the RD approval order: • File the RD Order with the Registrar of

Approval Companies (RoC), if required. • Amend the Articles of Association, if necessary, by

passing a Special Resolution and filing e-Form MGT-14. • Align future financial statements, Annual General Meetings (AGMs), statutory filings, and other compliances according to the revised financial year.

Note: This relaxation is available only to holding/subsidiary/associate companies of foreign entities for consolidation purposes. Normal Indian companies cannot change from the April–March cycle without exceptional approval.

Conclusion: SKP Limited should apply to the Central Government (through the concerned Regional Director) in e- Form RD-1 along with supporting documents justifying the need for a different financial year for consolidation with Herry Limited outside India. Upon approval, it can adopt the aligned financial year.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Section 2(41) definition of financial year.
2. Mention that approval is required from Regional Director through e-Form RD-1
3. Present procedure in step-wise format for better readability.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students wrongly state that Board approval alone is sufficient.
2. Many fail to mention RD approval and filing procedure.

Question 16 Johnson Limited goes for public issue of its shares. The issue was oversubscribed. A default was committed with respect to allotment of shares by the officers of the company. There were no Managing Director, Whole time Director or any other officer designated by the Board with the responsibility of complying with the provisions of the Act. State who are the persons considered as "officers in default" in this case?

(7 MARKS|9 MINUTES JULY 21)

Answer 16 Relevant Provisions: As per Section 2(60) of the Companies Act, 2013 (defining "officer who is in default"), for the purpose of any provision in this Act which enacts that an officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to any penalty or punishment by way of imprisonment, fine or otherwise, "officer who is in default" means any of the following officers of a company, namely: —

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 18

(i) whole-time director;

(ii) Key managerial personnel;

(iii) where there is no key managerial personnel, such director or directors as specified by the Board in this behalf and who has or have given his or their consent in writing to the Board to such specification, or all the directors, if no director is so specified;

(iv) any person who, under the immediate authority of the Board or any key managerial personnel, is charged with any responsibility including maintenance, filing or distribution of accounts or records, authorises, actively participates in, knowingly permits, or knowingly fails to take active steps to prevent, any default;

(v) Any person in accordance with whose advice, directions or instructions the Board of Directors of the company is accustomed to act, other than a person who gives advice to the Board in a professional capacity. (Note: The definition has remained consistent since enactment, with no major amendments altering the hierarchy for cases without KMP.)

Analysis: The default relates to allotment of shares in a public issue (governed primarily by Section 39 read with SEBI ICDR Regulations, but liability for officers in default under the Companies Act follows Section 2(60)). In the given case:

 There is no Managing Director (MD) or Whole-time Director (WTD), who are typically part of whole-time

directors or KMP.  There is no other officer designated by the Board with the responsibility of complying with the provisions of

the Act (i.e., no director(s) specified by the Board under clause (iii) who has/have given written consent to be charged with such responsibility).  Consequently, the fall back provision under clause (iii) applies: all the directors of the company shall be

deemed to be "officers in default".

This is a deeming fiction to ensure accountability when no specific executive/KMP or designated director is in place. (Note: Independent/non-executive directors may have limited liability under Section 149(12) in certain cases, but where the default is attributable and no designation exists, the general provision holds; however, for this question, the statutory default is all directors.)

Conclusion: In the given case, as Johnson Limited committed a default in allotment of shares and there was no Managing Director, Whole-time Director, Key Managerial Personnel, or any director specifically designated by the Board (with written consent) to be responsible for compliance with the provisions of the Act, all the directors of the company shall be considered as "officers in default" under Section 2(60) (iii) of the Companies Act, 2013.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quote Section 2(60) and explain hierarchy of responsibility.
2. Identify absence of MD/WTD/KMP and directly conclude that all directors become officers in default.
3. Keep explanation logical and sequential.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 19

Examiner Observations:

1. Students write only definitions without applying facts.
2. Many fail to identify the fallback provision applicable to all directors.

Question 17 H Ltd. is the holding company of S Pvt. Ltd. As per the last profit and loss account for the year ending 31st March 2024, S Pvt. Ltd. has a turnover of Rs. 1.80 crores and paid-up share capital of Rs. 80 lakhs. The company wants to avail the status of a "small company." Advice.

(MARKS 3 | MINUTES 3) (MAY 23)

Answer 17 Relevant Provisions: As per the proviso to Section 2(85) of the Companies Act, 2013, the status of a small company shall not apply to a holding company or a subsidiary company.

Conclusion: In the light of the above facts, although S Pvt. Ltd. meets the financial thresholds of turnover (not exceeding 40Cr) and capital (not exceeding 4Cr), it cannot be categorized as a small company because it is a subsidiary of H Ltd.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Directly mention that subsidiary companies cannot be small companies.
2. No need for lengthy calculation once subsidiary status is established.
3. Give a short and precise conclusion.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students unnecessarily discuss turnover and capital limits despite clear disqualification.
2. Many forget the exception relating to subsidiary companies.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 20

PART B

### Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Question 1. Green Ltd. is incorporated on 3rd January, 2022. As per the Companies Act, 2013, what will be the financial year for the company? (a) 31st March, 2022 (b) 31st December, 2022 (c) 31st March, 2023 (d) 30th September, 2023

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) 31st March, 2023 Reason: As per the Companies Act, 2013, the financial year for a company is from 1st April to 31st March of the following year. Since Green Ltd. was incorporated on 3rd January, 2022, its first financial year will start from the date of incorporation and end on 31st March, 2023, which is the end of the financial year for companies in India. Therefore, the first financial year will be from 3rd January, 2022 to 31st March, 2023

Question 2. Abhilasha and Amrita have incorporated a ‘not for profit’ private limited company which is registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013. One of their friends has informed them that their company can be categorized as a ‘small company’ because as per the last profit and loss account for the year ending 31st March, 2022, its turnover was less than Rs 100 crore and its paid up share capital was less than Rs 10 crore. Advice.

(a) Section 8 company, which meets the criteria of ‘turnover’ and ‘paid-up share capital’ in the last financial year, can avail the status of ‘small company’ only if it acquires at least 5% stake in another ‘small company’ within the immediately following financial year. (b) If the acquisition of minimum 5% stake in another ‘small company’ materializes in the second financial year (and not in the immediately following financial year) after meeting the criteria of ‘turnover’ and ‘paid-up share capital’ then with the written permission of concerned ROC, it can acquire the status of ‘small company’. (c) The status of ‘small company’ cannot be bestowed upon a ‘not for profit’ company which is registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013. (d) A section 8 company, if incorporated as a private limited company (and not as public limited company) can avail the status of ‘small company’ with the permission of concerned ROC, after it meets the criteria of ‘turnover’ and ‘paid-up share capital’.

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) The status of ‘small company’ cannot be bestowed upon a ‘not for profit’ company which is registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013. Reason: As per the Companies Act, 2013, a Section 8 company is a "not for profit" company and is formed with the primary objective of promoting commerce, art, science, religion, charity, etc. A Section 8 company, by ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 21

definition, cannot be a "small company" under the provisions of the Act, even if it meets the financial criteria of turnover (below Rs 100 crore) and paid-up share capital (below Rs 10 crore). The concept of a "small company" is applicable to private limited companies and One Person Companies (OPCs), but it does not apply to Section 8 companies (not-for-profit companies). Therefore, even though Abhilasha and Amrita's company may meet the financial criteria, it cannot be categorized as a small company due to its nature as a Section 8 company.

Question 3. A Ltd. is holding 61% shares in B Ltd. and B Ltd. holds 51% in C Ltd. State which is the correct statement here: (a) C Ltd. is the holding company to A Ltd. (b) C Ltd. is the holding company to B Ltd. (c) B Ltd. is the Subsidiary to C Ltd. (d) Both B Ltd. and C Ltd. are subsidiary to A Ltd.

(MTP Sep’22)

Answer: (d) Both B Ltd. and C Ltd. are subsidiary to A Ltd. Reason: A Ltd. holds 61% of shares in B Ltd.: This means A Ltd. has a controlling interest in B Ltd., making B Ltd. a subsidiary of A Ltd. according to the definition of a subsidiary company under the Companies Act, 2013 (where a company holds more than 50% of the shares in another company). B Ltd. holds 51% of shares in C Ltd.: This means B Ltd. has a controlling interest in C Ltd., making C Ltd. a subsidiary of B Ltd. However, since A Ltd. holds 61% of shares in B Ltd., and B Ltd. holds 51% of shares in C Ltd., A Ltd. is the ultimate holding company of C Ltd. through its control over B Ltd. Therefore, both B Ltd. and C Ltd. are subsidiaries of A Ltd., as A Ltd. has control over both companies.

Question 4. A Ltd. is the holding company of B Ltd. Another company C Ltd. is the subsidiary company of B Ltd. Is there any relationship between A Ltd. and C Ltd.? (a) There is no relationship between A Ltd. and C Ltd. (b) C Ltd. is deemed to be the subsidiary of A Ltd. (c) A Ltd. shall be deemed to be the holding company of C Ltd. provided A Ltd. acquires at least 10% stake in C Ltd. (d) C Ltd. shall be deemed to be the subsidiary of A Ltd. if the latter company acquires minimum 10% stake in the former company within six months after C Ltd. becomes subsidiary of B Ltd.

(RTP May ’19)

Answer: (b) C Ltd. is deemed to be the subsidiary of A Ltd. Reason: As per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, if a company (A Ltd.) is the holding company of another company (B Ltd.), and B Ltd. is the holding company of a third company (C Ltd.), then C Ltd. is deemed to be a subsidiary of A Ltd., even if A Ltd. does not directly hold any shares in C Ltd. This is based on the concept of indirect control. In this case, A Ltd. holds control over B Ltd., and B Ltd. in turn holds control over C Ltd. Therefore, A Ltd. is considered the ultimate holding company of C Ltd. through its control over B Ltd., making C Ltd. a subsidiary of A Ltd. Thus, there is a deemed relationship between A Ltd. and C Ltd., even though A Ltd. doesn't directly own shares in C Ltd.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 22

Question 5. “Associate company”, in relation to another company, means a company in which that other company has a significant influence, but which is not a subsidiary company of the company having such influence and includes a joint venture company. Here, the words ‘significant influence’ me Answer: (a) Control of at least 10% of total voting power (b) Control of at least 15% of total voting power (c) Control of at least 20% of total voting power (d) Control of at least 25% of total voting power

(Study Material) (MTP March ‘23)

Answer: (c) Control of at least 20% of total voting power Reason: As per the Companies Act, 2013, the term "significant influence" refers to the ability to participate in the financial and operating decisions of a company, but not to control those decisions. The Companies Act defines "significant influence" as the power to participate in the decisions of the company, typically evidenced by holding at least 20% of the voting power in that company. Therefore, significant influence means holding at least 20% of the total voting power in another company. This threshold is key to determining whether a company can be considered an associate company under the law. Hence, the correct answer is (c) Control of at least 20% of total voting power.

Question 6. Kaveri Goods Carriers Private Limited (KGCPL) issued 9% Non-convertible Debentures worth Rs 10 lakhs and thereafter, the directors contemplated to get them listed. After due formalities, these privately placed non- convertible debentures of Rs 10 lakhs were listed. Which of the following options is applicable in the given situation? (a) KGCPL shall be considered as a listed company. (b) KGCPL shall not be considered as a listed company. (c) KGCPL shall be considered as a listed company only when minimum amount of listed privately placed non- convertible debentures is Rs 15 lakhs. (d) KGCPL shall be considered as a listed company only when minimum amount of listed privately placed non- convertible debentures is minimum Rs 20 lakhs.

(Practice question)

Answer: (b) KGCPL shall not be considered as a listed company. Reason: As per the Companies Act, 2013 read with Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, certain private companies that have listed only their privately placed non-convertible debentures are excluded from the definition of a listed company. Therefore, even after listing privately placed non-convertible debentures of ₹10 lakhs, KGCPL will not be treated as a listed company.

Question 7. Such shares which are issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for a consideration other than cash for working extraordinary hard and achieving desired output is honoured with: (a) Equity Shares (b) Preference Shares (c) Sweat Equity Shares (d) Redeemable preference shares

(RTP Nov 21)

Answer: (c) Sweat Equity Shares ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 23

Reason: Sweat equity shares are issued by a company to its directors or employees as a reward for their hard work and efforts in contributing to the success of the company. These shares are typically issued at a discount or for a consideration other than cash, like providing valuable services or achieving desired results, rather than in exchange for monetary payment. The key point is that sweat equity shares recognize the contribution of an individual in the form of effort, skills, or expertise, rather than capital investment. This type of equity is generally offered to directors, employees, or even promoters, to honor their extraordinary contribution to the company. Therefore, the correct answer is (c) Sweat Equity Shares.

Question 8. A Public company may be formed by: (a) Only two persons (b) Not more than three persons (c) Not more than Seven Persons (d) Seven or more Persons

(PYP Nov’22)

Answer: (d) Seven or more Persons Reason: As per the Companies Act, 2013, a Public company must have a minimum of seven members to be formed. This is in contrast to a private company, which can be formed with a minimum of two members. For a public company:  The minimum number of members required is seven.  There is no maximum limit for the number of members in a public company. Hence, a public company can be formed by seven or more persons, which makes option (d) the correct answer

Question 9. The Best Dry Fruits Ltd was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. Whether the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 shall apply on it? a) No, the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 shall not apply on it. b) Yes, the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 shall apply on it. c) The Companies Act, 1913 was enacted by the British Government, hence only an Act made by British Government shall apply on such company. d) Since, this company was incorporated by the British Government, hence the Companies Act of UK Govt shall apply.

Answer: (b) Yes, the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 shall apply on it. Reason: The Companies Act, 2013 applies to all existing companies incorporated under previous company laws, including the Companies Act, 1913. Such companies continue to exist and are governed by the current Companies Act, 2013.

Question 10. P&Q were the only members of a company who died in a road accident. In this case, the company comes to an end on the death of P&Q. (a) True (b) False

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 24

(c) Partly True (d) Partly False

(MTP NOV 24)

Answer: (b) False Reason: A company is an artificial legal person having perpetual succession. The death or insolvency of members does not affect the existence of the company. Therefore, even if all members die, the company does not automatically come to an end.

Question 11. A company being a legal person is also a citizen under the Constitution of India. (a) True (b) False (c) Only company incorporated under Companies Act, 2013 is a citizen (d) Company having only individual members is a citizen.

(RTP/MTP JAN 25)

Answer: (b) False Reason: A company is an artificial legal person but not a citizen under the Constitution of India. Citizenship is available only to natural persons (human beings), not to companies.

Question 12. Word ‘Corporation’ is ‘Company’. (a)Wider than (b) Narrower than (c) Synonymous to (d) None of the above

Answer: (a) Wider than Reason: The term “Corporation” has a wider meaning than “Company” because it includes various incorporated bodies such as statutory corporations, corporations sole, municipal corporations, etc., whereas a company is only one type of corporation.

Question 23. Forest a Limited was registered as a public company. There are 240 members in the Company as noted below –

Question 24. In case of a company limited by guarantee, the liability of the members can be enforced\_\_\_\_ (a) At any time when the company so decides (b) Only at the time of winding-up of the company (c) Only by an order of NCLT (d) Only by order of Registrar of companies

Answer: b) Only at the time of winding-up of the company Reason: In a company limited by guarantee, members undertake to contribute a specified amount only when the company is wound up. Therefore, their liability can be enforced only during winding-up and not during the normal course of business.

Question 41. ‘Abhilasha and Amrita have incorporated a not for profit’ private limited company which is registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013. maximum 2 layers below the holding company). Explanation:  Layer 1 = Direct subsidiary of the holding company  Layer 2 = Subsidiary of the Layer 1 company  Layer 3 and beyond → Not permitted (prohibited)

Exemptions (companies to which this restriction does not apply):  Banking company  Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) registered with RBI  Insurance company  Government company For all other companies (public, private, listed, unlisted), the maximum permitted layers of subsidiaries is 2.

Question 45. The subscribers to the Memorandum of Association (a) May become members only if there is a specific provision to that effect in the Company’s Articles of Association. (b) Become a member as soon as company is registered. (c) Are members irrespective of any formality as to registration etc? (d) In a depository system, the following is considered to be a member of the company.

(MTP/RTP DEC 23) Answer: (b) become a member as soon as company is registered. Reason: As per Section 2(55) read with Section 9 of the Companies Act, 2013: The subscribers to the Memorandum of Association (MoA) are deemed to be the members of the company from the date of its incorporation/registration.

Key legal points:  The subscribers to the MoA automatically become the first members of the company.  No further formality (like allotment of shares, entry in register of members, or any provision in Articles) is

required.  Upon registration of the company, the subscribers are conclusively deemed to be members.  This is a statutory effect of registration under Section 9: “From the date of incorporation … the subscribers to

the memorandum … shall be deemed to have agreed to become members of the company.”

Chapter 2 Incorporation of Company and matters incidental thereto

PART A

Question 1. The object clause of the Memorandum of Vivek Industries Limited., empowers it to carry on real- estate business and any other business that is allied to it. Due to a downward trend in real-estate business, the management of the company has decided to take up the business of Food processing activity. The company wants to alter its Memorandum, so as to include the Food Processing Business in its objects clause. Examine whether the company can make such change as per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material)(Easy|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 1. Alteration of Objects Clause of Memorandum The Companies Act, 2013 has made alteration of the memorandum simpler and more flexible. Under section13 (1) of the Act, a company may, by a special resolution after complying with the procedure specified in this section, alter the provisions of its Memorandum.

In the case of alteration to the objects clause, section 13(6) requires the filing of the Special Resolution by the company with the Registrar. Section 13 (9) states that the Registrar shall register any alteration to the Memorandum with respect to the objects of the company and certify the registration within a period of thirty days from the date of filing of the special resolution by the company. Section 13 (10) further stipulates that no alteration in the Memorandum shall take effect unless it has been registered with the Registrar as above. Hence, the Companies Act, 2013 permits any alteration to the objects clause with ease. Vivek Industries Limited can make the required changes in the object clause of its Memorandum of Association.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Section 13 and directly mention that alteration of object clause requires Special Resolution and

ROC filing.

2. Write provisions in sequence: resolution → filing → registration by ROC → effectiveness. Avoid lengthy

introduction and conclude clearly that alteration is valid.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often forget that alteration becomes effective only after registration by ROC.
2. Many also miss mentioning Section 13(10), due to which marks are deducted.

Question 2. Mr. Dinesh incorporated a new Private Limited Company under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and desires to commence the business immediately. Please advice Mr. Dinesh about the procedure for commencement of business as laid under the provisions of the Section 10A of the Companies Act, 2013.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(MTP April 21)(Easy|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 37

Answer 2. As per Section 10A of the Companies Act, 2013, a company incorporated after the commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Second Ordinance, 2019 and having a share capital shall not commence any business or exercise any borrowing powers unless: (i) A declaration is filed by a director within a period of 180 days of the date of incorporation of the company in such form and verified in such manner as may be prescribed, with the Registrar that every subscriber to the memorandum has paid the value of the shares agreed to be taken by him on the date of making of such declaration; and (ii) The company has filed with the Registrar a verification of it registered office as provided in subsection (2) of section 12. Mr. Dinesh has to comply with the above requirements and procedure for commencing the business of the company.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Mention Section 10A first and write only the two mandatory conditions in point form.
2. Highlight “180 days declaration” and “verification of registered office” as keywords. Use short statutory

language for quick presentation.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students generally write unnecessary incorporation procedure instead of commencement requirements.

Missing the 180-day limit is a common mistake.

Question 3. Nadeem incorporated a "One Person Company" making his sister Nisha as the nominee. Nisha is leaving India permanently due to her marriage abroad. Due to this fact, she is withdrawing her consent of nomination in the said One Person Company. Taking into considerations the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 answer the questions given below. (A) If Nisha is leaving India permanently, is it mandatory for her to withdraw her nomination in the said One Person Company? (B) If Nisha maintained the status of Resident of India after her marriage, then can she continue her nomination in the said One Person Company?

Answer 3.
