According to section 20(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, a document may be served on Registrar or any member by sending it to him by post or by registered post or by speed post or by courier or by delivering at his office or address, or by such electronic or other mode as may be prescribed. Provided that a member may request for delivery of any document through a particular mode, for which he shall pay such fees as may be determined by the company in its annual general meeting.

Thus, if a member wants the notice to be served on him only by registered post at his residential address at Kanpur for which he has deposited sufficient money, the notice must be served accordingly, otherwise service will not be deemed to have been effected. Accordingly, the questions as asked may be answered as under: (i) The contention of Vijay shall be tenable, for the reason that the notice was not properly served. (ii) In the given circumstances, the company is bound to serve a valid notice to Vijay by registered post at his residential address at Kanpur and not outside India.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. State minimum members first, then separately explain consequences under Section 3A.
2. Use timeline-based explanation for six-month rule.

Examiner Observations:

1. State minimum members first, then separately explain consequences under Section 3A. Use timeline-based

explanation for six-month rule.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 67

Question 40. What is the minimum number of persons required to form a Private company and a Public company. Explain the consequences when the number of members falls below the minimum prescribed limit.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 40. According to section 3 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company may be formed for any lawful purpose by- (a) 7 or more persons, where the company to be formed is to be a public company; (b) 2 or more persons, where the company to be formed is to be a private company; According to section 3A,

- If at any time the number of members of a company is reduced, in the case of a public company, below 7, in

the case of a private company, below 2, and company carries on business for more than six months while number of members is so reduced, then

- every person who is a member of the company during the time that it so carries on business after those six

months and is cognizant (aware) of the fact that it is carrying on business with less than seven members or two members, as the case may be,

- shall be severally liable for the payment of the whole debts of the company contracted during that time (after

six months) and may be severally sued therefore.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. State minimum members first, then separately explain consequences under Section 3A.
2. Use timeline-based explanation for six-month rule.

Examiner Observations: Students often forget that liability arises only after business continues beyond six months with reduced members.

Question 41. Red Limited was incorporated on 1st April, 2014 is facing severe effects of depression of the economy. Owing to its bad financial status most of the members have started withdrawing their holding from the company. The company had 250 members on 10th January, 2019. By 15th January, 2019, 244 members had withdrawn their holding. No new member has invested in the company after 15th February till 15th August. Now, Mr. A, an existing member has approached you to advise him regarding his liabilities in such a situation.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(PYQ May 2018) (Medium | ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 41. According to section 3A of Companies Act, 2013, If at any time number of members of a company is reduced, in case of a public company, below 7, in case of a private company, below 2, and company carries on business for more than 6 months while number of members is so reduced, every person who is a member of company during the time that it so carries on business after those 6 months and is cognizant of the fact that it is carrying on business with less than 7 members or 2 members, as the case may be, shall be severally liable for payment of the whole debts of company contracted during that time, and may be severally sued therefor. Hence, in the given situation, the number of members in the said public company have fallen below 7 [250-244=6] and these members have continued beyond the specified limit of 6 months, the reduced members of the company during the period of 1 month shall be severally liable for the payment of the whole debts of the company

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 68

contracted during that time, and may be severally sued therefor.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Calculate number of members and duration carefully before applying Section 3A.
2. Mention “several liability” only for debts contracted after six months.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students commonly impose liability from the date membership reduced instead of after expiry of six months.

Question 42. Manglu and friends got registered a company in the name of Taxmann advisory private limited. Taxmann is a registered trademark. After 5 years when the owner of trademark came to know about the same, it filed an application with relevant authority. Can the company be compelled to change its name by the owner of trademark? Can the owner of registered trademark request the company and then company changes its name at its discretion?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(RTP May 2020 & MTP 2021) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 42. According to section 16 of the Companies Act, 2013 if a company is registered by a name which-

- in the opinion of the Central Government, is identical with the name by which a company had been previously registered, it may direct the company to change its name... within 3 months.
- is identical with a registered trade mark and owner of that trade mark apply to the Central Government within three years of incorporation... it may direct the company to change its name... within 3 months. In the given case, owner of registered trade-mark is filing objection after 5 years of registration of company with a wrong name. While it should have filed the same within 3 years. Therefore, the company cannot be compelled to change its name. As per section 13, company can anytime change its name by passing a special resolution and taking approval of Central Government. Therefore, if owner of registered trademark request the company for change of its name and the company accepts the same then it can change its name voluntarily by following the provisions of section 13.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Focus on limitation period of 3 years under Section 16.
2. Then separately explain voluntary name change under Section 13.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often miss the statutory time limit for trademark owner’s application.

Question 43. UINA Infra Projects Private Limited was incorporated on 1st June, 2022. Mr. X had already registered the trade name of "UINA Infra projects" on 1st April, 2018 under the Trade Marks Act, 1999. Mr. X was suffering from a pro-longed disease since 1st April, 2021. When Mr. X recovered from illness on 20th May, 2024 and joined his own office on 5th July, 2024, he came to know from his staff members that a company has been incorporated with the name UINA Infra Projects Private Limited. He lodged a complaint with the Regional Director on 10th July, 2024 requesting him to order the company to change its name. The Regional Director ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 69

examined the application of Mr. X and on 11th July, 2024, issued a direction to UINA Infra Projects Private Limited to change its name. Mr. D, a director of UINA Infra Projects Private Limited contended that the above direction of the Regional Director was bad in law and therefore not proper on the following grounds: A. That the name of the company is not too identical with or too nearly resembles to the name of any other company; and B. That the stipulated time period of two years of making any complaint with respect to the name in the above ground was already over on 31st May, 2024. Referring to the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, decide, whether the contention of Mr. D is tenable. Also advise UINA Infra Projects Private Limited the time period within which the company would be required to change its name in case the direction of the Regional Director was valid.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(RTP Nov 2022) (Medium| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 43. According to section 16 of the Companies Act, 2013... if a company... is registered by a name which... is of opinion... is identical with or too nearly resembles to the name by which a company in existence... or on an application by a proprietor of already registered trade mark under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, it may direct the company to change its name. The company shall change its name or new name... within a period of three months from the issue of such direction, after adopting an ordinary resolution for the purpose. Application by a proprietor of registered trade mark shall be made within three years of incorporation or registration or change of name of the company.

In terms of the above stated provisions and facts of the question: Part (i) - First Ground of Objection: In the first instance, the contention of Mr. D... is not tenable due to the fact that the restriction is not only with respect to the name of an existing company, but also as a result of an application filed before the appropriate authority by the proprietor of a registered trademark... Hence, the contention of Mr. D is not tenable. Part (ii) - Second Ground of Objection: In the second instance also, the contention of Mr. D is not tenable. The application should be made by the proprietor of a registered trademark within three years of incorporation... and not within two years.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Answer each objection separately and mention “three years” clearly.
2. End with the time limit of three months for changing the name.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students usually confuse “2 years” with “3 years” limitation period under Section 16.

Question 44. Anushka security equipments limited is a manufacturer of CCTV cameras. It has raised ₹ 100 crore through public issue of its equity shares for starting one more unit of CCTV camera manufacturing. It has utilized 10 crore rupees and then it realized that its existing business has no potential for expansion because government has reduced customs duty on import of CCTV camera. Hence imported cameras from China are cheaper than its own manufacturing. Now it wants to utilize remaining amount in mobile app development business by adding a new object in its memorandum of association. Does the Companies Act allow such change of object? If not, then what advise will you give to company. If yes, then give steps to be followed.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(PYQ Nov 2018) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 70

Answer 44. According to section 13 of the Companies Act, 2013 a company, which has raised money from public through prospectus and still has any unutilised amount out of the money so raised, shall not change its objects for which it raised the money through prospectus unless a special resolution is passed by the company and-

(i) the details in respect of such resolution shall also be published in the newspapers... and shall also be placed on the website of the company... indicating therein the justification for such change;

(ii) the dissenting shareholders shall be given an opportunity to exit by the promoters and shareholders having control in accordance with SEBI regulations. Company will have to file copy of special resolution with ROC and he will certify the registration within a period of thirty days. Looking at the above provision we can say that company can add object of mobile app development in its memorandum and divert public money into that business. But it will have to comply with above requirements.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Highlight that unutilized public money exists, so additional conditions under Section 13 apply.
2. Write Special Resolution, newspaper publication and exit opportunity in bullets.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often forget dissenting shareholders’ exit option under SEBI regulations.

Question 45. The Articles of Association of a Company may contain provisions for entrenchment under Section 5 of the Companies Act, 2013. What is meant by entrenchment provisions in this context? Also State the relevant provisions of the said Act dealing with entrenchment provisions.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 45. Entrenchment: Usually an article of association may be altered by passing special resolution but entrenchment makes it more difficult to change it. So entrenchment means making something more protective. Section 5 of the Companies Act, 2013 describes the provisions relating to entrenchment. Articles may contain provisions for entrenchment [Section 5(3)\]: The articles may contain provisions for entrenchment to the effect that specified provisions of the articles may be altered only if conditions or procedures as that are more restrictive than those applicable in the case of a special resolution, are met or complied with.

Manner of inclusion of the entrenchment provision [Section 5(4)\]: The provisions for entrenchment shall only be made either on formation of a company, or by an amendment in the articles agreed to by all the members of the company in the case of a private company and by a special resolution in the case of a public company. Notice to the registrar of the entrenchment provision [Section 5(5)\]: Where the articles contain provisions for entrenchment, whether made on formation or by amendment, the company shall give notice to the Registrar of such provisions in such form and manner as may be prescribed.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Define entrenchment briefly and then write Sections 5(3), 5(4) and 5(5) in sequence.
2. Point-wise presentation fetches quicker marks.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 71

Examiner Observations:

1. Define entrenchment briefly and then write Sections 5(3), 5(4) and 5(5) in sequence.
2. Point-wise presentation fetches quicker marks.

Question 46. The Board of Directors of Sindhu Limited wants to make some changes and to alter some Clauses of the Articles of Association which are to be urgently carried out, which include the increase in Authorized Capital of the company, issue of shares, increase in borrowing limits and increase in the number of directors. Discuss about the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 to be followed for alteration of Articles of Association.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(PYQ May 2018) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 46. Alteration in Articles of Association: Section 14 of the Companies Act, 2013, vests companies with power to alter or add to its articles. The law with respect to alteration of articles is as follows:

(1) Alteration by special resolution: Subject to the provisions of this Act and the conditions contained in its memorandum, if any, a company may, by a special resolution alter its articles.

(2) Filing of alteration with the registrar: Every alteration of the articles and a copy of the order of the Central Government approving the alteration, shall be filed with the Registrar, together with a printed copy of the altered articles, within a period of fifteen days in such manner as may be prescribed, who shall register the same.

(3) Any alteration made shall be valid: Any alteration of the articles registered as above shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be valid as if it were originally contained in the articles.

(4) Alteration noted in every copy: Every alteration made in articles of a company shall be noted in every copy of the articles, as the case may be.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Mention Special Resolution first, then filing with ROC within prescribed time.
2. Present provisions step-wise for better clarity.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often omit filing requirement and validity after registration.

Question 47. Sapphire Private Limited has registered its articles along with memorandum as on 1st July 2021. The directors of the company seeks your advice regarding the effect of registration of the company on the company itself and on its members.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 47. As per Section 9 and 10 of the Companies Act, 2013 following shall be the effect of registration of a company:

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 72

(1) From the date of incorporation, the subscribers to the memorandum and all members of the company, shall become a body corporate.

(2) Such a registered company shall be capable of exercising all the functions of an incorporated company with the perpetual succession with power to acquire, hold and dispose of property, and to contract and to sue and be sued.

(3) The memorandum and articles shall, when registered, bind the company and the members thereof to the same extent as if they respectively had been signed by the company and by each member, and contained covenants on its and his part to observe all the provisions of memorandum and of articles.

(4) All monies payable by any member to the company under the memorandum or articles shall be a debt due from him to the company.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Write effects under separate headings like body corporate, perpetual succession and binding effect of

MOA/AOA.

2. Keep points concise.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students usually forget contractual binding effect between company and members under Section 10.

Question 48. Explain in the light of the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, the circumstances under which a subsidiary company can become a member of its holding company.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 48. In accordance with the provisions of Section 19 of the Companies Act, 2013, a subsidiary company cannot either by itself or through its nominees hold any shares in its holding company and no holding company shall allot or transfer its shares to any of its subsidiary companies. Any such allotment or transfer of shares in a company to its subsidiary is void. The section however does not apply where:

(1) The subsidiary company holds shares in its holding company as the legal representative of a deceased member of the holding company, (2) the subsidiary company holds such shares as a trustee, or (3) the subsidiary company was a shareholder in the holding company even before it became its subsidiary.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with general prohibition under Section 19 and then write all three exceptions separately.
2. Comparative presentation saves revision time.

Examiner Observations:

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 73

1. Students often mention only one or two exceptions and leave the answer incomplete.

Question 49. Shri Laxmi Electricals Ltd. (S) is a company in which Hanuman power suppliers Limited (H) is holding 60% of its paid up share capital. One of the shareholder of H made a charitable trust and donated his 10% shares in H and ₹ 50 crore to the trust. He appoint S as the trustee. All the assets of the trust are held in the name of S. Can a subsidiary hold shares in its holding company in this way?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(PYQ Nov 2019) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 49. According to section 19 of the Companies Act, 2013 a company shall not hold any shares in its holding company either by itself or through its nominees... Any such allotment or transfer... shall be void. Following are the exceptions to the above rule; (a) Where the subsidiary company holds such shares as the legal representative of a deceased member...

(b) Where the subsidiary company holds such shares as a trustee; or

(c) Where the subsidiary company is a shareholder even before it became a subsidiary... In the given case, one of the shareholders of holding company has transferred his shares in the holding company to a trust where the shares will be held by subsidiary company. It means now subsidiary will hold shares in the holding company. But it will hold shares in the capacity of a trustee. Therefore, we can conclude that in the given situation S can hold shares in H.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Identify trustee capacity immediately and apply exception under Section 19 directly.
2. Avoid unnecessary discussion on prohibition rule.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students generally fail to connect trustee relationship with the statutory exception.

Question 50. Kavya Ltd. has a paid up share-capital of Rs. 80 crores. Amjali Ltd. holds a total of Rs. 50 crores of Kavya Ltd. Now, Kavya ltd. is making huge profits and wants to expand its business and is aiming at investing in Amjali Ltd. Kavya Ltd. has approached you to analyse whether as per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, they can hold 1/10th of the share capital of Amjali Ltd.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material ) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 50. In terms of section 2 (87) of the Companies Act 2013 "subsidiary company" or "subsidiary"... means a company in which the holding company-

(i) Controls the composition of the Board of Directors; or

(ii) Exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power... Since, Kavya ltd. is holding more than one half (50 crores out of 80 crores) of the total share capital of Kavya Ltd., it (Amjali Ltd.) is holding of Kavya Ltd.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 74

Further, as per the provisions of section 19... no company shall, either by itself or through its nominees, hold any shares in its holding company and no holding company shall allot or transfer its shares to any of its subsidiary companies and any such allotment or transfer... shall be void. In the given question, Kavya ltd. cannot acquire the shares of Amjali Ltd. as the acquisition of shares does not fall within the ambit of any of the exceptions provided in section 19.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. First establish holding-subsidiary relationship through voting power.
2. Then apply Section 19 prohibition and check for exceptions.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often confuse which company is holding company and which is subsidiary.

Question 51. ABC Limited issued equity shares worth ₹ 1,00,000 (10,000 shares of ₹ 10 each) on 1st April, 2023 which has been fully subscribed, whereby XYZ Limited holds 3,500 equity shares and PQR Limited holds 2,500 equity shares. Prior to the issue of equity shares, ABC Limited already held 20% of the equity shares of MNP Limited. Further, XYZ Limited holds 10% of MNP Limited’s equity shares as a trustee. MNP Limited controls the composition of the Board of Directors of XYZ Limited and PQR Limited on 01.07.2023. Examine with reference to the relevant provisions of the Companies Act, 2013- (i) Whether ABC Limited is a subsidiary of MNP Limited? (ii) Whether ABC Limited can hold shares of MNP Limited? (iii) Whether ABC Limited and XYZ Limited have the right to vote on the Annual General Meeting of MNP Limited held on 30th September, 2023?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(PYQ Jan 2021 & Nov 2020) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 51. This given question is based on section 2(87) read with section 19 of the Companies Act, 2013. For the purposes of this clause, Explanation is given providing that a company shall be deemed to be a subsidiary company of the holding company even if the control... is of another subsidiary company of the holding company. Whereas section 19 provides that, no company shall, hold any shares in its holding company... Provided further that the subsidiary company... shall have a right to vote at a meeting of the holding company only in respect of the shares held by it as a legal representative or as a trustee. Here, in the instant case... MNP Limited controls the composition of Board of Directors of XYZ Limited and PQR Limited... MNP Limited is a holding company of XYZ Limited and PQR Limited.

(i) ABC Limited shall be deemed to be a subsidiary company of the holding company (MNP Limited) as MNP Limited controls the composition of subsidiary companies XYZ Limited & PQR Limited as per explanation to section 2(87).

(ii) Yes. In this case ABC Limited is a subsidiary of MNP Limited as ABC Ltd. was holding 20% of equity shares of RS Ltd. even before it became a subsidiary company of the MNP Ltd., according to the exception to section 19.

(iii) ABC Limited cannot vote at AGM of MNP Limited held on 30th September, 2023. 2. XYZ Limited can vote at AGM of MNP Limited held on 30th September, 2023.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 75

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Solve step-wise: identify holding relationship → check shareholding exception → determine voting rights.
2. Use separate conclusions for each sub-part.

Examiner Observations: 1.Students commonly miss that voting rights are available only for shares held as trustee/legal representative.

Question 52. Explain the exceptions to the Doctrine of Indoor Management.

(4 marks|3 minutes)( Study Material) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 52. Exceptions to Doctrine of Indoor Management Relief on the ground of ‘indoor management’ cannot be claimed by an outsider dealing with the company in the following circumstances:

1. Knowledge of irregularity: In case this ‘outsider’ has actual knowledge of irregularity within the company, the

benefit under the rule of indoor management would no longer be available.

2. Negligence: If with a minimum of effort, the irregularities within a company could be discovered, the benefit of

the rule of indoor management would not apply...

3. Forgery: The rule does not apply where a person relies upon a document that turns out to be forged since

nothing can validate forgery.

4. Where the question is in regard to the very existence of an agency.

5. Where a pre-condition is required to be fulfilled before company itself can exercise a particular power.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Write all exceptions in bullet form with one-line explanation each.
2. Keywords like forgery, negligence and knowledge of irregularity are scoring areas.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students generally explain doctrine only and ignore exceptions asked in the question.

Question 53. The directors of Smart Computers limited borrowed a sum of money from Mr. Tridev. The company's articles provided that the directors may borrow on bonds such sums as may, from time to time, be authorized by resolution passed at a general meeting of the company. The shareholders claimed that there had been no such resolution authorizing the loan, and therefore, it was taken without their authority and the company is not bound to repay the loan to Tridev. In the light of the contention of shareholders, decide whether the company is bound to pay the loan.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(RTP May 2019) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 76

Answer 53. Doctrine of Indoor Management: According to this doctrine, persons dealing with the company need not enquire whether internal proceedings relating to the contract are followed correctly, once they are satisfied that the transaction is in accordance with the memorandum and articles of association. In the given question, Mr. Tridev being a person external to the company, need not enquire whether the necessary meeting was convened and held properly... even if the shareholders claim that no resolution authorizing the loan was passed, the company is bound to pay the loan to Mr. Tridev.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. First define the doctrine briefly, then directly apply facts.
2. Conclude clearly that outsider need not verify internal procedures.

Examiner Observations: 1.Students often unnecessarily discuss constructive notice instead of focusing on indoor management.

Question 54. State whether these statements are true/false along with reasons (i) To be a promoter one necessarily be associated with the initial formation of the company. (ii) Even a Non-Resident Indian can form and become member of OPC. (iii) Members who knowingly operating the company for more than six months with less than the minimum number of members specified in Section 3(1) are severally liable for the payment of all debts contracted by the company during the period since the number of members was first reduced.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(RTP May 2020) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 54. (i) False, one who subsequently helps company to keep going, raise fund & advice to board (other than in professional capacity) will equally be regarded as a promoter.

(ii) True. [As per Rule 3(1) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014.] Only a natural person, other than minor; who is an Indian citizen and whether resident in India or otherwise shall be eligible to incorporate a One Person Company.

(iii) False, refer section 3A of the Act. Such members are liable severally for the payment of the whole debts of the company contracted during that time (after elapse of six months).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Write “True” or “False” first, then give one statutory reason only.
2. Short and direct answers save maximum time.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students lose marks by giving lengthy explanations without clear conclusion.

Question 55. ABC Private Ltd. has two wholly owned subsidiary companies, D Private Limited and E Private Limited. Examine, whether, D Private Limited and E Private Limited will be treated as related party as per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013? ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 77

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material) (Easy| ICAI Fav | High chance for exam)

Answer 55. According to section 2(76)(viii) of the Companies Act, 2013, Related party, with reference to a company, means anybody corporate which is-

(A) A holding, subsidiary or an associate company of such company;

(B) A subsidiary of a holding company to which it is also a subsidiary; or

(C) an investing company or the venturer of the company; In the given question, D Private Limited and E Private Limited are wholly owned subsidiary companies of ABC Private Ltd. According to stated clause (B), above, D Private Limited and E Private Limited are related parties. However, as per the Notification No. G.S.R. 464(E) dated 5th June, 2015, clause (viii) shall not apply with respect to section 188 to a private company, though being a related parties.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Mention Section 2(76)(viii) directly and identify fellow subsidiaries as related parties.
2. Add note on exemption for private companies separately.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students usually forget the exemption notification relating to Section 188 for private companies.

Question 56. Explain the meaning of the followings terms as defined under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999: (i) Authorized person, (ii) Currency

(3 marks|2 minutes)(MTP Jan 2025)(Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 56. (i) Authorized person:- According to section 2(c) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, Authorized person means an Authorized dealer, money changer, off- shore banking unit or any other person for the time being Authorized under section 10(1) to deal in foreign exchange or foreign securities. (ii) Currency:- According to section 2(h) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, Currency includes all currency notes, postal notes, postal orders, money orders, cheques, drafts, travelers’ cheques, letters of credit, bills of exchange and promissory notes, credit cards or such other similar instruments, as may be notified by the Reserve Bank.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Definitions-based questions should be answered exactly in statutory language.
2. Underline keywords like “authorized dealer” and “foreign securities”.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often paraphrase definitions too much and miss important legal words.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 78

Question 57. Explain the following with reference to the provisions of the General Clauses Act, 1897: (i) Person (ii) Document

(3 marks|3 minutes)(MTP Jan 2025)(Easy|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 57. (i) Person: According to section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, ‘Person’ shall include any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not.

(ii) Document: According to section 3(18) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, ‘Document’ shall include any matter written, expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks or by more than one of those means which is intended to be used or which may be used, for the purpose or recording that matter.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Write section numbers and exact legal definitions in concise form.
2. Use headings separately for “Person” and “Document”.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students generally omit section numbers and fail to reproduce precise statutory wording.

Question 58. Explain the following with reference to the provisions of the General Clauses Act, 1897: (i) Affidavit (ii) Good Faith

(4 marks|3 minutes)(MTP May 2025)(Easy|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 58. (i) “Affidavit” [Section 3(3) of the General Clauses Act, 1897\]: ‘Affidavit’ shall include affirmation and declaration in the case of persons by law allowed to affirm or declare instead of swearing. The above definition is inclusive in nature. It states that Affidavit shall include affirmation and declarations. This definition does not define affidavit. However, we can understand this term in general parlance. Affidavit is a written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence in Court or before any authority.

(ii) “Good Faith” [Section 3(22) of the General Clauses Act, 1897\]: A thing shall be deemed to be done in “good faith” where it is in fact done honestly, whether it is done negligently or not. The question of good faith under the General Clauses Act is one of fact. It is to be determined with reference to the circumstances of each case. Thus, anything done with due care and attention, which is not malafide, whether it is done negligently or not is presumed to have been done in good faith.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. State definition first and then explain meaning in simple language.
2. Highlight that “good faith” depends on honesty even if negligence exists.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often confuse “good faith” under General Clauses Act with other Acts requiring due care and

attention.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 79

Queston 59. XY Ltd. has its registered office at Mumbai in the State of Maharashtra. For better administrative conveniences the company wants to shift its registered office from Mumbai to Nashik (within the State of Maharashtra). What formalities the company has to comply with under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 for shifting its registered office as stated above? Explain.

(MTP April 2019,MTP Oct 2019,ICAI Module)

Answer:- The Companies Act, 2013 under section 13 provides for the process of altering the Memorandum of a company. Since the location or Registered Office clause in the Memorandum only names the state in which its registered office is situated, a change in address from Mumbai to Nashik, does not result in the alteration of the Memorandum and hence the provisions of section 13 (and its sub sections) do not apply in this case.

However, under section 12 (5) of the Act which deals with the registered office of company, the change in registered office from one town or city to another in the same state, must be approved by a special resolution of the company.

Further, presuming that the Registrar will remain the same for the whole state of Maharashtra, there will be no need for the company to seek the confirmation to such change from the Regional Director.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Since the registered office is shifting within the same State.
2. Section 12(5) applies, not Section 13 relating to alteration of Memorandum.
3. Same State + Same ROC = Special Resolution only; No alteration of MOA and No Regional Director approval.

Examiner Observations:

1. The examiner expects you to clearly state that only Section 12(5) is applicable because the State mentioned

in the Memorandum remains unchanged.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 80

PART B

Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Question 1. \_\_\_\_\_ conceives the ideal of forming a company. (a) Directors (b) Shareholders (c) Promoters (d) Auditors (Study Material)

Answer: (c) Promoters Reason: Promoters are the individuals or entities who undertake the necessary preliminary steps to bring a company into existence, including conceiving the business idea, investigating its feasibility, and managing the registration process.

Question 2. The minimum number of members in a private company and public company are (a) 3 and 7 respectively (b) 2 and 7 respectively (c) 2 and 9 respectively (d) None of the above

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) 2 and 7 respectively Reason: Under the Companies Act, a private company requires a minimum of 2 members to be incorporated, while a public company requires a minimum of 7 members to start its operations.

Question 3. A private company shall have minimum\_\_\_and public company shall minimum \_\_\_ directors. (a) 2 : 3 (b) 2 : 7 (c) 3 : 7 (d) 1 : 2

(Study Material)

Answer: (a) 2 : 3 Reason: According to the Companies Act, a private company is required to have at least 2 directors, whereas a public company must have a minimum of 3 directors to manage its affairs.

Question 4. An individual citizen can become member of following number of one Person Company at one time (a) 10 (b) 20 (c) 01 (d) 05

(RTP Nov 2021)

Answer: (c) 01

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 81

Reason: Under the Companies Act, a natural person who is an Indian citizen and resident is permitted to be a member of only one One Person Company (OPC) at any given time to prevent the misuse of the corporate structure.

Question 5. Rukmani, a fresh science graduate, wants to make available the farmers good quality seeds and manure. For her business she is contemplating to form a company and is weighing various options. Sometimes before, she came to know that a ‘One Person Company’ has minimum one member and one director whereas a private company has minimum two members and two directors. As regards a public company she has vague idea that there should be minimum three directors but she does not know about the minimum members required in this case. Advice (a) When there is requirement of minimum three directors, the public company can be formed by minimum three persons. (b) There should be minimum five persons for formation of a public company though requirement of minimum directors shall remain three. (c) There should be minimum seven person for formation of a public company though requirement of minimum directors shall remain three. (d)There should be minimum nine person for formation of a public though requirement of minimum directors shall remain three

(MTP 2021)

Answer: (c) There should be minimum seven person for formation of a public company though requirement of minimum directors shall remain three. Reason: While a public company requires a minimum of 3 directors to manage operations, the law specifically mandates a minimum of 7 members (persons) to subscribe to the memorandum and form the entity.

Question 6. What are the conditions to become member in OPC? (a) Natural Person (b) Indian Citizen (c) Resident in India or Not (d) All of the above

(RTP May 2021)

Answer: (d) All of the above Reason: To form or become a member of an OPC, an individual must be a natural person (not a body corporate) and an Indian citizen; current laws also allow both residents and non-residents (those who stayed in India for less than 120 days) to qualify.

Question 7. Which of the following person can become member of OPC? (a) Individual (b) Company (c) LLP (d) All of the above

(Study Material)

Answer: (a) Individual

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 82

Reason: An OPC can only be formed by a natural person; artificial legal entities like a Company or an LLP are legally barred from becoming members or nominees of a One Person Company.

Question 8. Which of the following statement(s) is/are false? (a) OPC can be incorporated as section 8 company (b) OPC can carry out NBFC activity (c) A minor can be member of OPC (d) All of the above

(PYP Nov 2020)

Answer: (d) All of the above Reason: All three statements are legally prohibited under the Companies Act: an OPC cannot be formed for charitable objects (Section 8), it cannot engage in NBFC (Non-Banking Financial Investment) activities, and a minor is strictly barred from becoming a member or nominee.

Question 9. OPC can voluntarily convert into any other company only after the expiry of (a) 1 year (b) 2 years (c) 3 years (d) there is no minimum time period

(RTP Nov 2021)

Answer: (d) There is no minimum time period Reason: Following the 2021 amendments to the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, the mandatory two-year waiting period for voluntary conversion was removed, allowing an OPC to convert into a private or public company at any time.

Question 10. OPC should have minimum \_\_\_ director(s). (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 7

(Study Material)

Answer: (a) 1 Reason: Under the Companies Act, a One Person Company (OPC) is designed for individual entrepreneurs and is legally required to have a minimum of one director, who is typically the member themselves.

Question 11. Jatin is desirous of forming a ‘One Person Company (OPC)’ for which he wants to nominate his wife Jasmin who in the event of his death shall become the member of OPC. However, he is not aware of as to which document should contain the name of the nominee. Advise him in the matter. (a) Name of the nominee should be mentioned in the Articles of Association after the names of the directors. (b) Name of the nominee should be mentioned in the Memorandum of Association. (c) Either Articles of Association or Memorandum of Association may contain the name of the nominee. (d) There is no need to mention the name of he nominee in either Articles of Association or Memorandum of Association; a simple consent letter obtained from the nominee and kept in the records is sufficient. ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 83

(MTP Oct 2020)

Answer: (b) Name of the nominee should be mentioned in the Memorandum of Association. Reason: The Companies Act mandates that the Memorandum of Association (MoA) of an OPC must state the name of the person (nominee) who will become the member in the event of the subscriber's death or incapacity.

Question 12. Rajesh has formed a ‘One Person Company (OPC)’ with his wife Roopali as nominee. For the last two years his wife Roopali is suffering from terminal illness and due to this hard fact he wants to change her as nominee. He has a trusted and experienced friend Ramnivas who could be made nominee or his (Rajesh) son Rakshak who is of seventeen years of age. Whom should he nominate as nominee in place of his wife? (a) Since blood relation can only be appointed as nominee in case of OPC, Rajesh needs to appoint his son Rakshak. (b) Rajesh can appoint his friend Ramnivas as nominee in his OPC but not his son Rakshak (c) Roopali is not agreegable to the proposal of Rajesh and hence, Rajesh cannot change her as the nominee (d) Either Rakshak or Mr. Ramnivas can be appointed as nominee

(RTP May 2020)

Answer: (b) Rajesh can appoint his friend Ramnivas as nominee in his OPC but not his son Rakshak Reason: Under the Companies Act, only a natural person who is a major (18+ years old) can be a nominee; therefore, his son Rakshak is disqualified as a minor, while his friend Ramnivas is eligible regardless of blood relation.

Question 13. Abha formed a ‘One Person Company (OPC)’ on 15-10-2017 with her husband Akhil as nominee and ₹ 10 lacs as Authorized and paid-up share capital. In the month of April, 2018 she got in touch with a foreigner and is expecting to receive a substantial export order by May 2018 whose final delivery must be completed by December 2018. She is contemplating to convert her OPC into a private limited company before she receives the export order in May 2018. (a) Since Abha is the sole member of OPC she is having full discretion to voluntarily convert it into a private limited company any time after 15-10-2017 (b) Abha can voluntarily convert her OPC into a private limited company only after the expiry of first financial year by which the accounts are closed (i.e. after 31.3.2018 without any restriction.) (c) Abha can voluntarily convert her OPC into a private limited company only after she delivers duly audited first financial statements and Annual Return to the concerned Register of Companies by due date and without making payment of any additional fee. (d) Abha can voluntarily convert her OPC into a private limited company only after expiry of two years from 15-10- 2017 (i.e. on 15-10- 2019 or thereafter).

(RTP Nov 2021)

Answer: (a) Since Abha is the sole member of OPC she is having full discretion to voluntarily convert it into a private limited company any time after 15-10-2017 Reason: Following the 2021 amendments to the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, the previous mandatory two- year waiting period was removed, allowing an OPC to voluntarily convert into a private or public company at any time after its incorporation. ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 84

Question 14. Anupam got incorporated ‘One Person Company with his sister Alpana as the nominee and about three years have passed satisfactorily. From time- to-time Anupam does a number of Charitable works and is attached with three NGOs undertaking such assignments. In the meantime, his business under his OPC has also flourished. Now he is contemplating the convert the OPC either as a Section 8 company (i.e. formation of companies with charitable objects) or as a private or public company. Select the best option for him. (a) Since OPC belongs to Anupam, he has full discretion to convert the OPC either as a Section 8 Company or as a private or public company (b) Since OPC was formed as a private company, the only option available with Anupam is to get it converted into a private limited company. Moreover, there is specific prohibition on converting OPC into a public limited company. (c) There is specific prohibition on converting OPC into a Section 8 company; otherwise it can be converted into a private or public company without any hindrance. (d) Since Anupam does a lot of charitable works there is no prohibition if he converts his OPC into a Section 8 company (Companies formed with charitable objects.

(MTP March 2022)

Answer: (c) There is specific prohibition on converting OPC into a Section 8 company; otherwise it can be converted into a private or public company without any hindrance. Reason: Under Rule 3 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, a One Person Company is strictly prohibited from being incorporated as or converting into a Section 8 Company (charitable company); however, it can be voluntarily converted into a private or public company at any time.

Question 15. Vivek is in trading business whereby he supplies handmade gloves and socks to many charitable trusts who supports the elderly people. Vivek now wants to expand his business and wants to reap the benefits of company form of organization by opening his business as a OPC registered under section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013. Advise Vivek (a) Vivek cannot form an OPC as he is in trading business (b) Vivek cannot form an OPC to be registered under section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 (c) Vivek can form an OPC to be registered under section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 (d) Vivek can form an OPC as a private company and then convert it into a section 8 company

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Vivek cannot form an OPC to be registered under section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 Reason: Under the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, a One Person Company (OPC) is explicitly prohibited from being incorporated as or converting into a Section 8 company (a company with charitable objects); it must be a for-profit entity.

Question 16. Shruti a common friend of Suchitra and Sukanya, got incorporated OPC Sometimes before and during a chit-chat with her friends informed them that there is some limit on the maximum capital which her

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 85

OPC can have and she would have to convert her OPC either into a private or public limited company if such limit exceeded. Suchitra and Sukanya who are desirous of forming a private limited company for carrying on textile trading business, are unsure about the maximum capital which a private limited company can have. Advise. (a) A private limited company can have maximum of ₹ 1 crore as share capital. (b) A private limited company can have maximum of ₹ 2 crores as share capital. (c) A private limited company can have maximum of ₹ 5 crores as share capital as share capital. (d) A private limited company can have unlimited share capital.

(MTP April 2021)

Answer: (d) A private limited company can have unlimited share capital. Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013, while a company must specify an "Authorized Share Capital" in its Memorandum of Association, there is no legal upper limit or ceiling on how much this capital can be. A private company can increase its authorized capital to any amount by following the prescribed legal procedure and paying the requisite stamp duty to the government.

Question 17. Ram has incorporated a One-Person Company with the name of Food lovers Inc. His friends Ramesh is a member of another One Person Company. Juice loves Inc. Ramesh has appointed Ram as the nominee of his OPC, Juice lovers Inc. Unfortunately, Ramesh died and Ram becomes the member of Juice lovers Inc., by virtual of his being the nominee, Now Ram wants to know whether he can continue his membership in both the companies? (a) Yes, Ram can continue to hold the membership in both the OPCs (b) Ram needs to give up the membership in any one OPC within a period of 120 days (c) Ram needs to give up the membership in any one OPC within a period of 180 days (d) Ram needs to give up the membership in any one OPC within a period of 365 days.

(PYP Jan 2021)

Answer: (c) Ram needs to give up the membership in any one OPC within a period of 180 days Reason: Under the Companies Act, an individual can be a member of only one OPC at a time; if they become a member of a second OPC through nomination by death, they must rectify the situation and choose one company within a grace period of 180 days.

Question 18. If the number of members is reduced below statutory minimum members become personally liable after a period of (a) 1 month (b) 3 months (c) 6 months (d) 1 year

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) 6 months Reason: Under Section 3A of the Companies Act, 2013, if the number of members falls below the statutory minimum (2 for private, 7 for public) and the company carries on business for more than 6 months, every person who is a member during that time becomes personally liable for all debts contracted after that period. ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 86

Question 19. Which one of the following is not the content of the Memorandum of Association? (a) Name clause (b) Registered office clause (c) Objects clause (d) Board of directors clause

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) Board of directors clause Reason: The Memorandum of Association (MoA) contains the fundamental clauses upon which the company is built (Name, Situation, Objects, Liability, Capital, and Subscription); the details regarding the appointment and powers of directors are contained in the Articles of Association (AoA).

Question 20. Which of the following documents is the constitution of the company? (a) Memorandum of Association (b) Register of Members (c) Order of NCLT (d) None of the above

(Study Material)

Answer: (a) Memorandum of Association Reason: The Memorandum of Association (MoA) is considered the constitution or "Charter" of a company because it defines its objects, powers, and the scope of its operations beyond which the company cannot legally act.

Question 21. Which of the following documents contains internal regulation of the Company? (a) Memorandum of Association (b) Article of Association (c) Order of NCLT (d) None of the above

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Article of Association Reason: The Articles of Association (AoA) serve as the rulebook or "user manual" of the company, containing the specific rules, regulations, and bye-laws that govern internal management, such as the appointment of directors, conduct of meetings, and issuance of shares.

Question 22. MOA of an unlimited company not having a share capital is included in (a) Table B (b) Table C (c) Table D (d) Table E

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) Table D Reason: The Memorandum of Association (MOA) for an unlimited company not having a share capital is provided in Table D of Schedule I of the Companies Act, 2013. Each table in Schedule I provides a specific model form for different types of companies, as outlined in Section 4(6) of the Act. ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 87

Question 23. Situation clause in MOA contains the (a) The name of Registrar of companies (b) Complete postal address (c) Name of the state in which registered office is situated (d) Name of city/town only and not that of state.

(RTP May 2021)

Answer: (c) Name of the state in which registered office is situated Reason: The Situation Clause (or Registered Office Clause) must specify the state where the company’s registered office is located to determine the jurisdiction of the High Court and the specific Registrar of Companies (ROC) under which the company falls. While the exact address is shared later with the Registrar, the MOA itself only requires the name of the state.

Question 24. Liability clause in MOA is required by (a) Company limited by shares (b) Company limited by guarantee only (c) Company limited by guarantee having share capital (d) All of the above

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) All of the above Reason: The Liability Clause is mandatory for all companies with limited liability to define the extent to which members are responsible for the company's debts. This includes companies limited by shares (limited to unpaid share value) and those limited by guarantee (limited to the amount promised in the event of winding up).

Question 25. The term ‘Foundation’ may be allowed to be used in the name of only (a) Foreign Company (b) Section 8 Company (c) Nidhi company (d) Producer Company

(MTP May 2020)

Answer: (b) Section 8 Company Reason: Under the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, companies registered under Section 8 (not-for-profit organizations) are required to include words like Foundation, Forum, Association, Federation, or Council in their name to reflect their social or charitable objectives, instead of "Limited" or "Private Limited."

Question 26. The term ‘Federation’ may be allowed to be used in the name of only (a) Foreign Company (b) Section 8 Company (c) Nidhi Company (d) Producer Company

(MTP Nov 2021) ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 88

Answer: (b) Section 8 Company Reason: Similar to the term "Foundation," the word "Federation" is specifically reserved for companies registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, as it signifies a non-profit objective related to the promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, or charity.

Question 27. The term ‘electoral trust’ may be allowed to be used in the name of only (a) Foreign Company (b) Section 8 Company (c) Nidhi Company (d) Producer Company

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Section 8 Company Reason: Similar to the term "Foundation," the word "Federation" is specifically reserved for companies registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, as it signifies a non-profit objective related to the promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, or charity.

Question 28. Upon receipt of application, Register will reserve the name for an initial period of (a)20 days from the date of application (b) 20 days from the date of approval (c) 30 days from the date of application (d) 30 days from the date of approval

(RTP May 2022)

Answer: (b) 20 days from the date of approval Reason: According to Section 4(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Registrar reserves a name for a new company for a period of 20 days from the date of approval. For an existing company changing its name, the reservation period is 60 days from the date of approval.

Question 29. Upon receipt of application, Registrar reserved the name of a new company. However, the documents for incorporation of the company couldn’t be filled with the initial period permitted under the Companies Act, 2013. The application is ready to pay an additional fees of ₹ 1,000 but wants to know for how many days the name will be kept reserved. (a) 20 days from the date of approval (b) 30 days from the date of approval (c) 40 days from the date of approval (d) 60 days from the date of approval

(RTP May 2021)

Answer: (c) 40 days from the date of approval Reason: Under Rule 9A of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, a company can extend the initial 20-day reservation period to 40 days by paying a fee of ₹1,000 before the expiry of the original 20 days.

Question 30. Sapan and Sanjay made a name reservation application accompanied by requisite fee to the Registrar for forming a new private company. The Registrar accorded its approval for reservation of most ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 89

preferred name Sapanjay Softwares Private Ltd. On 6th July, 2018. In how many days, necessary documents for incorporation of the company must be submitted to the Registrar so that the reserved name does not get lapsed, in case, they do not intend to pay any additional fees. (a) Within 10 days from the date of approval (b) Within 20 days from the date of approval (c) Within 45 days from the date of approval (d) Within 60 days from the date of approval

(MTP Nov 2019)

Answer: (b) Within 20 days from the date of approval Reason: Under Section 4(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Registrar reserves a name for a new company for a period of 20 days from the date of approval. If the promoters (Sapan and Sanjay) do not wish to pay additional fees for an extension, they must file the incorporation documents within this initial 20-day window.

Question 31. Vinay and Sanjay made a name reservation application accompanied by requisite fee to the Registrar for forming a new private company. The Registrar accorded its approval for reservation of most preferred name Vinanjay Softwares Private Ltd. on 7th July, 2018. By which date necessary documents for incorporation of the company must be submitted to the Registrar so that the reserved name does not get lapsed, in case they do not intend to pay any additional fees. (a) Latest by 20th July, 2018 (b) Latest by 27th July, 2018 (c) Latest by 4th August, 2018 (d) Latest by 4th September, 2018

(PYP Nov 2018)

Answer: (b) Latest by 27th July, 2018 Reason: As per the Companies Act, 2013, the reserved name for a new company remains valid for 20 days from the date of approval. Since the approval was granted on 7th July, adding 20 days brings the deadline to 27th July, 2018\.

Question 32. Amar made an application, his wife Abhilasha being other proposed subscriber and got reserved a name for incorporation of a private limited company but the Registrar of Companies, Delhi and Haryana, much before the incorporation, found that the name was applied by furnishing wrong information. (a) The reserved name shall be cancelled by the ROC because the name was applied by furnishing wrong information and Amar who made the application shall be liable to a penalty up to Rs. One lac. (b) The reserved name, after seeking explanation from Amar and after the pays a penalty of Rs. One lac shall be allotted by the ROC and the company shall be incorporated by this name. (c) The reserved name shall be cancelled by the ROC but Amar shall not be liable to pay any penalty because cancellation of name in itself is a penalty. (d) Besides cancellation of the reserved name Amar and Abhilasha shall be debarred from making an application for reservation of name for one year from the date on which cancellation letter was issued by the ROC.

(Study Material)

Answer: (a) The reserved name shall be cancelled by the ROC because the name was applied by furnishing wrong information and Amar who made the application shall be liable to a penalty up to Rs. One lac. Reason: According to Section 4(5)(ii) of the Companies Act, 2013, if it is found that a name was reserved by furnishing wrong or incorrect information, and the company has not yet been incorporated, the Registrar shall ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 90

cancel the reserved name and the person who made the application (Amar) shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to one lakh rupees.

Question 33. \_\_\_\_contains the regulations for management of the company. (a) Memorandum of Association (b) Articles of Association (c) Schedules (d) Notifications

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Articles of Association Reason: Under Section 5 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Articles of Association (AOA) serve as the internal rulebook of a company. It contains the rules, bye-laws, and regulations that govern the internal management, the conduct of business, and the relationship between the company and its members.

Question 34. Articles of a company may be altered by complying with more restrictive provisions than Special Resolution. This is called (a) Doctrine of Constructive notice (b) Doctrine of Indoor Management (c) Doctrine of Ultra Vires (d) Entrenchment provision

(PYP Nov 2020)

Answer: (d) Entrenchment provision Reason: Under Section 5(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, "entrenchment" allows a company to specify that certain provisions in its Articles of Association can only be altered by following a procedure that is more restrictive than a Special Resolution (e.g., requiring 90% or 100% agreement instead of the usual 75%).

Question 35. To entrench its article after incorporation a public company (a) Will have to pass a special resolution (b) Will have to take consent of all members (c) s not allowed to do so (d) Will have to pass special resolution and take approval of Tribunal

(Study Material)

Answer: (a) Will have to pass a special resolution Reason: According to Section 5(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a public company wishes to include entrenchment provisions in its Articles of Association after its incorporation, it must do so by passing a Special Resolution. For a private company, however, the consent of all members (unanimous) is required.

Question 36. In case of a private company, the provisions for Entrenchment may be made at the time of formation of the company or by amendment of articles. (a) By passing a special resolution (b) With the consent of all the members (c) By passing a special resolution and approval of the Central Government (d) With the consent of all the members and approval of the Central Government

(MTP May 2022) ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 91

Answer: (b) With the consent of all the members Reason: Under Section 5(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, while a public company can entrench its articles by passing a Special Resolution, a private company must obtain the unanimous consent of all its members if the entrenchment provision is introduced through an amendment after incorporation.

Question 37. The Articles of a company limited by guarantee having share capital is in (a) Table F (b) Table G (c) Table H (d) Table I

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Table G Reason: Under Schedule I of the Companies Act, 2013, the model Articles of Association (AOA) for different types of companies are organized into specific tables. Table G is specifically prescribed for a company limited by guarantee and having a share capital.

Question 38. A model form of articles contained in Table F relates to a company limited by (a) Shares (b) Guarantee (c) Shares and guarantee (d) none of the above

(PYP May 2018)

Answer: (a) Shares Reason: Under Schedule I of the Companies Act, 2013, Table F provides the model Articles of Association (AOA) specifically for a company limited by shares. This table contains the standard regulations for managing internal affairs, such as share calls, forfeiture, and voting rights.

Question 39. A company has a right to provision of Model Articles. (a) Adopt (b) Exclude (c) Modify (d) All of the above

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) All of the above Reason: Under Section 5(7) and 5(8) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company has the full flexibility to adopt the model articles (Tables F to J) in their entirety, modify them to suit specific needs, or exclude them by drafting unique regulations—provided the custom rules do not contravene the Act.

Question 40. Every person dealing with the company is deemed to have read and understood the MOA and AOA. This is called (a) Doctrine of Ultra Vires (b) Doctrine of Constructive Notice (c) Doctrine of Indoor Management (d) Doctrine of Alter Ego ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 92

(PYP May 2018)

Answer: (b) Doctrine of Constructive Notice Reason: The Doctrine of Constructive Notice is a legal presumption that since the Memorandum of Association (MOA) and Articles of Association (AOA) are public documents registered with the Registrar, every person dealing with the company is deemed to have "constructive" (presumed) knowledge of their contents and cannot later claim ignorance.

Question 41. Doctrine of Indoor Management was laid down in the case of (a) Griffing vs. Paget (b) Royal British Bank vs. Turquand (c) Howard vs. Patent Ivory Co. (d) Rouben vs Great Fingal Consolidated

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Royal British Bank vs. Turquand Reason: The Doctrine of Indoor Management is often referred to as the "Turquand Rule" because it originated from this 1856 landmark case. The court held that while outsiders are expected to know a company's public documents (MOA/AOA), they are not required to investigate the regularity of internal proceedings, such as whether a specific resolution was actually passed.

Question 42. Doctrine of Indoor Management works in favour of the\_\_\_\_\_ and against the\_\_\_\_ (a) Company, outsiders (b) Outsiders, company (c) Company, directors (d) Directors, Company

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Outsiders, company Reason: The Doctrine of Indoor Management (also known as the Turquand Rule) protects third parties by allowing them to assume that a company’s internal proceedings have been carried out regularly; therefore, the company cannot avoid liability by claiming internal procedural irregularities.

Question 43. Certificate of incorporation is issued in Form \_\_\_ (a) INC – 1 (b) INC – 10 (c) INC – 11 (d) INC – 32

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) INC – 11 Reason: Once the Registrar of Companies (ROC) is satisfied that all legal requirements for registration have been met, they issue the Certificate of Incorporation in Form INC-11 as per the Companies Act.

Question 44. Company is incorporated using

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 93

(a) INC – 1 (b) INC – 10 (c) INC – 11 (d) SPICe + : INC – 32

(RTP May 2020)

Answer: (d) SPICe +: INC – 32 Reason: Under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) "Ease of Doing Business" initiative, SPICe+ (Simplified Proforma for Incorporating Company Electronically Plus) is the integrated web-based form used for company incorporation. It acts as a single window for multiple services, including name reservation, DIN allotment, and mandatory PAN/TAN applications.

Question 45. SPICe + stands \_\_\_\_\_\_ (a) Specified Proforma for Incorporating Company Electronically Plus (b) Simplified Proforma for Incorporating Company Electronically Plus (c) Specified Proforma for Incorporating Company Easily Plus (d) Simplified Proforma for Incorporating Company Easily Plus

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Simplified Proforma for Incorporating Company Electronically Plus Reason: SPICe+ is an integrated web form introduced by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) to streamline the incorporation process by offering 10 different services (like PAN, TAN, and DIN) across three central government departments in a single application.

Question 46. Corporate Identification Number is a \_\_\_ digit alphanumeric number. (a) 10 (b) 11 (c) 16 (d) 21

(MTP Oct 2021)

Answer: (d) 21 Reason: The Corporate Identification Number (CIN) is a unique 21-digit alphanumeric code assigned by the Registrar of Companies (ROC) to every company registered in India to track its identity and status.

Question 47. If a company is registered by incorrect information, then its winding up may be ordered by (a) Central Government (b) Registrar of Companies (c) NCLT (d) Court

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) NCLT Reason: According to Section 7(7) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a company is incorporated by furnishing false or incorrect information, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) has the power to order its winding up, direct the removal of its name from the register, or pass any other order it deems fit.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 94

Question 48. Section 8 companies are also known as \_\_\_\_\_\_ (a) Government company (b) Licensed Company (c) Dormant Company (d) Nidhi Company

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Licensed company Reason: Under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is formed for promoting commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, or environmental protection. It is called a Licensed Company because it must obtain a specific license from the Central Government to operate without using the words "Limited" or "Private Limited" in its name.

Question 49. Where a company is granted licence under section 8, it is not required to use the following word even though it is a limited company. (a) Guarantee company (b) Limited Liability Partnership (c) Limited or Private Limited, as the case may be (d) Development Authority

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) Limited or Private Limited, as the case may be Reason: Under Section 8(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Central Government grants a license to companies with charitable or non-profit objectives, allowing them to be registered as limited companies without the addition of the words "Limited" or "Private Limited" to their name.

Question 50. \_\_\_ may, by order, revoke the license of Section 8 Company. (a) NCLT (b) Central Government (c) Special Court (d) High Court

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Central Government Reason: Under Section 8(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Central Government has the authority to revoke the license of a Section 8 company if it violates any of the conditions of the license, acts fraudulently, or operates in a manner prejudicial to public interest.

Question 51. Mr. Pushpa wishes to start his own venture with an idea of recycling of plastic waste as charitable organisation. He approaches you for your advice so as to decide on which type of entity he should incorporate mainly based on the aspects of taxation, capital funding and other monetary benefits to the promoters. Kindly suggest a suitable form of entity from the following: (a) Limited Liability Partnership (b) Private Limited Company (c) Section 8 Company (d) Producer Company

(RTP May 2021)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 95

Answer: (c) Section 8 Company Reason: Since Mr. Pushpa's primary objective is to run a charitable organization (recycling plastic waste for social/environmental good), a Section 8 company is the most suitable as it is specifically designed for non-profit objectives and offers significant tax exemptions (under Section 12AB and 80G of the IT Act) and access to grants/CSR funding.

Question 52. Ravi and Ragini have formed a Section 8 company: date of incorporation being 18.02.2018 and they being the directors and also the shareholders. During June, 2018, two unsuitable articles in AOA were required to be altered for smooth functioning of the company. Advise. (a) Since articles regulate the internal management of the company, both Ravi and Ragini being directors and shareholders are themselves capable of altering the articles. (b) In case of section 8 company, articles can be altered only if the company shows profits consecutively for two years. (c) In case of Section 8 company, prior approval of the Central Government is required to be obtained before its articles are altered. (d) In case of Section 8 company, at least one year must elapse from the date of its incorporation before its articles are altered but there is no need to obtain prior permission of the Central Government.

(PYP Nov 2020)

Answer: (c) In case of Section 8 Company, prior approval of the Central Government is required to be obtained before its articles are altered. Reason: According to Section 8(4)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company registered under this section cannot alter the provisions of its Memorandum (MOA) or Articles of Association (AOA) except with the previous approval of the Central Government.

Question 53. A not for profit company shall not alter the provisions of its memorandum or articles. (a) False, it can freely change it (b) False, it can do so with the permission of CG (c) True, because it will be violative of terms of license (d) True, because MOA/AOA of a section 8 company is unalterable

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) False, it can do so with the permission of CG Reason: Under Section 8(4)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013, a Section 8 company (not-for-profit) is allowed to alter the provisions of its Memorandum of Association (MOA) or Articles of Association (AOA), provided it obtains the previous approval of the Central Government.

Question 54. A director of a company has to file a declaration that every subscriber has paid the value of the shares agreed to be taken by him within days of incorporation. (a) 30 (b) 90

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 96

(c) 120 (d) 180

Question 55. A company shall within\_\_days have a registered office from days of incorporation. (a) 10 (b) 15 (c) 30 (d) 60

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) 30 Reason: According to Section 12(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is required to have a registered office capable of receiving and acknowledging all communications and notices within 30 days of its incorporation.

Question 56. If a company has changed its name, it shall affix the former name along with new name for \_\_ year(s). (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4

(PYP Nov 2018)

Answer: (b) 2 Reason: Under the proviso to Section 12(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a company has changed its name during the last two years, it must paint, affix, or print its former name(s) along with the new name on all its business letters, billheads, and official publications.

Question 57. A company can shift its registered office outside the City, town or village only after the approval by way of (a)Board resolution (b) Ordinary resolution (c) Special resolution (d) written consent from Central Government

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) Special resolution Reason: Under Section 12(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a company wishes to shift its registered office outside the local limits of the city, town, or village where it is currently situated, it must obtain the approval of the members by passing a Special Resolution in a General Meeting.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 97

Question 58. If a company wants to shift its registered office from one RoC-Mumbai to RoC-Pune, but within Maharashtra, then approval of is required (a)NCLT (b) Central Government (c) Regional Director (d) Special Court

(RTP May 2022)

Answer: (c) Regional Director Reason: According to the proviso to Section 12(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, when a company shifts its registered office from the jurisdiction of one Registrar (ROC) to another within the same state (as is the case between Mumbai and Pune in Maharashtra), it must obtain prior confirmation from the Regional Director (RD).

Question 59. If a company wants to shift its registered office from one RoC to another within the same state, then approval of Regional Director is filed with the Registrar within days. (a) 15 (b) 30 (c) 60 (d) 90

Answer: (c) 60 Reason: According to Section 12(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, once the Regional Director (RD) confirms the shifting of the registered office from one ROC to another within the same state, the company must file a copy of the RD’s order with the Registrar of Companies (ROC) within 60 days of receiving the confirmation.

Question 60. Omni Limited was incorporated on 1st July 2019. It has to establish its registered office on or before (a) 1st October 2019 (b) 1st December 2019 (c) 16th July 2019 (d) 31st July 2019

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) 31st July 2019 Reason: Under Section 12(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is required to have a registered office within 30 days of its incorporation. Since Omni Limited was incorporated on 1st July 2019, the 30-day window expires on 31st July 2019.

Question 61. SNDT Ltd decided to shift its registered office from jurisdiction of one Registrar to the jurisdiction of another Registrar. By when SNDT Ltd has to file that confirmation with the Registrar? (a) 11th July, 2017 (b) 25th July, 2017 (c) 11th August, 2017 (d) 25th August, 2017

Answer: (d) 25th August, 2017 Reason: Under Section 12(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company must file the confirmation order received from the Regional Director (RD) with the Registrar (ROC) within 60 days from the date of the order.

Question 62. Indian Company decided to shift its registered office within the jurisdiction of same Registrar in a Board meeting held on 25th May, 2017. Within how many days Company shall intimate such change to Registrar of Companies? (a) Within 15 days from the date of such change (b) Within 30 days from the date of such change (c) Within 15 days from the date of Board meeting (d) Within 30 days from the date of Board meeting

(RTP Nov 2019)

Answer: (b) Within 30 days from the date of such change Reason: Under Section 12 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company must provide notice of any change in the situation of its registered office to the Registrar within 30 days of the change, verified in the prescribed manner.

Question 63. If a company changes its name: which of the following is most accurate. (a) It is not allowed to use old name in any way. (b) New name should not be identical with the old name. (c) Old name should be painted/printed for next 1 year along with new name. (d) Old name should be painted/printed for next 2 years along with new name.
