(vii) in respect of the issue or transfer of any shares of a company, the share transfer agents, registrars and merchant bankers to the issue or transfer;

In the given case, as stated Johnson Limited, committed a default with respect to the allotment of shares by the officers. As in company there were no managing director, whole time director, or any other officer/person designated by the Board with the responsibility of complying with the provisions of the Act. Therefore, in such situation, all the directors of the company may be treated as officers in default.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Define “officer in default” under Section 2(60) and apply it to the facts given.
2. In absence of KMP/WTD/designated officer, directly conclude that all directors become liable.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often reproduce the entire definition without applying it to the case.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 129

Question 33. Grab Ltd., an unlisted company, intends to make a public offer of securities. However, they are not sure about the compliance requirements for issuing securities in dematerialised form. You being an expert, guide Grab Ltd. on the relevant provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and whether Grab Ltd. is eligible to issue its securities?

(5 marks|6 minutes)( RTP Nov 2020)(Medium)

Answer 33. Section 29 deals with the Public Offer of Securities to be in dematerialised form. It provides that every company making a public offer and such other class or classes of companies as may be prescribed, have to issue their securities only in dematerialised form by complying with the provisions of the Depositories Act, 1996 and regulations made under it. Sub-section 1A provides that in case of prescribed class/classes of unlisted companies, the securities shall be held or transferred only in dematerialised form by complying with the provisions of the Depositories Act, 1996 and regulations made under it.

Accordingly, in the given case, Grab Ltd., an unlisted company, if it falls in the prescribed classes of companies, have to comply with the provisions given under section 29(1A) and the relevant Rule 9A of Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014. Grab Ltd. must ensure that its securities are issued and transferred in dematerialised form in compliance with the Depositories Act, 1996.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Explain Section 29 and determine whether the unlisted company falls within the prescribed class.
2. Highlight the key phrase “issue and transfer only in dematerialized form.”

Examiner Observations:

1. Candidates confuse provisions of demat issue with listing requirements.

Question 34. Explain the manner in which a company may issue Global Depository Receipts in a foreign country.

(6 marks|7 minutes)( Study material)(Medium)

Answer 34. The companies (issue of global depository receipts) rules, 2014, lays the manner in which a company may issue depository receipts in a foreign country. Manner for issue of depository receipts- (1) The depository receipts can be issued by way of public offering or private placement or in any other manner prevalent abroad and may be listed or traded in an overseas listing or trading platform.

(2) The depository receipts may be issued against issue of new shares or may be sponsored against shares held by shareholders of the company in accordance with such conditions as the Central Government or Reserve Bank of India may prescribe or specify from time to time.

(3) The underlying shares shall be allotted in the name of the overseas depository bank and against such shares, the depository receipts shall be issued by the overseas depository bank abroad.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 130

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. State the manner of issue under the Companies (Issue of Global Depository Receipts) Rules, 2014.
2. Remember the three points—Issue Method, Underlying Shares, Overseas Depository Bank.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students generally explain GDR meaning but miss the procedural requirements.

Question 35. Ruhi and her brother Sohit were offered jointly 1000 equity shares of ₹ 100 each by Soumya Software Private Limited under the issue of shares on private placement basis. Offer-cum-application letter addressed to both containing their names as “Ms. Ruhi, Mr. Sohit”. From whose account the company is required to take subscription money for 1000 equity shares?

(3 marks|4 minutes)( RTP may 2020)(Medium| ICAI Fav |High chance for exam)

Answer 35. According to the first Proviso of Rule 14(5) of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, monies payable on subscription to securities to be held by joint holders shall be paid from the bank account of the person whose name appears first in the application.

Since Ruhi’s name appears first in the application, therefore the subscription of ₹ 1,00,000 shall be payable by her from her account. It is obligatory for the company to ensure that the money is paid from her bank account and not from the bank account of her brother Sohit.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Apply Rule 14(5) and identify whose name appears first in the application.
2. Remember: Subscription money must come from the bank account of the first applicant.

Examiner Observations:

1. Candidates often answer based on joint ownership rather than the statutory rule.

Question 36. Swati Limited is intending to issue its securities on private placement basis. Explain to the directors of the company, the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, on the following matters: (i) Meaning of Private Placement (ii) 'Time Limit for Allotment of Securities' and 'repayment of application money in case of default in allotment.'

(6 marks|7 minutes)( PYQ Nov 2018)(Medium| ICAI Fav |High chance for exam)

Answer 36.(i) Meaning of ‘Private Placement’: As per Explanation I to section 42(3), the term "private placement" means any offer or invitation to subscribe or issue of securities to a select group of persons by a company (other than by way of public offer) through private placement offer - cum-application, which satisfies the conditions specified in section 42.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 131

(ii) ‘Time Limit for Allotment of Securities’: A company making an offer or invitation under section 42 shall allot its securities within sixty days from the date of receipt of the application money for such securities. If the company is not able to allot the securities within that period, it shall repay the application money to the subscribers within fifteen days from the expiry of sixty days. If the company fails to repay the application money within the aforesaid period, it shall be liable to repay that money with interest at the rate of twelve per cent per annum from the expiry of the sixtieth day.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. First define private placement, then discuss allotment timeline and refund/interest provisions.
2. memorized 60 days allotment + 15 days refund + 12% interest.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students frequently forget the interest rate or calculate timelines incorrectly.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 132

PART-B Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Question 1. Trident Limited is in process of making private placement of securities. It received application money on 2nd March 2023. It shall allot its securities by, if failed then repay application money to the subscribers by, else liable to repay that money with interest at the rate of. (a) 1st April, 16th April, and 12% respectively (b) 1st May, 16th May, and 12% respectively (c) 1st April, 16th April, and 6% respectively (d) 16th April, 1st May, and 12% respectively

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) 1st May, 16th May, and 12% respectively Reason: As per Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 (Private Placement):

1. Allotment of securities must be completed within 60 days from receipt of application money.  Application money received: 2 March 2023  60 days expire on 1 May 2023
2. If allotment is not made within 60 days, the company must refund the money within 15 days thereafter.

 Refund deadline: 16 May 2023

3. If the company fails to refund within those 15 days, it must pay interest @ 12% p.a. from the expiry of the 60th day.

Question 2. Modern Furniture Limited, issued a document containing offer of securities for sale that is considered as deemed prospectus under section 25, which requires such document must contains certain matters/disclosures in addition to those required under section 26. Which of following are correct requirements; i. A statement of the net amount received or to be received as consideration for the securities to which the offer relates ii. The persons making the offer were named in the prospectus as promoters of the company. iii. The time and place at which the underlying contract for allotment may be inspected. (a) i or ii only (b) i or iii only (c) ii or iii only (d) All of i, ii and iii

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) i or iii only Reason: Under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 2013 (Deemed Prospectus), where securities are offered for sale to the public, the document must contain, in addition to Section 26 disclosures: (i) A statement of the net amount received or to be received as consideration for the securities. (iii) The time and place at which the contract for allotment may be inspected. (ii) is incorrect because the requirement is not that the persons making the offer were named as promoters in the prospectus.

Question 3. Section 40 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires every company shall make an application to one or more recognized stock exchange or exchanges before making public offer. Madhav Casting Limited filed an application to three exchanges for the securities to be dealt with in such stock exchanges, it received permission from couple of them and proceed with public issue. There will be: (a) No penalty, as application has been filed (b) Penalty on Madhav Casting Limited ranging from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 50 lakh (c) Penalty on Madhav Casting Limited ranging from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 50 lakh and every officer of the company who is in default ranging from Rs 50 thousand to Rs 3 lakh (d) Penalty on Madhav Casting Limited ranging from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 50 lakh and every officer of the company who is in default ranging from Rs 50 thousand to Rs 3 lakh and/or Imprisonment upto one year.

Study Material)

Answer: (c) Penalty on Madhav Casting Limited ranging from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 50 lakh and every officer of the company who is in default ranging from Rs 50 thousand to Rs 3 lakh Reason: As per Section 40 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company making a public offer must obtain permission from all the recognized stock exchanges named in the prospectus before proceeding with the issue. If the company proceeds without obtaining the required permissions, it is liable to:  Company: Penalty of ₹5 lakh to ₹50 lakh  Officer in default: Penalty of ₹50,000 to ₹3 lakh There is no imprisonment prescribed under this section for such default.

Question 4. A prospectus which does not include complete particulars of the quantum or price of the securities included therein is called: (a) A deemed Prospectus (b) A Shelf Prospectus (c) An Abridged Prospectus (d) A Red Herring Prospectus

(MTP Oct ‘21)

Answer: (d) A Red Herring Prospectus Reason: As per Section 32 of the Companies Act, 2013, a Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) is a prospectus that does not contain complete particulars of the quantum or price of the securities being offered. It is issued before the final prospectus and helps investors understand the offer while the final issue price and quantity are yet to be determined.

Question 5. Rig exploration and refinery limited (RERL) decided to raise capital through issue of a shelf prospectus. Company secretary explains the requirement to board that RERL shall be required to file an information memorandum with the Registrar within, prior to the issue of a second or subsequent offer of securities under the shelf prospectus. (a) 15 days (b) 21 days (c) 30 days (d) 1 month

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) 1 month Reason: As per Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013, when a company issues a Shelf Prospectus, it must file an Information Memorandum with the Registrar within 1 month prior to the issue of the second or subsequent offer of securities under the shelf prospectus.

Question 6. Modern Furniture decided to raise capital by issue for which prospectus need to be issued. Answer: (d) every director or proposed director Reason: As per Section 26 of the Companies Act, 2013, a copy of the prospectus filed with the Registrar must be signed by every person who is named therein as a director or proposed director of the company or by their duly authorized attorney.

Question 7. Which of following shall be considered as securities for purpose of section 23 of the Act; (i) Unit linked insurance policy (ii) Actionable claim regarding mortgaged debt (iii) Securities issued by National Asset Reconstruction Ltd (a) (iii) only (b) Both (i) and (iii) only (c) Both (ii) and (iii) only (d) none of the (i), (ii), and (iii)

(Practice question)

Answer: (c) Both (ii) and (iii) only Reason: For the purposes of Section 23 of the Companies Act, 2013, the definition of "securities" is taken from the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956. False (i) Unit Linked Insurance Policy (ULIP) is excluded from the definition of securities. True (ii) Security receipt / actionable claim relating to mortgaged debt issued by an Asset Reconstruction Company is treated as a security. True (iii) Securities issued by National Asset Reconstruction Ltd. (NARCL) are also considered securities.

Question 8. In case of variation in terms of contract or objects in prospectus, which of the followings statement are not true; (i) Ordinary resolution shall be passed at general meeting (ii) Notice given to shareholder shall also be published in two newspapers (iii) Amount so raised can be invested only in equity share of prescribed class of companies. (a) (i) only (b) Both (i) and (ii) only (c) Both (i) and (iii) only (d) Both (ii) and (iii) only

(Practice question)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 135

Question 9. When a copy of the contract for the payment of underwriting commission is required to be delivered to the Registrar: (a) Three days before the delivery of the prospectus for registration (b) At the time of delivery of the prospectus for registration (c) Three days after the delivery of the prospectus for registration (d) Five days after the delivery of the prospectus for registration

(MTP Oct ’20 & Sep ‘23)

Answer: (b) At the time of delivery of the prospectus for registration Reason: As per Section 40(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, where underwriting commission is payable, a copy of the contract for payment of such commission must be delivered to the Registrar along with the prospectus at the time of its registration.

Question 10. Which of the following statements is not true? (a) In case of shares, the rate of underwriting commission to be paid shall not exceed five percent of the issue price of the share. (b) Underwriting commission should not be more than the rate specified by the Article of Association. (c) In case of debentures, the rate of underwriting commission shall not exceed five percent of the issue price of the debentures. (d) Amount of commission may be paid out of profits of the company.

(MTP Oct 21)

Answer: (c) In case of debentures, the rate of underwriting commission shall not exceed five percent of the issue price of the debentures. Reason: As per Section 40(6) of the Companies Act, 2013: Underwriting commission on shares cannot exceed 5% of the issue price (or the rate authorized by the Articles, whichever is lower). Commission should not exceed the rate specified in the Articles of Association. Commission may be paid out of profits and/or securities premium account. For debentures, the maximum underwriting commission is 2.5%, not 5%.

Question 11. (Practice question)

Answer: (c) Shall refund all the monies received as subscription within fifteen days Reason: As per Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013 (Shelf Prospectus and Information Memorandum), if an applicant applies for securities before changes disclosed in the Information Memorandum come to his knowledge, he may withdraw the application within the prescribed time. In such a case, the company must refund the entire subscription amount within 15 days, without any deduction.

Question 12. The minimum amount of subscription in a public issue shall be received within days from the date of issue of prospectus. (a) 30 (b) 60 (c) 90 (d) 120

If the minimum subscription is not received within this period, the application money must be refunded.

Question 13. Dwapar Equipment Finance Limited, a non-banking finance company (NBFC), is desirous of offering secured, redeemable, non-convertible 9% Debentures to the public in three or more tranches over a certain period of time. Which kind of prospectus it is required to issue so that its purpose is served and there arises no need to take out a fresh prospectus for second and subsequent offer of securities. (a) Deemed Prospectus. (b) Shelf Prospectus. (c) Red Herring Prospectus. (d) Abridged prospectus.

(MTP Oct’19 & Oct ‘23)

Answer: (b) Shelf Prospectus Reason: As per Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013, a Shelf Prospectus may be issued by prescribed classes of companies, including eligible NBFCs, when they intend to offer securities in two or more issues/tranches over a period of time. Once a Shelf Prospectus is filed, there is no need to issue a fresh prospectus for second and subsequent offers, subject to filing an Information Memorandum.

Question 14. Part of the capital for which application have been received from the public and shares allotted to them: (a) Nominal capital (b) Issued capital (c) Subscribed capital (d) called up capital

Answer: (c) Subscribed capital Reason: Subscribed Capital is that part of the issued capital for which applications have been received from the public and shares have been allotted by the company. Question 15. The paid up share capital of ABC Ltd. (c) Company itself whose shareholding they want to offload. (d) Any competent officer of the company.

Answer: (c) Company itself whose shareholding they want to offload. Therefore, the promoters can authorize ABC Ltd. itself to act on their behalf for the offer of sale.

Question 17. Being in need of further capital, Rimsi Cotton-Silk Products Limited opted to offer 50.00 lacs equity shares of Rs. 1 each to 50 identified persons on ‘private placement’ basis and accordingly a letter of offer accompanied by serially numbered application form was sent to them after fulfillment of due formalities including passing of special resolution. One of the applicants, Rajan made a written complaint to the company highlighting the fact that the letter of offer was incomplete as well as illegal, for the same did not contain ‘renunciation clause’ though he wanted to exercise his ‘right of renunciation’ in favour of one of his son Uday. By choosing the correct option, advise the company in this matter. (a) As the ‘Right of Renunciation’ cannot be denied, the company needs to rectify its mistake by including the same in the letter of offer and the application form. (b) The company is prohibited from providing ‘Right of Renunciation’ and therefore, the letter of offer and the application form need not include any such clause. (c) Instead of absolute prohibition, the company needs to provide ‘Right of Renunciation’ limited to twenty five percent of offering. (d) Instead of absolute prohibition, the company needs to provide ‘Right of Renunciation’ limited to fifty percent of offering.

(MTP Oct’19)

Answer: (b) The company is prohibited from providing ‘Right of Renunciation’ and therefore, the letter of offer and the application form need not include any such clause Reason: As per Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 (Private Placement), the offer can be made only to the identified persons whose names are recorded by the company before the invitation is made. Therefore, the right of renunciation is not available in a private placement. The identified person cannot transfer or renounce the offer in favour of any other person.

Question 19. Delight Sports Garments Limited is contemplating to raise funds through issue of prospectus in which, according to the directors, a sum of Rs 50 crores should be stated as the minimum amount that needs to be subscribed by the prospective subscribers. The funds shall be raised in four instalments consisting of application, allotment, first call and second & final call. Advise the company by which instalment it should receive the minimum subscription stated in the prospectus. (a) Along with amount subscribed as application money. (b) Along with amount subscribed as final call money. (c) Along with amount subscribed as first call money. (d) Along with amount subscribed as second and final call money.

(RTP Nov-19)

Answer: (a) Along with amount subscribed as application money. Reason: As per Section 39 of the Companies Act, 2013, the minimum subscription stated in the prospectus must be received at the time of application itself, before the company can proceed with allotment of securities. Question 20. A Limited made a public issue of Debentures. The articles of the company authorises the payment of underwriting commission at 2 per cent of the issue price. The company has negotiated with the proposed underwriters, Gama Brokers and has finalised the rate at 2.25 per cent. The amount that the company is eligible to pay as underwriting commission is: (a) 5% (b) 2% (c) 2.5% (d) 2.25%

(RTP Nov 21) (MTP Sep ’23)

Answer: (b) 2% Reason: In this scenario, the company, A Limited, has authorized the payment of underwriting commission at 2% in its Articles of Association. However, the proposed underwriters, Gama Brokers, have negotiated a higher commission rate of 2.25%. The Companies Act, 2013 and the Articles of Association of the company govern the payment of underwriting commission. According to the Act, the company is eligible to pay underwriting commission at a rate specified in its Articles of Association, but not exceeding the rate approved by the members in a general meeting. In this case, the Articles of Association specify that the company can pay up to 2% of the issue price as underwriting commission. Therefore, even though the underwriters have agreed to a rate of 2.25%, the company is only eligible to pay a maximum of 2% under the provisions of the Articles of Association. Thus, the correct answer is 2%, and option (b) is the right choice.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 140

Question 21. The term ‘Public Offer’ does not include (a) Offer for sale (b) Initial Public Offer (c) Further Public Offer (d) preferential allotment

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) preferential allotment Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a "Public Offer" refers to the process of raising funds from the general public. It specifically includes Initial Public Offers (IPO), Further Public Offers (FPO), and an Offer for Sale (OFS) to the public. In contrast, a preferential allotment is considered a "Private Placement" because the shares are offered to a select, pre-identified group of people rather than the public at large. Therefore, it does not fall under the legal definition or procedural requirements of a Public Offer.

Question 22. Under section 25, unless contrary is proved, it is evidence that allotment of securities was made with a view to offer them for sale to public, if offer for sale to the public was made within (a) 30 days (b) 60 days (c) 6 months (d) 1 year

(PYQ Nov 2020)

Answer: (c) 6 months Reason: Under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 2013, a document is deemed a "Deemed Prospectus" if a company allots securities with the intent of offering them to the public. The law provides two specific conditions to prove this intent: first, if the offer for sale to the public is made within six months after the allotment or agreement to allot; or second, if the company has not received the full consideration for the securities at the date of the public offer. This ensures that intermediaries cannot be used to bypass formal public issue requirements.

Question 23. No prospectus shall be valid if it is issued more than\_\_\_\_days after the date on which a copy thereof is delivered to Registrar for registration. (a) 30 (b) 60 (c) 90 (d) 180

(RTP May 2023)

Answer: (c) 90 Reason: According to Section 26(8) of the Companies Act, 2013, a prospectus becomes invalid if it is not issued to the public within a specific timeframe after its registration. Specifically, no prospectus shall be valid if it is issued more than 90 days after the date on which a copy was delivered to the Registrar of Companies (RoC). This requirement ensures that the financial information and material facts contained in the prospectus remain current and relevant for potential investors at the time of the actual offer.

Question 24. A company can change terms of contract mentioned in prospectus by way of: (a) Ordinary resolution though postal ballot (b) Ordinary resolution in meeting ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 141

(c) Special resolution in meeting (d) Special resolution through postal ballot

(PYQ May 2018)

Answer: (d) Special resolution through postal ballot Reason: Under Section 27 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 7 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, a company cannot vary the terms of a contract or the objects for which the prospectus was issued unless it passes a Special Resolution. Furthermore, the law specifically mandates that this resolution must be passed through a postal ballot. This stringent requirement ensures that all shareholders, particularly those who may not be able to attend a physical meeting, have the opportunity to vote on significant changes that deviate from the original promises made during the fund-raising process

Question 25. Offer for sale is dealt by section (a) 28 (b) 29 (c) 30 (d) 31

(Study material)

Answer: (a) 28 Reason: Section 28 of the Companies Act, 2013, governs the "Offer of Sale of shares by certain members of a company." This section allows existing shareholders (such as promoters or large investors), in consultation with the Board of Directors, to offer their holdings to the public. Under this provision, the document used for the sale is treated as a deemed prospectus, and the selling members must reimburse the company for all expenses incurred during the process. While Section 25 deals with "Deemed Prospectus" in general, Section 28 specifically focuses on the mechanism where existing members sell their shares directly to the public through the company.

Question 26. The paid-up share capital of XYZ Ltd. is 50,00,000 shares of ₹ 200 each. 20% of its paid-up share capital is held by 4 of its promoters, who wants to off load their holding by making an offer of sale to the public by issuing a prospectus. They want to authorize someone to take all actions and complete all formalities related to such offer of sale. Form the following who can be Authorized by them to do so (a) Any person who has agreed to fulfil all the formalities related to such offer to sale (b) Any one or more director of the company (c) Company itself whose shareholding they want to offload. (d) Any competent officer of the company.

(MTP Oct 2021)

Answer: (c) Company itself whose shareholding they want to offload. Reason: According to Section 28 of the Companies Act, 2013, when certain shareholders (such as promoters) propose to offer their holding to the public through an Offer for Sale (OFS), they must consult the Board of Directors. The Act specifically provides that the members may authorize the company to take all necessary actions and complete all formalities related to the offer. Even though the shares belong to the individuals, the company acts as the vehicle for the public offer, and any expenses incurred by the company in this process must be reimbursed by the selling shareholders.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 142

Question 27. In case of offer of sale of shares by certain members of the company, which of the following options is applicable (a) The provisions relating to minimum subscription are not applicable (b) Entire minimum subscription amount is required to be received within three days of the opening date (c) 25% of the minimum subscription amount is required to be received on the opening date and the remaining 75% within three days thereafter (d) 50% of the minimum subscription is required to be received by the second day of the opening date and the remaining 50% within next three days after the second day

(RTP Nov 2021)

Answer: (a) The provisions relating to minimum subscription are not applicable Reason: An Offer for Sale (OFS) under Section 28 of the Companies Act, 2013, involves the sale of existing shares by current shareholders (like promoters) to the public, rather than the issuance of new shares by the company. Since the company’s capital remains unchanged and no new funds are being raised for company projects, the Minimum Subscription requirement (which ensures a company raises enough capital to commence its business) does not apply. The shares being sold are already fully paid-up, making the protective requirement of minimum subscription unnecessary for this specific type of transaction.

Question 28. Neptune Metal Tools Limited was incorporated on 2nd December, 2018 with twenty five subscribers and authorized capital of ₹ 50,00,000 (5,00,000 equity shares of ₹ 10 each). As the directors of the company are in a dilemma whether to issue physical share certificates to the subscribers or keep the shares in dematerialized form, they need to be advised correctly in this respect. (a) Being a unlisted company, Neptune may either issue physical share certificate to the subscribers or alternatively, issue them in dematerialized form. (b) Neptune needs to issue shares to the subscribers only in dematerialized form. (c) A company having more than 100 share holders needs to issue shares in dematerialized form and therefore. Neptune may issue physical share certificates to the subscribers (d) A company having authorized capital of ₹ Fifty lakhs and above needs to issue shares in dematerialized form and therefore. Neptune may issue physical share certificates to the subscribers

(RTP May 2022)

Answer: (b) Neptune needs to issue shares to the subscribers only in dematerialized form. Reason: As per Section 29 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 9A of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, every unlisted public company must issue its securities only in dematerialised form. Since Neptune Metal Tools Limited has 25 subscribers (exceeding the maximum of 7 for a public company but within the nature of an unlisted public entity), it is legally obligated to facilitate the dematerialisation of all its securities. The law mandates that any new issue of shares or even a transfer of existing shares by such companies cannot be processed in physical mode. Therefore, the directors have no choice but to issue the shares in demat form to comply with the current regulatory framework.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 143

Question 29. Russian Equipment Finance Limited, a non- banking finance company (NBFC), is desirous of offering secured, redeemable, non- convertible 9% Debentures to the public in three or more tranches over a search period of time. Which kind of prospectus it is required to issue so that its purpose is served and there arises no need to take out a fresh prospectus for second and subsequent offer of securities. (a) Deemed Prospectus (b) Shelf Prospectus (c) Red Herring Prospectus (d) Abridged prospectus

(PYQ 2019, study material)

Answer: (b) Shelf Prospectus Reason: Under Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013, a Shelf Prospectus is a specific type of prospectus that allows a company to issue securities in one or more tranches over a period of time without the need to file a fresh prospectus for each subsequent offer. This is particularly useful for entities like NBFCs that require frequent capital. The shelf prospectus remains valid for a period of one year from the date of the first opening of the offer. For every subsequent issue within that year, the company only needs to file an Information Memorandum (Form PAS-2) to update investors on material changes in its financial position or new charges created, effectively "taking the prospectus off the shelf" whenever needed.

Question 30. Shelf prospectus remains valid up to (a) 6 months (b) 1 year (c) 2 years (d) 5 years

(MTP 2020, Study material)

Answer: (b) 1 year Reason: Under Section 31(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a Shelf Prospectus is valid for a period of one year. This period commences from the date of the opening of the first offer of securities under that prospectus. Within this one-year window, the company can issue multiple tranches of securities without the need to file a fresh prospectus for each issue. This helps eligible companies (like NBFCs or public financial institutions) save on administrative costs and respond quickly to market changes. For every subsequent offer during this year, the company only needs to file an Information Memorandum to update investors on any material changes.

Question 31. A shelf prospectus field with the ROC shall remain valid for a period of (a) One year from the date of registration (b) One year from the date of closing of first issue (c) One year from the date of opening of first issue (d) Ninety days from the date on which a copy was delivered to ROC

(PYQ May 2019)

Answer: (c) One year from the date of opening of first issue Reason: According to Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013, the validity of a shelf prospectus is strictly defined as one year. This period starts specifically from the date of opening of the first offer of securities under that prospectus. During this tenure, the issuer is not required to file a fresh prospectus for subsequent offers of

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 144

securities. It is important to note that the countdown does not begin when the document is filed or when the first issue closes, but precisely when the first subscription window opens to the public.

Question 32. Extra Limited is a growing Company and requires additional funds for expansion from time to time. They are following the same process for making an offer to public and then issue those shares. This is very time and energy consuming for them. Kindly advise them if there is any way out. (a) During first offer they shall file prospectus with a validity on one year, so subsequent offer issued during the period of validity of that prospectus, no further prospectus is required. (b) During first offer they shall file prospectus with a validity on two years, so subsequent offer issued during the period of validity of that prospectus, no further prospectus is required. (c) During first offer they shall file shelf prospectus with a validity on one year, so subsequent offer issued during the period of validity of that prospectus, no further prospectus is required. (d) During first offer they shall file shelf prospectus with a validity on two years, so subsequent offer issued during the period of validity of that prospectus, no further prospectus is required.

(Study material)

Answer: (c) During first offer they shall file shelf prospectus with a validity on one year, so subsequent offer issued during the period of validity of that prospectus, no further prospectus is required. Reason: Under Section 31 of the Companies Act, 2013, companies that require frequent funding can save time and resources by filing a Shelf Prospectus. This document allows the issuer to make multiple offers of securities without filing a fresh prospectus for each stage, provided they are made within a validity period of one year from the date of the opening of the first offer. The company only needs to file an Information Memorandum (Form PAS-2) prior to the second and subsequent issues to update any material changes in the financial position or charges created. This mechanism effectively eliminates the repetitive and exhaustive process of registering a full prospectus for every new fund-raising round.

Question 33. A prospectus issued in the form of advertisement must state. (a) The objects for which the company has been formed (b) The liability of members (c) The amount of share capital of company (d) All of the above

(Study material)

Answer: (d) All of the above Reason: When a company issues a prospectus in the form of an advertisement, Section 30 of the Companies Act requires it to be a comprehensive disclosure for potential investors. It must include the objects clause to inform the public about the company's business goals, the liability of members to clarify the financial risks involved, and the share capital structure to show the company's financial scale. These details are mandatory to ensure transparency and protect investors from misleading information. Providing this data allows the public to make an informed decision regarding the company's stability and future prospects before investing their capital.

Question 34. Which of the following prospectus is filed in case of book-building issue?

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 145

(a) Deemed prospectus (b) Red-herring prospectus (c) Shelf prospectus (d) Abridged prospectus

(RTP Nov 2022)

Answer: (b) Red-herring prospectus Reason: A Red-herring prospectus is specifically used during the book-building process because it does not contain details regarding the final price or the exact number of shares being offered. Instead, it provides a price band, allowing the market to determine the actual price through investor bidding. Once the bidding process is complete and the price is "discovered," the final prospectus with the determined price and quantity is filed with the Registrar. This mechanism is essential for Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) where the company wants to gauge market demand before finalizing the issue price.

Question 35. Red-herring prospectus must be filed at least days prior to opening of the subscription list. (a) 3 (b) 10 (c) 15 (d) 30

(RTP Nov 2020)

Answer: (a) 3 Reason: According to Section 32(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company proposing to issue a Red-herring prospectus must file it with the Registrar of Companies (ROC) at least three days prior to the opening of the subscription list and the offer. This mandatory window ensures that the document is on public record and available for regulatory scrutiny before investors begin placing their bids. Since a Red-herring prospectus contains all financial and legal details except the final price and quantity of shares, this period allows the market to process the company's information. Filing it within this timeframe is a critical compliance step in the book-building process to maintain transparency and investor protection.

Question 36. A prospectus which does not include complete particulars of the quantum or price of the securities included therein is called: (a) A deemed Prospectus (b) A shelf Prospectus (c) An Abridged Prospectus (d) A Red Herring Prospectus

(Study material)

Answer: (d) A Red Herring Prospectus Reason: Under Section 32 of the Companies Act, 2013, a Red Herring Prospectus is defined as a prospectus that lacks specific details regarding the price of the securities offered or the quantum (total number) of securities being issued. It is typically used during a Book Building process to test market demand before the final price is determined. This document allows potential investors to evaluate the company's fundamentals while the final pricing and quantity are finalized just before the issue opens or closes.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 146

Question 37. PQR Limited decided to make an offer for purchase of securities. Application Forms for the purchase were issued to public. However, it was not accompanied by an abridged prospectus. For this default company is liable for penalty. How much penalty Company has to bear? (a) ₹ 25,000 (b) (c) ₹ 100,000 (d) ₹ 500,000

(MTP 2022)

Answer: (b) ₹ 50,000 Reason: According to Section 33 of the Companies Act, 2013, every application form issued for the purchase of any securities of a company must be accompanied by an abridged prospectus. This ensures that investors have access to essential information before investing. If a company defaults on this provision, it shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees (₹ 50,000) for each such default. This is a strict compliance requirement to protect investor interests and ensure transparency during a public offer.

Question 38. Which of the following persons are entitled to damages for mis-statement in prospectus? (a) Subscriber to securities (b) A person who bought securities from stock exchange after relaying on prospectus (c) A person who purchased shares from subscriber after relaying on prospectus (d) All of the above

(PYQ Nov 2019)

Answer: (a) Subscriber to securities Reason: Under Section 35 of the Companies Act, 2013, only a person who has subscribed for securities on the basis of a misleading prospectus is entitled to claim damages. Since a prospectus is an invitation to the public to subscribe to shares directly from the company, the liability for misstatement does not extend to subsequent buyers who purchase shares from the secondary market (stock exchange) or from existing shareholders.

Question 39. If a person makes multiple applications in different names; then which of the following statements are not true; (a) He shall be liable for action under section 447 (b) Above provision shall be prominently reproduced in prospectus (c) Court may also order disgorgement of gain (d) Disgorged gain will be transferred to Insolvency and Bankruptcy fund

(RTP May 2021)

Answer: (d) Disgorged gain will be transferred to Insolvency and Bankruptcy fund Reason: Under Section 38 of the Companies Act, 2013, if a person makes multiple applications for securities in different names (personation), the law mandates that any disgorged gain or sale proceeds of seized securities must be credited to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF), not the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Fund. Statements (a), (b), and (c) are all legally correct as per the Act, making (d) the only false statement.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 147

Question 40. As per Companies Act, 2013; the minimum subscription is (a) 50% (b) 80% (c) 90% (d) Amount stated in the prospectus

(Study material)

Answer: (d) Amount stated in the prospectus Reason: Under Section 39(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, "minimum subscription" is defined simply as the amount stated in the prospectus as being necessary to provide for the items specified therein. While SEBI regulations separately mandate a 90% threshold for public issues to be successful, the Companies Act itself leaves the specific amount to be determined and disclosed by the company in its prospectus.

Question 41. The minimum amount of subscription in a public issue shall be received within\_\_\_ days from the date of issue of prospectus. (a) 30 (b) 60 (c) 90 (d) 120

(MTP April 2022)

Answer: (a) 30 Reason: According to Section 39(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the minimum subscription amount must be received by the company within 30 days from the date of issue of the prospectus (or such other period as may be specified by SEBI). If this amount is not received within the prescribed time, the application money must be refunded to the applicants within 15 days from the closure of the issue to avoid interest penalties.

Question 42. If minimum subscription is not received within 30 days, the amount shall be returned within \_\_\_ days. (a) 10 (b) 15 (c) 30 (d) 45

(MTP April 2023)

Answer: (b) 15 Reason: As per Section 39(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 11 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, if the minimum subscription is not received within 30 days, the application money must be returned within 15 days from the closure of the issue. Failure to repay within this period makes the directors jointly and severally liable to repay the money with interest at the rate of 15% per annum.

Question 43. On which offer of securities, commission is permitted to be paid to any underwriter by the company. (a) When securities are offered on rights basis (b) When securities are offered in the form of bonus issue (c) When securities are offered on private placement basis (d) When securities are offered to the public for subscription ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 148

(Study material)

Answer: (d) When securities are offered to the public for subscription Reason: As per Section 40(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, a company is permitted to pay underwriting commission only when securities are offered to the public. Furthermore, Rule 13(e) explicitly states that no commission shall be paid to any underwriter on securities which are not offered to the public for subscription. This is because underwriting is intended to mitigate the risk of a public issue failing to meet minimum subscription requirements.

Question 44. The underwriting commission on shares must not exceed (a) 2% of the issue price (b) 2.5% of the issue price (c) 5% of the issue price (d) 5.5% of the issue price

(PYQ Nov 2020)

Answer: (c) 5% of the issue price Reason: According to Rule 13 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, the commission paid to underwriters for shares shall not exceed 5% of the price at which the shares are issued, or the rate authorized by the company's Articles of Association (AOA), whichever is less. This statutory cap ensures that the cost of raising capital remains reasonable and protects the company's funds.

Question 45. The underwriting commission on debenture must not exceed (a) 2% of the issue price (b) 2.5% of the issue price (c) 5% of the issue price (d) 5.5% of the issue price

(PYQ Jan 2021)

Answer: (b) 2.5% of the issue price Reason: According to Rule 13 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, the commission payable to underwriters in the case of debentures shall not exceed 2.5% of the price at which the debentures are issued, or the rate authorized by the Articles of Association (AOA), whichever is lower. This limit is strictly half of the maximum commission allowed for shares (5%).

Question 46. ABC Limited made a public issue of Debentures. The articles of the company authorizes the payment of underwriting commission at 2 percent of the issue price. The company has negotiated with the proposed underwriters, Gama Brokers and has finalized the rate at 2.5 percent. The amount that the company is eligible to pay as underwriting commission is: (a) 5% (b) 2% (c) 2.5% (d) 2.25%

(RTP Nov 2022)

Answer: (b) 2%

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 149

Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013, the underwriting commission for debentures cannot exceed 5% of the issue price or the rate authorized by the Articles of Association (AOA), whichever is lower. Since ABC Limited's AOA specifically limits the commission to 2%, the company cannot pay the negotiated rate of 2.5%, as the AOA's lower limit takes precedence over both the statutory maximum and private negotiations.

Question 47. Which of the following is not true? (a) In case of shares; the rate of underwriting commission to be paid shall not exceed five percent of the issue of the share. (b) Underwriting commission should not be more than the rate specified by the Article of Association. (c) In case of debentures; the rate of underwriting commission shall not exceed five percent of the issue price of the debentures. (d) Amount of commission may be paid out of profits of the company.

(MTP 2021)

Answer: (c) In case of debentures; the rate of underwriting commission shall not exceed five percent of the issue price of the debentures. Reason: This statement is false because, under the Companies Act, 2013, the maximum rate of underwriting commission for debentures is limited to 2.5% of the issue price. The 5% limit mentioned in the option applies specifically to the issue of shares, not debentures. All other options are correct as commission can be paid out of profits and must comply with the limits set by the company's Articles of Association.

Question 48. When a copy of the contract for the payment of underwriting commission is required to be delivered to Registrar: (a) Three days before the delivery of the prospectus for registration (b) At the time of delivery of the prospectus for registration (c) Three days after the delivery of the prospectus for registration (d) Five days after the delivery of the prospectus for registration

(Study material)

Answer: (b) At the time of delivery of the prospectus for registration Reason: According to the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, a copy of the underwriting contract must be delivered to the Registrar of Companies (ROC) simultaneously with the delivery of the prospectus for registration. This ensures transparency regarding the costs of the issue and confirms that the commission rates comply with the law and the company's Articles. Failure to file this contract at the time of registration is considered a non-compliance with the statutory requirements for a public issue.

Question 49. GDRs can be issued after passing (a) Ordinary Resolution (b) Special Resolution (c) Board resolution (d) Unanimous Resolution of board

(RTP May 2019)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 150

Answer: (b) Special Resolution Reason: Under Section 41 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with the Companies (Issue of Global Depository Receipts) Rules, a company must pass a Special Resolution at a general meeting of its shareholders to issue GDRs. This requirement ensures that existing shareholders approve the potential dilution of equity and the issuance of securities in a foreign market. Additionally, the Board of Directors must also approve the proposal before it is put to the shareholders.

Question 50. In case of GDR, the name of the\_\_\_\_is entered in the Registered of members. (a) Foreign Investors (b) Overseas Depository (c) Domestic Custodian Bank (d) Overseas Custodian Bank

(Study material)

Answer: (b) Overseas Depository Reason: According to the Companies (Issue of Global Depository Receipts) Rules, 2014, until the GDRs are actually redeemed or converted into underlying shares by the investors, the name of the Overseas Depository Bank is entered in the Register of Members of the company. The Depository acts as the "registered owner" of the shares, while the foreign investors hold the GDRs. The Domestic Custodian Bank simply holds the physical share certificates or electronic shares as an agent of the Overseas Depository but its name is not entered as the member.

Question 51. Offer of securities or invitation to subscribe securities under private placement shall be made to maximum \_\_\_ number of persons in the aggregate in a financial year. (a) 50 (b) 100 (c) 150 (d) 200

(PYQ Jan 2021)

Answer: (d) 200 Reason: Under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 14 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, a company can make a private placement to a maximum of 200 persons in the aggregate in a financial year. This limit excludes "Qualified Institutional Buyers" (QIBs) and employees offered securities under a scheme of employees' stock option. If a company exceeds this limit, the offering is treated as a public offer and must follow much stricter regulatory requirements.

Question 52. Innovation Limited intends to invite subscription to ₹ 1.10 crores equity shares of ₹ 10 each on private placement basis. The persons identified as potential subscribers are within the statutory limit and also include the two other categories to which such statutory limit is not applicable On such category is employees of the company who are offered equity shares under Employees ‘Stock Option Scheme, by choosing the correct option, name the other excluded category. (a) Quality Institutional Buyers (b) Qualified Institutional Buyers. (c) Qualification Institutional Buyers. (d) Qualified Investing Institutional Buyers

(RTP Nov 2021)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 151

Answer: (b) Qualified Institutional Buyers Reason: According to Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, the limit of 200 persons for a private placement does not include two specific groups: Employees (offered shares under an ESOP) and Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs). QIBs are professional investors, such as mutual funds or venture capital funds, who are deemed to possess the expertise to evaluate investments and therefore do not require the same regulatory protections as retail investors.

Question 53. In case of private placement, the value of offer per person shall not be less than (a) INR 10,000 of face value of securities (b) INR 20,000 of face value of securities (c) INR 30,000 of face value of securities (d) No minimum limit

(RTP May 2021)

Answer: (d) No minimum limit Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, there is currently no minimum investment amount or face value prescribed for an offer made to a single person under private placement. While an earlier version of the rules (Rule 14) required a minimum investment of INR 20,000, this requirement was deleted by the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Second Amendment Rules, 2018. Consequently, companies now have the flexibility to determine the offer value per person based on their specific funding requirements.

Question 54. Which of the following statement is contrary with the provisions of the Companies Act 2013? (a) A private company can make a private placement of its securities (b) Company has to pass a special resolution for private placement (c) Minimum offer per person should have Market Value of ₹ 20,000 (d) A public can company can make a private placement of its securities

(MTP 2022)

Answer: (c) Minimum offer per person should have Market Value of ₹ 20,000 Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013, statements (a), (b), and (d) are all legally valid: both private and public companies can make private placements, and a special resolution is a mandatory requirement. Statement (c) is contrary to the law because the original requirement for a minimum investment of ₹ 20,000 was based on the face value of securities, not the market value. Furthermore, even this "face value" requirement was officially removed by the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Second Amendment Rules, 2018, meaning there is currently no such minimum limit at all.

Question 55. Guru Govind Publishers Limited has received application money of ₹ 20,00,000 (2,00,000 equally shares of ₹ 10 each) on 10th October, 2019 from the applicants who applied for allotment of shares in response to a private placement offer of securities made by the company to them. Select the latest date by which the company must allot the shares against the application money so received (a) 9th November, 2019 (b) 24th November, 2019

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 152

(c) 9th December, 2019 (d) 8th January, 2020

(RTP Nov 2023)

Answer: (c) 9th December, 2019 Reason: According to Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company making a private placement must allot its securities within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application money. Since the money was received on 10th October, 2019, counting 60 days leads to 9th December, 2019 (21 days in October + 30 days in November

- 9 days in December). If the company fails to allot the shares within this period, it must repay the application

money to the subscribers within 15 days from the expiry of the sixty-day limit.

Question 56. XYZ Private Limited made private placement offer to identified people. It was clearly stated that such people have no right of renunciation. Company received shares application money within given period of time however could not allot shares within 60 days from receipt. Now it is duty of XYZ Private Limited to repay the share application money. Company will be liable to pay interest if they fail to do so. Within how many days Company has to repay the share application money to avoid interest payment? (a) 15 days (b) 30 days (c) 60 days (d) 90 days

(MTP Oct 2023)

Answer: (a) 15 days Reason: Under Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a company is unable to allot securities within 60 days of receiving the application money, it must repay that money to the subscribers within 15 days from the date of expiry of the 60-day period. If the company fails to repay the money within these 15 days, it becomes liable to pay interest at the rate of 12% per annum from the expiry of the 60th day. This dual-timeline ensures that companies act promptly to either finalize the allotment or return the investors' capital.

Question 57. If company fails to refund the application money within time in case of Private placement, then the company is liable to pay interest at the rate of (a) 10% (b) 12% (c) 15% (d) 18%

(PYQ Nov 2020)

Answer: (b) 12% Reason: Pursuant to Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a company fails to allot securities within 60 days and subsequently fails to repay the application money within the following 15 days, it is liable to repay that money with interest. The statutory interest rate is 12% per annum, calculated from the expiry of the sixtieth day. This interest serves as a penalty for the delay in returning the investors' funds after the allotment window has closed.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 153

Question 58.A public company sent private placement offer letter to 200 persons of its choice in march 20xx and allotted shares to them in April 20xx. Can it send private placement offer letter to 200 new people in May 20xx? (a) Yes (b) No (c) Yes with the permission of ROC (d) Yes with the permission of NCLT

(Study material)

Answer: (a) Yes Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company can make a private placement to a maximum of 200 persons in a single financial year. Since the first offer was made in March (the end of one financial year) and the second offer is made in May (the beginning of a new financial year), the limit resets. As long as each offer complies with the 200-person limit per financial year and follows the prescribed allotment procedures, the second offer is legally valid.

Question 59. Nitin Goel Limited raised ₹ 10 crore through private placement. The company wants to utilized these funds as soon as possible. Which of the following statements is true with respect to utilization of funds? (a) The company can utilize the funds immediately on receipt of application money. (b) The company shall not utilize the funds unless the allotment is made. (c) The company shall not utilize the funds unless the allotment is made and return of allotment is filed. (d) The company can utilize the funds after 30 days from the date of filing return of allotment.

(RTP Nov 2023)

Answer: (c) The company shall not utilize the funds unless the allotment is made and return of allotment is filed. Reason: According to Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is strictly prohibited from utilizing any money raised through a private placement until two conditions are met: the allotment of securities is completed and the Return of Allotment (Form PAS-3) is filed with the Registrar of Companies (ROC). This ensures that the legal process of issuing shares is officially recorded before the capital is touched. Until then, the money must remain in a separate bank account.

Question 60. Being in need of further capital, Rimisi Cotton – Silk Products Limited opted to offer 50.00 lacs equity shares of ₹ 1 each to 50 identified person on private placement basis and accordingly a letter of offer accompanied by serially numbered application form was sent to them after fulfillment of due formalities including passing of special resolution. One of the applicants, Rajan made a written complaint to the company highlighting the fact that the letter of offer was incomplete as well as illegal, for the same did not contain ‘renunciation clause’ through he wanted to exercise his ‘right of renunciation’ in favour of one of his son Uday. By choosing the correct option, advise the company in this matter. (a) As the ‘Right of Renunciation’ cannot be denied, the company needs to rectify its mistake by including the same in the letter of offer and the application. (b) The company is prohibited from providing ‘Right of Renunciation’ and therefore, the letter of offer and the application form need not include any such clause.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 154

(c) Instead of absolute prohibition, the company needs to provide ‘Right of Renunciation’ limited to twenty five percent of offering. (d) Instead of absolute prohibition, the company needs to provide ‘Right of Renunciation’ limited to fifty percent of offering.

(MTP 2022)

Answer: (b) The company is prohibited from providing ‘Right of Renunciation’ and therefore, the letter of offer and the application form need not include any such clause Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a Private Placement is an offer of securities to a specific, identified group of persons and is distinct from a Rights Issue. According to the provisions governing private placements, the offer is made specifically to the persons whose names are recorded by the company prior to the invitation; therefore, the Right of Renunciation does not apply. Since the offer is non-transferable and intended only for the identified persons, Rajan cannot renounce his shares in favor of his son, and the company is not legally required to include such a clause.

Chapter 4 Share Capital and Debentures

PART A

Question 1. Pride Pvt. Limited, a start-up by a few qualified professionals, was incorporated in 2018. The company is booming and favouring the younger generation to work. The Capital Structure of the company is as follows:

Particulars INR (Crore) Authorized Share Capital 1,00,00,000 Equity Shares of Rs 10 each 10 Issued, Subscribed and Paid-up Share Capital 50,00,000 Equity Shares of Rs 10 each 5 Share Premium 1 General Reserve 3.52 Profit & Loss Account 1.58 The company decided to issue 30% of its equity share capital as sweat equity shares to a class of directors and permanent employees with the objective of motivating them and making them partners in the company's growth. The proposed sweat equity shares will be subject to a lock-in period of five years. Accordingly, the company passed a resolution in its general meeting authorizing the issuance of 15 lakh sweat equity shares at a current market price of Rs 25 per share, to be issued for a consideration of Rs 5 per share to the identified class of directors and employees. In light of the above facts and in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, examine the following: (i) Whether size of issue of sweat equity shares was appropriate? (ii) Whether lock-in period was justifiable?

(6 marks|5 minutes)(RTP Sep 2025)(Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 1. Issue of Sweat Equity Shares: As per section 53, a company shall not issue shares at a discount, except as provided in section 54. Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013 states that sweat equity shares are issued to keep the employees of a company motivated by making them partner in the growth of the company. Section 54 mentions the provisions which need to be adhered to by a company if it desires to issue sweat equity shares.

Conditions: According to section 54(1), a company may issue sweat equity shares of a class of shares already issued, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely— (a) The issue is authorized by a special resolution passed by the company; (b) The resolution specifies the number of shares, the current market price, consideration, if any, and the class or classes of directors or employees to whom such equity shares are to be issued.

Limit on issue of Sweat Equity Shares: According to provision to Rule 8 (4) of the Companies (Share Capital & Debentures) Rules 2014, w.r.t a start-up company, it may issue sweat equity shares not exceeding fifty percent of its paid-up capital up to ten years from the date of its incorporation or registration.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 156

Lock-in Period: Rule 8(5) of the Companies (Share Capital & Debentures) Rules 2014, states that the sweat equity shares issued to directors or employees shall be locked in/non-transferable for a period of three years from the date of allotment.

Accordingly, in the given instance, (i) Size of issue of sweat equity shares was appropriate, as the decision of the company to issue 30% sweat equity shares to a class of directors and employees was within the prescribed limit of 50% (in case of start up company). Resolution containing 15 lakh sweat equity shares was also within the limit of 25 lakh sweat equity shares (i.e.,50% of paid-up capital) with the details as to the current market price and with the consideration to be issued.

(ii) No, as per law, lock-in period will be of three years from the date of allotment. Here, it states five years which is against the law.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Identify Sec. 54 and Rule 8. First check whether the company qualifies as a start-up, then verify the

percentage of sweat equity proposed and lock-in period.

2. Directly compare 30% issue with the 50% limit applicable to start-ups and quote the prescribed lock-in

period of 3 years.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often write 25% limit instead of 50% for start-ups and incorrectly accept a 5-year lock-in period.

Mention both points specifically.

Question 2. The Directors of Mars Motors India Ltd. desire to alter Capital Clause of the Memorandum of Association of their company. Advise them about the ways in which the said clause may be altered under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.

(5 marks|5 minutes)(Study Material)(Medium|ICAI Fav|high chance for exam)

Answer 2. Alteration of Capital: Under section 61 (1) a limited company having a share capital may, if authorized by its Articles, alter its Memorandum in its general meeting to: (i) Increase its authorized share capital by such amount as it thinks expedient;

(ii) Consolidate and divide all or any of its share capital into shares of a larger amount than its existing shares; However, no consolidation and division which results in changes in the voting percentage of shareholders shall take effect unless it is approved by the Tribunal on an application made in the prescribed manner.

(iii) Convert all or any of its paid- up shares into stock and reconvert that stock into fully paid shares of any denomination.

(iv) Sub-Divide its shares, or any of them, into shares of smaller amount than is fixed by the Memorandum;

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 157

(v) Cancel shares which, at the date of the passing of the resolution in that behalf, have not been taken or agreed to be taken by any person, and diminish the amount of its share capital by the amount of the shares so cancelled.

Further, under section 64 where a company alters its share capital in any of the above-mentioned ways, the company shall file a notice in the prescribed form with the Registrar within a period of thirty days of such alteration, along with an altered memorandum. The capital clause of memorandum, if authorized by the articles, shall be altered by passing an ordinary resolution as per Section 61 (1) of the Companies Act, 2013.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Begin with Sec. 61 and list all five methods of alteration of share capital. Conclude with ROC filing

requirement under Sec. 64.

2. Present the five alterations in bullet points rather than lengthy explanations.

Examiner Observations:

1. Many students mention only increase and reduction of capital and miss consolidation, subdivision,

conversion into stock and cancellation.

Question 3. Ramesh, a resident of New Delhi, sent a transfer deed duly signed by him as transferee and his brother Suresh as transferor, for registration of transfer of shares to Ryan Entertainment Private Limited at its Registered Office in Mumbai. He did not receive the transferred shares certificates even after the expiry of four months from the date of dispatch of transfer deed. He lodged a criminal complaint in the Court at New Delhi. Decide, under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, whether the Court at New Delhi is competent to act in the said matter?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material)(Medium|high chance for exam)

Answer 3. Jurisdiction of Court, now Tribunal under the Companies Act, 2013: According to Section 56 (4) of the Companies Act, 2013 every company, unless prohibited by any provision of law or of any order of court, Tribunal or other authority, shall deliver the certificates of all shares transferred within a period of one month from the date of receipt by the company of the instrument of transfer.

Further, as per Section 56 (6), where any default is made in complying with the provisions of subsections (1) to (5), the company and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees.

In this case, the jurisdiction binding on the company is that of the State in which the registered office of the company is situated i.e. Mumbai. Hence, the Court at Delhi is not competent to act in the matter.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Apply Sec. 56 and identify the location of the registered office. Jurisdiction depends upon the registered

office of the company.

2. Focus directly on the registered office being in Mumbai and conclude that Delhi Court lacks jurisdiction.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 158

Examiner Observations:

1. Students frequently discuss transfer procedure but fail to answer the jurisdiction issue asked in the

question.

Question 4. Due to insufficient profits, Silver Robotics Limited is unable to redeem its existing preference shares amounting to Rs. 10,00,000 (10,000 preference shares of Rs. 100 each) though as per the terms of issue they need to be redeemed within next two months. It did not, however, default in payment of dividend as and when it became due. What is the remedy available to the company in respect of outstanding preference shares as per the Companies Act, 2013?

(6 marks|5 minutes)(Study Material)(Medium|ICAI Fav|high chance for exam)

Answer 4. According to Section 55(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, where a company is not in a position to redeem any preference shares or to pay dividend, if any, on such shares in accordance with the terms of issue (such shares hereinafter referred to as unredeemed preference shares), it may—

- With the consent of the holders of three-fourths in value of such preference shares, and
- With the approval of the Tribunal on a petition made by it in this behalf,

issue further redeemable preference shares equal to the amount due, including the dividend thereon, in respect of the unredeemed preference shares, and on the issue of such further redeemable preference shares, the unredeemed preference shares shall be deemed to have been redeemed. Provided that the Tribunal shall, while giving approval under this sub-section, order the redemption forthwith of preference shares held by such persons who have not consented to the issue of further redeemable preference shares.

In view of the provisions of Section 55 (3), Silver Robotics Limited can initiate steps for the issue of further redeemable preference shares equal to the amount due i.e. Rs. 10,00,000. For this purpose, it shall obtain the consent of the holders of three-fourths in value of such preference shares and also seek approval of the Tribunal by making a petition. In case, there are certain preference shareholders who have not accorded their consent for the proposal of issuing further redeemable preference shares, the Tribunal may order the company to redeem forthwith such preference shares.

Accordingly, Silver Robotics Limited must be ready with sufficient funds for the redemption of preference shares held by those who have not consented. On the issue of such further redeemable preference shares by the company, the unredeemed preference shares shall be deemed to have been redeemed.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Apply Sec. 55(3). Mention consent of 3/4th preference shareholders and approval of Tribunal.
2. Remember the two mandatory conditions—3/4th consent and NCLT approval.

Examiner Observations:

1. Many answers mention only shareholder approval and forget Tribunal approval, resulting in loss of marks.

Question 5. Trisha Data Security Limited was incorporated on 1st August, 2019 with a paid- up share capital of Rs. 200 crores. Within such a small period of about one year in operation, it has earned sizeable profits and has topped the charts for its high employee-friendly environment. The company wants to issue sweat equity to its employees. A close friend of the CEO of the company has told him that the company cannot issue sweat equity shares as minimum 2 years have not elapsed since the time company commenced its business. The CEO of the company has approached you to advice about the essential conditions to be fulfilled before the issue of sweat equity shares especially since their company is just about a year old.

(5 marks|5 minutes)(Study Material)(Easy|ICAI Fav|high chance for exam)

Answer 5. Sweat equity shares of a class of shares already issued. According to section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company may issue sweat equity shares of a class of shares already issued, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely—

(i) The issue is authorized by a special resolution passed by the company;

(ii) The resolution specifies the number of shares, the current market price, consideration, if any, and the class or classes of directors or employees to whom such equity shares are to be issued;

(iii) where the equity shares of the company are listed on a recognised stock exchange, the sweat equity shares are issued in accordance with the regulations made by the Securities and Exchange Board in this behalf and if they are not so listed, the sweat equity shares are issued in accordance with such rules as prescribed under Rule 8 of the Companies (Share and Debentures) Rules, 2014,

The rights, limitations, restrictions and provisions as are for the time being applicable to equity shares shall be applicable to the sweat equity shares issued under Section 54 and the holders of such shares shall rank pari passu with other equity shareholders. Trisha Data Security Limited can issue Sweat equity shares by following the conditions as mentioned above. It does not make a difference that the company is just about a year old because no such minimum time limit of 2 years in operations is specified under Section 54.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. State Sec. 54 conditions and clarify that no minimum period of business operation is prescribed.
2. Write only the statutory conditions and directly reject the friend's view regarding 2 years.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students unnecessarily discuss commencement of business and confuse sweat equity with ESOP provisions.

Question 6. Walnut Foods Limited has an authorized share capital of 2,00,000 equity shares of Rs. 100 per share and an amount of Rs. 2 crores in its Securities Premium Account as on 31-3-2020. The Board of Directors seeks your advice about the application of securities premium account for its business purposes. Please give your advice.

(6 marks|5 minutes)(Study Material)(Medium|ICAI Fav|high chance for exam)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 160

Answer 6. Amount lying to the credit of Securities Premium Account is required to be utilised for certain prescribed purposes. According to section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013, where a company issues shares at a premium, whether for cash or otherwise, a sum equal to the aggregate amount of the premium received on those shares shall be transferred to a "securities premium account" and the provisions of this Act relating to reduction of share capital of a company shall, except as provided in this Section, apply as if the securities premium account were the paid-up share capital of the company.

The securities premium account may be applied by the company— (a) Towards the issue of unissued shares of the company to the members of the company as fully paid bonus shares;

(b) In writing off the preliminary expenses of the company;

(c) In writing off the expenses of, or the commission paid or discount allowed on, any issue of shares or debentures of the company;

(d) In providing for the premium payable on the redemption of any redeemable preference shares or of any debentures of the company; or

(e) For the purchase of its own shares or other securities under section 68. The securities premium account may be applied by such class of companies, as may be prescribed and whose financial statement comply with the accounting standards prescribed for such class of companies under section 133,—

(a) in paying up unissued equity shares of the company to be issued to members of the company as fully paid bonus shares; or

(b) In writing off the expenses of or the commission paid or discount allowed on any issue of equity shares of the company; or

(c) For the purchase of its own shares or other securities under section 68.

(d) Keeping the above points in view Walnut Foods Limited should proceed to utilised the amount of Securities Premium Account.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quote Sec. 52 and list all permissible uses of Securities Premium Account.
2. Memorize the five permitted uses and write them in points.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students frequently include payment of dividend or general business expenses, which are not permitted

uses.
