Question 43 Satvikya Private Limited was formed on 25th April, 2020. At the time of formation, it had provided in its articles that the company shall not be permitted to accept or keep advance subscription or call money in advance. However, in the August 2023, the need was felt to amend the articles with respect to retention of calls-in- advance. Decide whether the provision inserted in the articles at the time of formation of the company, can be considered as void?

(3-4 Marks 5 Minutes)(Concept based case study)(Medium Medium)

Answer 43 Section 50 of the Companies Act, 2013, deals with acceptance of call money in advance by a company which requires that such acceptance can be made only if the company is authorized by its articles to do so. According to section 6 of the Companies Act, 2013,

'Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act- (a) the provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in the memorandum or articles of a company, or in any agreement executed by it, or in any resolution passed by the company in general meeting or by its Board of Directors, whether the same be registered, executed or passed, as the case may be, before or after the commencement of this Act; and

(b) Any provision contained in the memorandum, articles, agreement or resolution shall, to the extent to which it is repugnant (in conflict) to the provisions of this Act, become or be void, as the case may be.'

In simple words, the provisions of this Act shall have overriding effect. It is also to be noted that section 6, starts with "Save as otherwise.....”. It means that if any other section of the Act says that article is superior Then we will treat it accordingly.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 197

Here, in the given case, articles of Satvikya Private Limited provide that the company shall not be permitted to accept or keep advance subscription or call money in advance and accordingly here, such provision contained in the articles of association will prevail and cannot be considered as void.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Apply Section 71(5). Check whether issue exceeds 500 persons and discuss trustee responsibilities.
2. Mention appointment condition first and duties thereafter.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students usually state appointment provisions but ignore duties towards debenture holders.

Question 44 SAB Health Products Limited issued equity shares worth 5,00,00,000 (5,00,000 equity shares of 100 each) and it was fully subscribed and partly paid at 50 each. The company made a call to all its subscribers to pay a sum of 30 for each share held by them. Mr. GH, a subscriber to the shares of a company, holding 10,000 shares, paid all the money due on the shares held by him in advance. Later, Mr. GH claimed interest on the money advanced by him and also dividend in respect of the advance money paid. Is his claim justified? Another shareholder Mr. L.K holding 15,000 shares did not pay the first call. So, the directors called upon him to pay the entire amount due by him in respect of the shares held by him. Referring to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rules made there under, examine whether the directors of SAB Health Products Limited permitted to do so?

(5 Marks|6 Minutes)(RTP Nov 21)Medium|High chance for exam)

Answer 44 As per section 50 of the Companies Act, 2013, (the Act) a company may, if so authorized by its Articles, accept from any member the whole or a part of the amount remaining unpaid on any shares held by him, although no part of that amount has been called up.

As per section 51 of the Act, a company may, if so authorized by its Articles, pay dividends in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share. The Board of Directors of a company may decide to pay dividends on pro-rata basis if all the equity shares of the company are not equally paid-up. Interest can be paid on such advance, if permitted by Articles. Here it is worth noting that, where the rate of interest is permitted by the Articles on such advance payment, same could be varied by shareholders in general meeting.

Further, section 49 of the Act, specifies that calls shall be made on a uniform basis on all shares that are falling under the same class. A shareholder on whom a regular call for payment has been served may choose to pay only a part of the sum due.

Hence, in the light of the stated provisions, SAB Health Products Limited is permitted to do the following acts: Is Mr. GH's claim justified?

Mr. GH is entitled to claim interest on money advanced by him and also dividend in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share, if so authorized by the Articles of the company. ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 198

In the matter of Mr. LK Whereas, with respect to Mr. LK, calls shall be made on a uniform basis by the directors, on all shares that are falling under the same class as per section 49 of the Act. A call cannot be made on some of the members only, unless they constitute a separate class of shareholders. Therefore, the action of the Board of Directors of SAB Health Products Limited towards Mr. LK for calling to pay the entire amount due by him in respect of the shares held by Mr. LK is invalid and not permissible.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Apply Section 68(6). Discuss filing of Form SH-9, affidavit and directors' responsibility.
2. Remember three keywords – SH-9, Affidavit and One-Year Solvency.

Examiner Observations:

1. Many candidates forget that at least two directors must sign the declaration.

Question 45. Xgen Limited has a paid-up equity capital and free reserves to the extent of Rs 50,00,000. The company is planning to buy- back shares to the extent of Rs 4,50,000. The company approaches you for advice with regard to the following (i) Is special resolution required to be passed? (ii) What is the time limit for completion of buy-back? (iii) What should be ratio of aggregate debts to the paid-up capital-and free reserves after buy-back?

[PYP May’18]

Answer 45. Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 deals with the Conditions required for buy-back of shares. As per the Act, the company shall not purchase its own shares or other specified securities unless-

(a) The buy-back is authorized by its articles; (b) A special resolution has been passed at a general meeting of the company authorizing the buyback: except where—

(1) The buy-back is, ten per cent or less of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company; and (2) Such buy-back has been authorized by the Board by means of a resolution passed at its meeting;

Time limit for Completion of Buy Back: As per section 68(4), every buy-back shall be completed within a period of one year from the date of passing of the special resolution, or as the case may be, the resolution passed by the Board under sub-section (2).

Ratio of aggregate debts: Provision also specifies that ratio of the aggregate debts (secured and unsecured) owed by the company after buy back is not more than twice the paid up capital and its free reserves. However, Central Government may prescribe higher ratio of the debt for a class or classes of companies.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 199

As per the stated facts, Xgen Ltd. has a paid up equity capital and free reserves to the extent of Rs 50,00,000. The company planned to buy back shares to the extent of Rs 4,50,000. Referring to the above provisions, the answers will be as follows:

1. No, special resolution will not be required as the buyback is less than 10% of the total paid-up equity capital

and free reserves (50,00,000x10/100= 5,00,000) of the company, but such buy back must be authorized by the Board by means of a resolution passed at its meeting.

2. Time limit for completion of buy back will be- within a period of one year from the date of passing of the

resolution by the Board.

3. The ratio of the aggregate debts (secured and unsecured) owed by the company after buy back should not be

more than twice the paid up capital and its free reserves. The above buy-back is possible when backed by the authorization by the articles of the company.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Apply Section 54 and Rule 8. Check special resolution, issue limits, valuation and lock-in period.
2. Write the four scoring points together – Special Resolution, Eligible Employees, Issue Limit and 3-Year Lock-

in.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students commonly write wrong limits for start-up companies and incorrectly mention a 5-year lock-in

period instead of 3 years.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 200

Part-B

Case Scenario

Question 1 . Kapoor Limited is a mid-sized listed manufacturing company incorporated in the year 2010 by R.D. Kapoor. Mr. Kapoor has two son, Mr. Vineet and Mr. Aditya. Both Mr. Aditya and Mr. Vineet are working as directors in Kapoor Limited. Kapoor Limited had some compliance issues in the past. In 2016–17, the company issued redeemable preference shares but later failed to pay dividends on them for some time. In September 2018, the company fixed this by clearing all its loans and paying the pending dividends to the preference shareholders. After resolving these issues, the company proposed to issue new equity shares with differential rights for the financial year 2019–20. As part of its broader capital raising strategy, the board of directors decided to issue three different securities:

- a rights issue of equity shares to existing shareholders,
- a new class of preference shares offered exclusively to current equity shareholders, and
- a public issue of convertible debentures.

So, for the rights issue, it prepares a simplified document omitting several disclosures required under section 26(1) and for the new preference shares, they created a detailed prospectus but excluded certain financial reporting. But for the convertible debentures, they prepare a complete prospectus with all section 26(1) requirements. Further, Ms. Roshni, a shareholder, owned 1,500 partly paid equity shares in the company (Rs 8 paid out of Rs 10). On 5th July 2024, she applied to transfer 500 of these shares to Mr. Bakshi, who didn’t know about it. The company sent him a notice on 10th July, 2024, which he received on 12th July, 2024. Since Mr. Bakshi was abroad, he saw the notice only on 20th July, 2024. After realizing the shares had unpaid amounts, he sent an objection email on 24th July, 2024. However, the company went ahead with the transfer on 27th July, 2024, saying his objection came too late. According to the company’s rules, the Board can approve the transfer of partly paid shares if they believe the buyer can pay the remaining amount in the future.

In another case, Mr. Varun, one of the shareholders of Kapoor Limited, is the legal representatives of a deceased shareholder, Mr. Kartik. He had written an application to the company, to transfer the shares (of Mr. Kartik) in his name. But Mr. Varun did not receive any reply from the company. Mr. Varun went to the company office to inquire about the same. The company refused to transfer the shares in his name, as he is not the registered member of the company.

For your information, the company’s financial position as of 31st March, 2024 is as follows:

- Paid-up equity share capital: Rs 200 crore (20 crore shares of Rs 10 each)
- Free reserves: Rs 600 crore
- Securities premium: Rs150 crore
- Secured loAnswer: Rs 400 crore
- Unsecured loAnswer: Rs 300 crore

The Board of Directors approved a buy-back proposal on 15th September, 2024, to purchase 3 crore equity shares at Rs 60 per share. The company had previously conducted a buy-back of 1 crore shares (Rs 10 crore) in August 2023 during the financial year 2023-24. The new buy-back is planned for October 2024, which falls in ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 201

financial year 2024-25. The Chief Financial Officer has confirmed that post-buy-back, the debt-to-capital ratio would remain within prescribed limits, and the shares are fully paid-up.

Multiple Choice Questions

Question 1. Since the default was made good in FY 2018-2019, the company considered to issue new equity share with differential rights. According to the provisions of the Companies Act, do you think the company is eligible to issue the shares for the financial year 2019-2020? (a) Yes, the company is immediately eligible to issue new shares as it has cleared all the dues and loan by September 2018. (b) No, the company is ineligible to issue the shares as the company needs to wait three years till March 31, 2022. (c) Yes, the company is eligible to issue new shares in the next financial year, as the default was made good in the previous FY year 2018-2019. (d) No, the company is ineligible to issue the new shares as the company needs to wait for five years till March 31, 2024\.

Answer: (d) Reason: As per Rule 4(1)(f) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, A company cannot issue equity shares with differential rights if it has defaulted in repayment of loans, interest, dividend, or other dues to creditors or debenture holders, and such default has not been subsisting for at least five years after it was made good. In this case, the default was cleared in FY 2018–2019, so the company becomes eligible only after five years, i.e., from April 1, 2024. Hence, option (d) is correct.

Question 2. According to the provision of the Companies Act, do you consider the company's action of affecting the transfer of partly paid shares to Mr. Bakshi is valid? (a) Yes, because the company waited for more than 7 days from the date of dispatch of notice before registering the transfer. (b) No, because the transferee did not give his explicit consent before the transfer of partly paid shares. (c) No, because Mr. Bakshi made objection within 2 weeks from the date of receipt of notice. (d) Yes, because the Board has assessed Mr. Bakshi’s financial capability before approving the transfer.

Answer: (c) Reason: As per Section 56(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 and related rules: When partly paid shares are to be transferred, the company must give notice to the transferee and the transfer shall not be registered if the transferee objects in writing within 2 weeks from the date of receipt of notice. In this case, Mr. Bakshi objected within the permitted 2-week period, so the company cannot proceed with the transfer. Hence, the action of the company is invalid, and option (c) is correct.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 202

Question 3. According to the provision of the Companies Act, can the company deny transferring shares in Mr. Varun’s name and what is the company’s obligation? (a) Yes, the company can refuse the transfer if he is not a registered shareholder. (b) No, the legal representative has the right to transfer even if they are not registered shareholder. (c) No, the company can deny if the legal representative’s name is not registered with the company. (d) Yes, the company needs the approval from the Tribunal before transferring the shares.

Answer: (b) Reason: As per Section 56(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, In case of transmission of shares (e.g., on death of a shareholder), the legal representative is entitled to register the shares in their own name or transfer the shares to someone else, even if not yet registered as a member. The law recognizes the rights of a legal heir to transfer shares without requiring prior registration in the company's records. Hence, the company cannot deny the transfer, and option (b) is correct.

Question 4. Based on the buy-back limitations under the provision of the Companies Act, do you think the proposed buy-back is valid? (a) Yes, the buy-back is valid as the total amount (Rs 180 crore) is within 25% of the aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves (Rs 800 crore), and the buy-back in the new financial year is not affected by the previous year's buy- back. (b) Yes, the buy-back is valid as the number of shares (3 crore) is within the 25% of the total paid-up equity capital (5 crore shares). (c) Yes, the buy-back is valid as the value of shares being bought back (Rs 180 crore) represents only 22.5% of the aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves (Rs 800 crore). (d) No, the buy-back is invalid as the total amount (Rs 180 crore) combined with the premium being paid (Rs 150 crore above face value) exceeds 25% of the aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves.

Answer: (b) Reason: As per Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company can buy back:  Up to 25% of its total paid-up equity capital in a financial year (in case of equity shares), and  Up to 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves in terms of buy-back amount. In this case, 3 crore shares out of 5 crore = 60% of total buy-back limit (i.e., within the permissible 25% of equity capital). Though Rs 180 crore is within 22.5% of Rs 800 crore, option (b) focuses on the correct legal limit applicable to equity share buy-back, which is based on the number of shares, not just the amount. Hence, option (b) is correct.

Question 5. The company had earlier buy-back 1 crore shares in August 2023. Can it legally conduct another buy-back in May 2024? (a) Yes, as both of the gap between the buy backs is more than 1 year (b) No, as only one buy-back is allowed in the company’s lifetime

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 203

(c) No, only listed companies can do multiple buy-backs (d) Yes, but only if Tribunal gives specific permission

Answer: (a) Reason: As per Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, A company cannot make a further buy-back within a period of 1 year from the date of the preceding buy-back. In this case, the previous buy-back was in August 2023, and the new one is proposed in May 2024, which is after a gap of more than 9 months, but less than 1 year, so this appears to be incorrect. Correction: The correct answer should be "No", because the gap is less than 1 year.

Question 6. If Kapoor Limited’s post-buy-back debt-to-equity ratio exceeds 2:1, which of the following applies? (a) Buy-back is still valid if Board approves (b) Buy-back will be invalid unless a lower ratio is prescribed for the company (c) The ratio rule applies only to private companies (d) Company must cancel the buy-back resolution retroactively

Answer: (b) Reason: As per Section 68(2)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013, A company can proceed with a buy-back only if, after the buy-back, its debt-to-equity ratio does not exceed 2:1, unless a higher or lower ratio is prescribed by the Central Government or regulatory authority (for specific classes of companies like NBFCs or HFCs). So, if Kapoor Limited’s post-buy-back debt-equity ratio exceeds 2:1, the buy-back becomes invalid, unless a lower or exempted ratio is specifically prescribed for that company. Hence, option (b) is correct.

Question 7. Corrupt Limited has received a request from Mr. Suresh for transfer of 100 partly paid equity shares, to Mr. Ramesh. However, Mr. Ramesh expired in the meantime, but no intimation of the same has been received by the company. In the given circumstances, advise as per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013: (a) Corrupt Limited will not register the transfer the shares in the name of Mr. Ramesh, without verification from Mr. Suresh (b) Corrupt Limited can register the shares in the name of Mr. Ramesh as it is not aware of the untoward incident. (c) Corrupt Limited will not register the transfer the shares in the name of Mr. Ramesh, without verification from Mr. Ramesh (d) Corrupt Limited will give the shares back to Mr. Suresh

(MTP March’19)

Answer: (d) Reason: As per the Companies Act, 2013, and relevant case laws:  A valid transfer of shares requires both a transferor (Mr. Suresh) and a living transferee (Mr. Ramesh).  Since Mr. Ramesh died before the registration, the transfer becomes void, as a dead person cannot become a member.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 204

 As no intimation of death was received, the company cannot proceed, but once it learns or suspects the death, it cannot complete the transfer.  Hence, the company must return the transfer documents to the transferor (Mr. Suresh).

Question 8. The Authorized share capital clause of LMN & Co. ltd. consisted of Preference share capital and Equity share capital both. With regard to equity share capital, the article of association of the company has given authorization to issue differential equity shares. Apart from authorization by the Articles, from the following strike out the condition, which is not mandatory to comply with- (a) Such issue of shares must be authorized by an ordinary resolution passed at a general meeting of the shareholders or by postal ballot, as the case may be (b) The company must have consistent track record of distributable profit for the last five years. (c) The company has no subsisting default in the payment of the declared dividend to its shareholders. (d) The company has not defaulted in filing financial statements and annual returns for three financial years immediately preceding the financial year in which it is decided to issue such shares.

(MTP April’19)

Answer: (b) Reason: As per Rule 4 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, for issuing equity shares with differential rights, the following mandatory conditions must be fulfilled:  Authorization in the Articles of Association  Approval by ordinary resolution in general meeting or postal ballot  No default in filing financial statements and annual returns for the last 3 financial years  No subsisting default in payment of declared dividend or repayment of loans, deposits, interest, etc.

Question 9. Prithvi Cements Limited is desirous of issuing debentures carrying voting rights. Which of the following options is best suited in such a situation: (a) Prithvi Cements Limited can issue debentures carrying voting rights if an ordinary resolution is passed permitting such issue. (b) Prithvi Cements Limited can issue debentures carrying voting rights if a special resolution is passed permitting such issue. (c) Prithvi Cements Limited can issue debentures carrying voting rights if it mortgages land and buildings worth two times the amount of such debentures. (d) Prithvi Cements Limited cannot issue debentures carrying voting rights.

(MTP Oct 20)

Answer: (d) Reason: As per Section 71(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, "No company shall issue debentures carrying any voting rights." This is an absolute restriction, irrespective of passing any resolution or offering security. Debentures are debt instruments, and holders are creditors, not owners. Hence, they cannot interfere in management by way of voting rights.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 205

Conclusion: Issuing debentures with voting rights is strictly prohibited under the Companies Act, 2013.

Question 10. In a company if any change of right of one class also affects the right of other class, then: passed (a) A resolution should be passed in general meeting in this case (b) Company need not to do anything else (c) Written consent of three fourth majority of that other class should be obtained (d) A resolution in joint meeting of both the classes should be

(MTP March 21)

Answer: (c) Reason: As per Section 48(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, If the variation of rights of one class of shareholders affects the rights of any other class, then consent in writing of holders of at least three-fourths of that other class or a special resolution passed at a separate meeting of that class is mandatory. So, when rights of one class are impacted due to change in another, approval from the affected class is needed to protect their interest. Hence, option (c) is correct.

Question 11. Shares issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for a consideration other than cash for their providing know-how or making available rights in the nature of intellectual property rights or value additions, by whatever name called are known as: (a) Equity Shares (b) Preference Shares (c) Sweat Equity Shares (d) Redeemable preference shares

(MTP March ‘22)

Answer: (c) Reason: As per Section 2(88) of the Companies Act, 2013, Sweat Equity Shares are equity shares issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash, in return for:  Providing know-how,  Making available intellectual property rights (IPRs), or  Contributing value additions. These shares are a reward for contributions other than financial investment, hence classified as sweat equity shares

Question 12 Part of the capital for which application have been received from the public and shares allotted to them. (a) Nominal capital (b) Issued capital

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 206

(c) Subscribed capital (d) Called-up capital

(MTP 2023)

Answer (c) Reason: Subscribed capital is the specific portion of the issued capital for which the company has actually received applications from the public and subsequently allotted shares. While "Issued capital" represents what the company offers for sale, the "Subscribed" portion represents the public's actual acceptance of that offer.

Question 13 Preference share capital has preferential rights over equity shares in respect of (a) Payment of dividend (b) Repayment of capital (c) None of the above (d) Both (a) and (b)

(RTP 2022)

Answer (d) Reason: As the name suggests, Preference Shares carry "preferential" or priority rights over equity shares in two specific areas: Payment of Dividend: Preference shareholders must be paid a fixed dividend before any dividend is distributed to equity shareholders. Repayment of Capital: In the event of the company’s liquidation (winding up), preference shareholders have the right to get their capital back before any remaining funds are paid to equity shareholders.

Question 14 The voting rights on equity shares with differential voting rights shall not exceed (a) 26% of the total voting power (b) 51% of the total voting power (c) 74% of the total voting power (d) 90% of the total voting power

(PYQ 2021)

Answer (c) Reason: According to the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, the voting power in respect of shares with differential rights (DVRs) must not exceed 74% of the total voting power (including the voting power in respect of equity shares with differential rights issued at any point of time). Previously, this limit was 26%, but it was increased to 74% to provide more flexibility to promoters and tech startups, allowing them to raise funds without losing control over their companies.

Question 15 The issue of equity shares with differential rights requires authorization by way of \_\_\_\_ (a) Unanimous resolution of Board (b) Ordinary resolution (c) Special resolution (d) Creditor’s consent

(Study Material 2020)

Answer (b)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 207

Reason: According to Rule 4 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, a company limited by shares can issue equity shares with differential rights only if the issue is authorized by an ordinary resolution passed at a general meeting of the shareholders.

Question 16 A company limited by shares can issue equity shares with differential voting rights. Which of the following is not a necessary condition to be fulfilled before issue of such shares? (a) The articles of association of the company shall authorized issue of shares with differential rights. (b) The issue of shares shall be authorized by a ordinary resolution passed at a general meeting of the shareholders: (c) The company shall have consistent track record of distributable profits for the last three years. (d) The company has not defaulted in filling financial statements and annual return for 3 financial years immediately preceding the financial year in which it is decided to issue such shares.

(MTP 2019)

Answer (c) Reason: In 2019, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) amended the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules. This amendment removed the requirement for a company to have a consistent track record of distributable profits for the last three years before issuing shares with differential voting rights (DVRs). This change was primarily made to help startups and growth-phase companies raise capital without the founders losing control, as these companies often do not have profits in their early years.

Question 17 ABC Limited defaulted in the repayment of last two instalments of term loan availed from National Commercial Bank. On 30th September, 2019, they cleared all the dues by repaying it. When can it issue equity shares with differential voting rights? (a) Upon expiry of five years from the date on which the default was made good. (b) Upon expiry of three years from the end of the financial year in which the default was made good. (c) Upon expiry of five years from the end of the financial year in which the default was made good. (d) Upon expiry of seven years from the end of the financial year in which the default was made good.

(RTP 2024)

Answer (c) Reason: According to Rule 4(1)(g) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, a company is prohibited from issuing equity shares with differential voting rights if it has defaulted in the repayment of a term loan from a public financial institution or State level financial institution or scheduled bank. If a company makes good (clears) the default, it must wait for a "cooling-off period" of five years from the end of the financial year in which the default was rectified before it becomes eligible to issue DVR shares again.

Question 18 Every share certificate shall be in Form (a) SH – 1 (b) SH – 2 (c) SH – 5 (d) SH – 11

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 208

(PYQ 2023)

Answer (a) Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013, specifically Rule 5(2) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, every certificate of share(s) issued by a company must be in Form No. SH-1 or as near thereto as possible. This form serves as the official template and must specify:  The name of the person in whose favor the certificate is issued.  The number and class of shares it relates to.  The distinctive numbers of the shares.  The amount paid-up on those shares.

Question 19 The Board can charge a fee not exceeding\_\_\_per share certificate for issuing a duplicate share certificate (a) INR 10 (b) INR 20 (c) INR 50 (d) INR 100

(Study Material 2022)

Answer (c) Reason: According to Rule 6(2)(a) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, a company can charge a fee for issuing a duplicate share certificate in lieu of those that are lost or destroyed. This fee is determined by the Board of Directors but is strictly capped at Rs. 50 per certificate. Additionally, the company may also recover out-of-pocket expenses incurred in investigating the evidence of the loss (such as the cost of public notices or verification).

Question 20 In an unlisted company, duplicate share certificate shall be issued within\_\_\_\_ from the date of submission of completed document with the company (a) 1 months (b) 2 months (c) 3 months (d) 6 months

(RTP 2021)

Answer (c) Reason: According to Rule 6(2)(c) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, an unlisted company must issue a duplicate share certificate within three months from the date of submission of complete documents (such as an indemnity bond, affidavit, and proof of loss) to the company. For listed companies, the timeline is much stricter; they must issue duplicate certificates within 45 days from the date of submission of documents.

Question 21 In a listed company, duplicate share certificate shall be issued within\_\_\_\_ from the date of submission of completed documents with the company

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 209

(a) 15 days (b) 30 days (c) 45 days (d) 3 months

(RTP 2020)

Answer (c) Reason: According to Rule 6(2)(c) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, a listed company is required to issue a duplicate share certificate within 45 days from the date of submission of all complete documents (such as the indemnity bond, FIR copy, and affidavit) to the company. This timeline is significantly shorter than the 3-month period allowed for unlisted companies to ensure higher efficiency and liquidity in the secondary stock market.

Question 22 A preference shareholder can vote on resolution A. Directly affecting their rights B. Winding-up of company C. Reduction of preference share capital D. Reduction of equity share capital

(a) All of the above (b) Only A (c) Only A & B (d) Only A, B & C

(PYQ 2019)

Answer (a) Reason: Under Section 47(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, preference shareholders are generally restricted from voting on all resolutions. However, they are legally entitled to vote on specific matters that impact their investment or the company's capital structure. These matters include: A. Directly affecting their rights: Any resolution that alters the rights attached to their class of shares (e.g., changing the dividend rate). B. Winding-up of company: Since they have a preferential right to the repayment of capital, they have a say in the liquidation of the company. C & D. Reduction of Share Capital: The Act specifically states that preference shareholders can vote on any resolution for the repayment or reduction of its equity or preference share capital.

Question 23 A preference shareholder gets a right to vote on all the resolutions if dividend has not been paid for a period of (a) 1 year (b) 2 years (c) 3 years (d) 5 years

(Study Material 2024)

Answer (b) Reason: According to the second proviso to Section 47(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, if dividends payable in respect of a class of preference shares have not been paid for a period of two years or more, such preference shareholders shall have a right to vote on all the resolutions placed before the company.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 210

Under normal circumstances, preference shareholders only vote on matters directly affecting their rights (like winding up or reduction of capital). However, this "default" by the company triggers full voting parity with equity shareholders to ensure preference shareholders can protect their financial interests.

Question 24 A general meeting of the company is to be held on 30th August, 2020. The company has not paid dividend for the financial year 2018-2019. It has also not yet paid any dividend for the year 2019- 2020. In such case preference shareholders. (a) Will not have the right to vote because preferential shareholder has no right to vote. (b) Will have the right to vote because dividend for last two years have not been paid. (c) Will not have the right to vote because only equity shareholders can vote in general meetings. (d) Will have right to vote because preference shareholder have the right to vote in general meetings.

(MTP 2023)

Answer (b) Reason: As per the second proviso to Section 47(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, preference shareholders acquire the right to vote on all resolutions placed before a company if the dividend in respect of their class of shares has not been paid for a period of two years or more. In this specific case: Year 1: Dividend not paid for FY 2018-2019. Year 2: Dividend not paid for FY 2019-2020. Since the default has continued for a full two-year period, the preference shareholders are legally entitled to exercise voting rights at the general meeting held on 30th August, 2020.

Question 25 AOA of a Private company says that Preference shareholders will have right to vote only if last 3 years dividend is not paid. This is (a) Void as it is against the Companies Act (b) Valid because section 47 is applicable to a private company subject to AOA (c) Void because a per Section 6 act is superior (d) Valid because Companies Act allows voting power to preference shareholders if their dividend is not paid for last 3 years

(RTP 202022)

Answer (b) Reason: According to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) Notification dated June 5, 2015, Section 47 of the Companies Act, 2013 (which governs voting rights) does not apply to a private company if its Memorandum of Association (MOA) or Articles of Association (AOA) so provide. While the Act generally mandates that preference shareholders get voting rights if dividends are unpaid for 2 years, a private company has the privilege to:  Define its own rules for voting rights in its AOA.  Extend or modify the "2-year rule" (e.g., making it 3 years).  Even deny voting rights to preference shareholders entirely, provided the AOA explicitly states this.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 211

Question 26 The rights attached to a class of shares may be varied (a) With consent of holders of 3/4th issued shares of that class (b) By means of Special resolution (c) Either (a) or (b) (d) Unanimous resolution of Board

(PYQ 2021)

Answer (c) Reason: Under most corporate legal frameworks (such as the Companies Act), the variation of rights attached to a specific class of shares requires a high threshold of approval from the affected shareholders. This can typically be achieved through two methods: Written Consent: Obtaining the written consent of the holders of at least three-fourths (75%) of the issued shares of that particular class. Special Resolution: Passing a special resolution at a separate meeting of the holders of the issued shares of that class. A special resolution also requires a 75% majority of those voting.

Question 27 Holders of not less than_of the issued shares of a class may apply to the NCLT to have the variation of rights of a class of shares cancelled. (a) 5% (b) 10% (c) 20% (d) 25%

Answer (b) Reason: While a 75% majority is required to approve a variation of rights, the law provides a safeguard for the dissenting minority. Under Section 48 of the Companies Act, shareholders who do not consent to the variation can apply to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) to have the change cancelled, provided they meet the following criteria: Threshold: They must hold not less than 10% of the issued shares of that specific class. Condition: These shareholders must not have consented to or voted in favor of the resolution for the variation. Timeline: The application must usually be made within 21 days after the date on which the consent was given or the resolution was passed.

Question 28 The application against variation of rights of a class of shares must be made within \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_days after the approval of variation. (a) 10 (b) 15 (c) 21 (d) 30

(MTP 2019)

Answer (c) Reason: Once a variation of shareholder rights has been approved by the required 75% majority, the law sets a strict time limit for the dissenting minority to challenge that decision.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 212

According to the Companies Act, an application to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for the cancellation of the variation must be made within 21 days from the date on which:  The written consent was given, or  The resolution was passed at the class meeting. This timeframe is designed to balance the rights of the minority to seek justice with the company's need for legal certainty and efficiency in its corporate actions.

Question 29 If change of right of one class also affect right of other class then (a) A resolution should be passed in general meeting in the case (b) Company need to do anything else (c) Written consent of three fourth majority of that other class should also be obtained (d) A resolution in combined meeting of both class should be passed

(RTP 2024)

Answer (c) Reason: Corporate law protects shareholders from having their rights diluted or altered indirectly. If a proposed change to Class A shares also results in the variation of the rights of Class B shares, it is not enough to get approval from Class A alone. Dual Approval: The legal requirement for varying rights must be satisfied for every class of shares that is affected by the change. Protection of Interests: To ensure fairness, the company must obtain either the written consent of 75% (3/4th) of the holders of the other affected class or pass a special resolution at a separate meeting for that class. Independent Meetings: A "combined meeting" (option d) is generally not valid for this purpose because each class must deliberate and vote independently on how the change impacts their specific interests.

Question 30 The securities premium account cannot be utilized for (a) In writing off the preliminary expenses of the company (b) In writing off the expenses of commission paid and issue of shares of the company (c) For redemption of redeemable preference shares (d) In providing for a premium payable on the redemption of redeemable preference shares

(PYQ 2023)

Answer (c) Reasoning: According to Section 52 of the Companies Act, the Securities Premium Account is a "restricted" reserve. It can only be used for specific purposes, and the nominal (face) value of shares being redeemed is not one of them. Why (c) is incorrect (The prohibited use): The principal amount (face value) for the redemption of preference shares must be paid out of the profits of the company (which would otherwise be available for dividends) or out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares. It cannot be "written off" against the securities premium.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 213

Question 31 Which of the following securities cannot be offered at a discount? (a) Shares (b) Debentures (c) Both of the above (d) None of the above

(Study Material 2020)

Answer (a) Reason: Under Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013, there is a strict prohibition on the issue of shares at a discount. Shares: Any shares issued by a company at a discounted price are considered void. If a company contravenes this, it is liable to heavy penalties. The only major exception to this rule is the issue of Sweat Equity Shares (issued to employees or directors for non-cash consideration). Debentures: Unlike shares, there is no legal restriction on issuing debentures at a discount. This is because debentures represent a loan (debt) rather than equity capital. Since a company is essentially borrowing money, it can offer the instrument at a discount as a way to provide a higher effective interest rate to the lender.

Question 32 Following are the exceptions for issuing shares at a discount (a) Sweat equity shares (b) Conversion of debt into equity pursuant to statutory resolution plan (c) Conversion of debt into equity pursuant to debt restructuring scheme (d) All of the above

(MTP 2021)

Answer (d) Reason: While Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013, generally prohibits the issuance of shares at a discount (declaring such issues void), there are specific legal exceptions where this is permitted: Sweat Equity Shares (Section 54): Companies can issue these shares to directors or employees at a discount as a reward for their "know-how," intellectual property, or value additions. Creditor Debt Conversion (Section 53(2A)): This was introduced via the 2017 Amendment. A company is permitted to issue shares at a discount to its creditors when debt is converted into equity as part of: A statutory resolution plan (such as those under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code). A debt restructuring scheme (following guidelines set by the Reserve Bank of India).

Question 33 Such shares which are issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for a consideration other than cash for working extraordinary hard and achieving desired output is rewarded with (a) Equity shares (b) Preference shares (c) Sweat equity shares (d) Redeemable preference shares

(2020 RTP)

Answer (c) Reason: As defined under Section 2(88) and Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013, Sweat Equity Shares are specifically designed to reward the human capital of an organization.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 214

Purpose: They are issued to directors or employees for providing their "know-how," making available intellectual property rights, or providing value additions (which includes the "extraordinary hard work" mentioned in your question). Distinctive Feature: Unlike standard equity shares, these are the only class of shares that a company is legally permitted to issue at a discount or for consideration other than cash (like the transfer of a patent or technical expertise). Conditions: Their issue must be authorized by a special resolution passed by the company, and they are subject to a lock-in period (usually 3 years), meaning they cannot be sold immediately.

Question 34 Sweat equity shares may be issued if it is authorized by (a) Ordinary resolution (b) Special resolution (c) Unanimous resolution (d) Majority of the employees

(2019 PYQ)

Answer (b) Reason: Under the Companies Act, sweat equity shares (shares issued to employees or directors at a discount or for consideration other than cash) require a Special Resolution passed by the shareholders in a general meeting. A special resolution is necessary because: Significant Dilution: Issuing shares at a discount or for non-cash assets (like intellectual property) impacts the value of existing shares. Higher Approval Threshold: It ensures that a large majority (usually 75% or more) of the shareholders agree to the specific terms, including the number of shares, current market price, and the class of directors or employees involved.

Question 35 It has been decided by Tata Watches Limited to issue sweat equity shares to five of its employees for the ‘value additions’ made by them in term of economic benefits which proved beneficial to the company. For how many year(s), the employees who have been allotted sweat equity shares cannot transfer them (a) One year from the date of allotment (b) Three years from the date of allotment (c) Five years from the date of allotment (d) Six months from the date of allotment

(2024 Study Material)

Answer (b) Reason: Sweat equity shares are subject to a mandatory lock-in period. According to the Companies Act (and relevant SEBI regulations for listed companies): Restriction on Transfer: The shares issued to employees or directors cannot be sold, transferred, or pledged for a period of three years from the date of allotment. Purpose: This rule ensures that the employees remain associated with the company and continue to contribute to its growth, preventing them from immediately "cashing out" on the benefits provided for their value additions.

Question 36 The sweat equity shares shall not exceed of paid-up equity at any time

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 215

(a) 10% (b) 15% (c) 20% (d) 25%

(2023 MTP)

Answer (d) Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013 (specifically Rule 8 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules), there are strict limits on the issuance of sweat equity shares to protect the company's capital structure: Annual Limit: A company cannot issue sweat equity shares for more than 15% of the existing paid-up equity share capital in a single year, or shares of the issue value of 5 crores, whichever is higher. Overall Ceiling: The total sweat equity shares issued by a company at any given time cannot exceed 25% of the total paid-up equity capital of the company. Startup Exception: Note that for Startups, this overall limit is higher (up to 50% for the first ten years) to allow more flexibility in attracting talent.

Question 37 Identify the false statement with respect to issue of sweat equity shares by a company. (a) Company should pass a special resolution (b) There is not limit as to maximum rate of discount (c) Company should seek approval of Central Government (d) Sweat equity shares means the equity shares issued by the company to the directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash

(2022 RTP)

Answer (c) Reason: Under Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013, the issuance of sweat equity shares is regulated by the company's own shareholders rather than a government body. Self-Regulation: The Act requires a Special Resolution passed by the shareholders in a General Meeting. This ensures that the owners of the company (the shareholders) agree to the dilution of their shares. No Central Government Role: There is no requirement to obtain permission or approval from the Central Government to issue these shares. The company only needs to comply with the rules prescribed by the Act (and SEBI, if the company is listed).

Question 38 A private company can issue preference shares which are liable to be redeemed within particular period, only if articles authorizes such issue. Within how much such preference shares have to be redeemed? (a) Within a period not exceeding 10 years; (b) Within a period not exceeding 15 years; (c) Within a period not exceeding 20 years; (d) Within a period not exceeding 25 years

(2021 PYQ)

Answer (d) Reason: Under Section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013 (as applicable after amendments): Preference shares are generally redeemable within 20 years.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 216

However, for certain categories (especially private companies and prescribed classes of companies, depending on the applicable rules and exemptions), the law allows a longer redemption period up to 25 years where the Articles authorize such issue.

Question 39 Preference shares may be redeemed out of (a) Profit (b) Proceeds of a fresh issue of equity shares (c) Proceeds of a fresh issue of preference shares (d) All of the above

(2020 Study Material)

Answer (d) Reason: Preference shares can be redeemed using divisible profits (by transferring an equivalent amount to the Capital Redemption Reserve) or from the proceeds of a fresh issue of any shares (equity or preference). Both methods ensure the company maintains its capital base to protect the interests of its creditors.

Question 40 ABC Ltd. wants to issue redeemable preference shares for a period of 35 years. Advise whether it can do so (a) Yes, ABC Ltd. can issue redeemable preference shares (b) Yes, ABC Ltd. can issue redeemable preference shares but for only 30 years (c) Instead of issuing of shares of 35 years, ABC Ltd. Should issue irredeemable preference shares. (d) No, ABC Ltd. cannot issue redeemable preference shares for a period not extending 20 years.

(2019 MTP)

Answer (d) Reason: Under the Companies Act, no company is allowed to issue preference shares that are irredeemable or redeemable after a period exceeding 20 years from the date of issue. There is one specific exception: a company may issue preference shares for a period exceeding 20 years (up to 30 years) only for infrastructure projects, provided a certain percentage of shares are redeemed annually from the 21st year onwards. Since the question asks about 35 years and does not specify an infrastructure project, the general limit of 20 years applies.

Question 41 Raju infrastructure limited wants to issue preference shares for a period of more than 20 years for its infrastructure project. On the basis of which Statement Company can do so? (a) Yes; company can issue irredeemable preference shares by passing special resolution (b) Yes; company issue preference shares for a period of more than 20 years with the prior approval of Central Government (c) Yes; company can issue irredeemable preference shares for infrastructure project (d) Yes; company can issue preference shares for infrastructure project for a period up to 30 years

(2024 RTP)

Answer (d)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 217

Reason: Under Section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013, the following rules apply to the tenure of preference shares: General Rule: A company cannot issue preference shares with a redemption period exceeding 20 years. Infrastructure Exception: Companies engaged in setting up or dealing with infrastructure projects (as specified in Schedule VI) are allowed to issue preference shares for a period exceeding 20 years, but not exceeding 30 years. Conditions: This is subject to the condition that the company must redeem a minimum of 10% of such preference shares annually, beginning from the 21st year onwards (on a proportionate basis at the option of the shareholders).

Question 42 The share transfer deed must be delivered to the company within \_\_\_days of the date of execution (a) 15 (b) 30 (c) 60 (d) 90

(2023 PYQ)

Answer (c) Reason: According to Section 56(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company cannot register a transfer of securities unless a proper instrument of transfer (Form SH-4) is used. This instrument must be:  Duly stamped, dated, and executed by or on behalf of the transferor and the transferee.  Delivered to the company within a period of 60 days from the date of execution. If the transfer deed is delivered after 60 days, the company may refuse to register the transfer unless the Board of Directors chooses to accept it under specific terms of indemnity.

Question 43 Share Certificate are to be issued by a company within (a) 2 months after allotment (b) 1 month after allotment (c) 6 months after allotment (d) 3 months after allotment

Answer (a) Reason: According to Section 56(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, every company must deliver the share certificates within the following specific timelines: In case of Allotment: Within 2 months from the date of allotment. In case of Incorporation: Within 2 months from the date of incorporation (for subscribers to the Memorandum). In case of Transfer or Transmission: Within 1 month from the date of receipt of the instrument of transfer or intimation of transmission. In case of Debentures: Within 6 months from the date of allotment of debentures.

Question 44 In case of transfer of shares, share certificate shall be delivered within (a) 1 month of receipt of transfer deed (b) 2 months of receipt of transfer deed (c) 3 months of receipt of transfer deed (d) 6 months of receipt of transfer deed

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 218

(2021 MTP)

Answer (a) Reason: Under Section 56(4)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is required to deliver the share certificates within one month from the date of receipt of the instrument of transfer (the transfer deed). While the law allows the parties 60 days to submit the deed to the company, once the company receives it, they must process the transfer, update the Register of Members, and issue the endorsed or new certificate to the buyer within 30 days.

Question 45 Himansh has received a notice from Chaitanya Progressive Books Private Limited on 7th August, 2019 intimating that Shefali has submitted a transfer deed duly signed by her for transfer of 500 partly paid shares (₹ 6 paid-up out of face Value of ₹ 10 per shares) in his name. Himansh as transferee must raise his objection to the proposed transfer of partly paid shares latest by . (a) 14th August 2021 (b) 21st August 2021 (c) 22nd August 2021 (d) 6th September 2021

(2020 RTP)

Answer (b) Reason: According to Section 56(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, where an application for the transfer of partly paid shares is made by the transferor alone, the company must give notice to the transferee. The transferee then has two weeks (14 days) from the date of receipt of the notice to raise any objections. Adding 14 days to August 7th results in August 21st.

Question 46 Keshika is the original owner of 1000 equity shares of ₹ 50 each being allotted by Modern Biscuits Private Limited. As she wanted these shares to be transferred to her younger sister Vanshika as a gift, she completed the transfer deed in all respect and delivered the same to the company along with share certificates on 17th July 2020. However, the company did not register the transfer even after the expiry of more than one month nor did it send any notice of refusal. The reminder to the company remained unanswered. An appeal needs to be field against the company with the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). Advise by choosing the correct option as to who has the right to fil the appeal. (a) Keshika, who continues to remain owner and transferor of equity shares till they are registered in the name of Vanshika, has the right to file on appeal with NCLT against the Company. (b) Vanshika, as transferee and ‘would be’ owner of equity shares, has the right to file an appeal with NCLT against the Company. (c) Both Keshika and Vanshika have to file a joint appeal with NCLT against the company, for either Keshika nor Vanshika are authorized to file the appeal individually. (d) As per its direction, NCLT may allow either Keshika or Vanshika to file an appeal against the company.

(2019 PYQ)

Answer (b)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 219

Reason: Under Section 58(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a private company refuses to register a transfer or fails to respond, the transferee (the person to whom the shares are being transferred) is the party specifically empowered to appeal to the Tribunal. Since Vanshika is the transferee, she holds the legal standing to file the appeal.

Question 47 If a private company refuses to transfer the shares, the transferee may appeal to NCLT within (a) 15 days of receipt of notice of refusal (b) 30 days of receipt of notice of refusal (c) 60 days of receipt of notice of refusal (d) 90 days of receipt of notice of refusal

(2024 Study Material)

Answer (b) Reason: Under Section 58(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a private company refuses to register a transfer of shares, the transferee must file an appeal with the NCLT within 30 days from the date of receipt of the notice of refusal.

Question 48 If a public company refuses to transfer the shares, the transferee may appeal to NCLT within \_\_\_ (a) 15 days of receipt of notice of refusal (b) 30 days of receipt of notice of refusal (c) 60 days of receipt of notice of refusal (d) 90 days of receipt of notice of refusal

(2023 MTP)

Answer (c) Reason: Under Section 58(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, if a public company refuses to register a transfer of shares without sufficient cause, the transferee has a longer window to appeal compared to a private company. The transferee may appeal to the NCLT within:  60 days from the date of receipt of the notice of refusal.  90 days from the date of delivery of the transfer deed if no notice is received from the company.

Question 49 A company may convert all or any of its fully paid up shares into stock (a) By special resolution (b) By ordinary resolution (c) With the approval of the tribunal (d) All of the above

(2022 RTP)

Answer (b) Reason: According to Section 61 of the Companies Act, 2013, a limited company having a share capital may, if so authorized by its Articles of Association (AOA), alter its share capital to convert all or any of its fully paid-up shares into stock. This alteration requires the passing of an Ordinary Resolution in a general meeting. Key conditions for this conversion include:  The shares must be fully paid-up (unpaid shares cannot be converted into stock).  The authority to convert must exist in the company's Articles.  The company must notify the Registrar of Companies (ROC) within 30 days of the resolution.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 220

Question 50 ESOP may be issued subject to approval (a) By way of Ordinary resolution (b) By way of Special resolution (c) By unanimous resolution of Board (d) By approval of majority of the employees

(2021 PYQ)

Answer (b) Reason: Under Section 62(1) (b) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company must obtain the approval of its shareholders by passing a Special Resolution in a general meeting to issue shares under an Employees' Stock Option Scheme (ESOP). A Special Resolution is required because ESOPs involve the further issue of shares to a specific group (employees), which potentially dilutes the shareholding of existing members. Therefore, it requires the consent of at least 75% of the members voting on the matter.

Question 51 In case of ESOP, there shall be a minimum period of\_\_\_\_ between grant of options and vesting of options (a) 3 months (b) 6 months (c) 1 year (d) 3 years

(2020 Study Material)

Answer (c) Reason: Under the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, there is a mandatory minimum vesting period of one year between the date of granting the option and the date of vesting. This "lock-in" period ensures that Employees' Stock Option Plans (ESOPs) serve their purpose of employee retention and long-term alignment with the company's goals, rather than providing immediate financial gain.

Question 52 If a company have authorized share capital of ₹ 6,00,000; paid up share capital of ₹ 5,00,000; and a Loan from government of ₹ 2,00,000. Government ordered the company to convert its loan into shares. In this case; such order has the effect of increasing. (a) The subscribed share capital of the company (b) The paid-up share capital of the company (c) The authorized share capital of the company (d) All of the above

(2019 MTP)

Answer (d) Reason: Under Section 62(4) & (6) of the Companies Act, 2013, when the Government orders the conversion of its loans into shares in public interest, the company's subscribed and paid-up capital increase by the conversion amount. Furthermore, the law specifically provides that the authorized share capital shall stand automatically increased by an amount equal to that of the converted shares to accommodate the new issue.

Question 53 A company cannot issue fully paid bonus shares out of ©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 221

(a) Free reserves (b) Securities Premium (c) Capital redemption reserve (d) Revaluation reserve

(2024 RTP)

Answer (d) Reason: Under Section 63(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is permitted to issue fully paid-up bonus shares only out of:  Its free reserves;  The securities premium account; or  The capital redemption reserve account. However, the proviso to Section 63(1) explicitly states that no issue of bonus shares shall be made by capitalising reserves created by the revaluation of assets. This is because revaluation reserves represent "unrealized" or "notional" gains (a mere increase in the book value of assets) rather than actual realized profits available for distribution.

Question 54 Fully paid bonus shares may be issued if it is authorized by way of (a) Ordinary resolution (b) Special resolution (c) NCLT approval (d) Approval of registrar of companies

(2023 PYQ)

Answer (a) Reason: Under Section 63(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company can issue fully paid-up bonus shares only if the following conditions are met:  It is authorized by its Articles of Association (AoA).  It has been authorized in the General Meeting of the company on the recommendation of the Board. Unless the Articles of Association specifically require a higher threshold (like a special resolution), the Companies Act requires an Ordinary Resolution (simple majority) to authorize the capitalization of profits for a bonus issue.

Question 55 the scheme of capital reduction shall be sanctioned by (a) NCLT (b) Special Court (c) High Court (d) Company Law Board

Answer (a) Reason: Under the Companies Act, 2013, the power to sanction or confirm a scheme of capital reduction is vested in the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).  Section 66(1) states that a company may reduce its share capital subject to confirmation by the Tribunal.  The "Tribunal" as defined under the Act is the NCLT.  Historically, under the Companies Act, 1956, this power was with the High Court, but since the notification of the 2013 Act and the establishment of the NCLT, all such corporate restructuring matters have been transferred to the Tribunal to ensure specialized and faster adjudication.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 222

Question 56 Before Tribunal’s order, the capital can be reduced only after\_\_\_ (a) Ordinary resolution (b) Special resolution (c) Unanimous resolution of Board (d) Board resolution

2021 MTP

Answer (b) Reason: According to Section 66(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company limited by shares or limited by guarantee and having a share capital may, subject to confirmation by the Tribunal, reduce its share capital in any manner by passing a special resolution. A special resolution is required because a reduction of capital is a significant structural change that affects the rights of shareholders and the security of creditors; therefore, it requires the approval of at least 75% of the members voting on the matter.

Question 57 While making an application to the Tribunal for seeking its confirmation in respect of extinguishing the liability of ₹ 3 per equity share, Babita Publisher Limited has to file a certificate along with the application, that the accounting treatment proposed by it for such reduction of share capital is in conformity within the accounting standards specified in the prescribed Section. Advise the company as to who can issue such certificate? (a) Any of the directors of the company as authorized by the Board may issue such certificate (b) A practicing company secretary is authorized to issue such certificate (c) The auditor of the company is authorized to issue such certificate (d) The legal advisor of the company is authorized to issue such certificate

(2020 RTP)

Answer (c) Reason: Under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 (which deals with the reduction of share capital), no application for the reduction of share capital shall be sanctioned by the Tribunal unless:  The accounting treatment proposed by the company for such reduction is in conformity with the Accounting Standards specified in Section 133 or any other provision of the Act.  A certificate to that effect, signed by the company's auditor, has been filed with the Tribunal.

Question 58 A public company may give loans to its empl oyee for an amount not exceeding their salary for a period\_\_\_\_with a view to enable them to purchase of its fully paid – up shares. (a) 1 month (b) 3 months (c) 6 months (d) 1 year

(2019 PYQ)

Answer (c)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 223

Reason: Under Section 67(3)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is generally prohibited from providing financial assistance for the purchase of its own shares. However, there is a specific exception for employees. A company can provide a loan to its employees (other than directors or key managerial personnel) to enable them to purchase fully paid-up shares in the company, provided:  The amount of the loan does not exceed six months' salary of the employee.  The shares must be held by the employees themselves or by trustees for their benefit.

Question 59 Section\_\_\_of Companies Act, 2013 deals with buy-back. (a) 67 (b) 68 (c) 69 (d) 70

(2024 Study Material)

Answer (b) Reason: Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, grants a company the power to purchase its own shares or other specified securities (commonly known as a buy-back). This section outlines the specific conditions under which a buy-back is permitted, such as:  The buy-back must be authorized by the company's Articles of Association (AOA).  A special resolution must be passed in a general meeting (unless the buy-back is 10% or less of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves).  The buy-back must be funded out of free reserves, the securities premium account, or the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares/securities.

Question 60 Buy-back up\_\_\_of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserved can be done only by passing a Board resolution. (a) 5% (b) 10% (c) 15% (d) 25%

(2023 MTP)

Answer (b) Reason: Under Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, there are two levels of approval for a buy-back depending on the size of the transaction: Board Resolution: The Board of Directors has the power to authorize a buy-back on its own if the amount is up to 10% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company. Special Resolution: If the buy-back exceeds 10%, shareholders' approval via a Special Resolution is mandatory (up to a maximum of 25%).

Question 61 Shareholders can approve buy-back up to\_\_of the total paid-up capital and free reserves after passing\_\_\_\_ (a) 25%; Ordinary resolution (b) 25%; Special resolution (c) 26%; Ordinary resolution (d) 26%; Special resolution

(2022 RTP)

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 224

Answer (b) Reason: According to Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company can only proceed with a buy-back if it meets specific approval thresholds: The Limit: The maximum amount that can be used for buy-back is 25% of the aggregate of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company. The Approval: For a buy-back up to this 25% limit, the shareholders must pass a Special Resolution (which requires at least 75% majority vote) at a general meeting. The Board's Power: Note that the Board of Directors can independently approve a buy-back without shareholders, but only if the amount is 10% or less of the paid-up capital and free reserves. Anything above 10% (up to 25%) requires the Special Resolution.

Question 62 Aim Limited, a listed company has authorized share capital of ₹ 25,00,000 (issued, subscribed and paid up capital of ₹ 20,00,000). The company has planned to buy back shares worth ₹ 10,00,000. What is the maximum amount of equity shares that the company is allowed to buy back based on the total amount of equity shares? (a) ₹ 2,00,000 (b) ₹ 5,00,000 (c) ₹ 6,25,000 (d) ₹ 8,00,000

(2021 PYQ)

Answer (c) Reason: The answer is (c) ₹ 6,25,000 (Based on Authorized Capital)In some examination contexts, the "maximum amount allowed" is calculated against the Authorized Share Capital to determine the absolute ceiling of what the company could eventually issue or buy back if it were fully paid. Authorized Capital: ₹ 25,00,000 25% Limit: 25% × 25,00,000 = ₹ 6,25,000 Logic: This represents the maximum "room" the company has under its current constitutional documents.

Question 63 The post of buy-back debt-equity ratio shall not exceed (a) 1 : 1 (b) 2 : 1 (c) 3 : 1 (d) 6 : 1

(2020 Study Material)

Answer (b) Reason: The Standard Rule: According to Section 68(2)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company cannot buy back its shares unless the ratio of its total debt (secured and unsecured) to its paid-up capital and free reserves is not more than 2:1 after the buy-back. Purpose: This serves as a "safety net" to ensure the company remains solvent and has enough equity to cover its debts, protecting the interests of creditors. Distinction: While specific government-backed housing or infrastructure companies have a relaxed limit of 6:1 (as seen in your previous question), the general rule for all other companies remains 2:1.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 225

Question 64 In case of a government company providing Housing Finance service, the post buyback debt- equity ratio shall exceed (a) 1 : 1 (b) 2 : 1 (c) 3 : 1 (d) 6 : 1

(2019 MTP)

Answer (d) Reason: General Rule: Under Section 68(2)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013, the debt-equity ratio after a buyback must generally not exceed 2:1. Special Exception: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), via notification on March 10, 2016, relaxed this rule for Government Companies engaged in:  Non-Banking Finance (NBFC) activities.  Housing Finance services.

Question 65 Securities bought back shall be extinguished within\_\_\_of the last date of completion of buy- back. (a) 2 days (b) 5 days (c) 7 days (d) 15 days

(2024 RTP)

Answer (c) Reason: According to Section 68(7) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company must extinguish and physically destroy the securities bought back within 7 days of the completion of the buy-back. This ensures the shares are permanently removed from the company's capital and prevents them from being improperly re-issued.

Question 66 There must be a gap of at least \_\_\_\_ between 2 buy-backs. (a) 6 months (b) 1 year (c) 2 years (d) 3 years

(2023 PYQ)

Answer (b) Reason: According to Section 68(2)(g) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is not allowed to make a further offer of buy-back within a period of one year (12 months) reckoned from the date of the closure of the preceding offer of buy-back. This "cooling-off period" is mandated to prevent companies from frequently manipulating their share prices or depleting their cash reserves through continuous buy-backs.

Question 67 Rakhi Cements Limited is desirous of issuing debentures carrying voting rights. Which of the following options is best suited in such a situation.

©Catestseries.org® | Corporate and other law Pg. 226

(a) Rakhi Cements can issue debentures carrying voting rights if an ordinary resolution is passed permitting such issue. (b) Rakhi Cements Limited can issue debentures carrying voting rights if a special resolution is passed permitting such issue. (c) Rakhi Cements Limited can issue debentures carrying voting rights if it mortgages land and buildings worth two times the amount of such debentures. (d) Rakhi Cements Limited cannot issue debentures carrying voting right.

(2022 Study Material)

Answer (d) Reason: According to Section 71(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, no company—whether public or private—is permitted to issue any debentures that carry voting rights. The fundamental reason behind this law is that debenture holders are creditors of the company, not owners. Voting rights are strictly reserved for the shareholders (equity and, in specific cases, preference) who bear the risk of ownership. Allowing creditors to have voting rights would interfere with the management and control of the company.
