Question 46. Explain the following in brief with reference to Companies Act 2013: (i) National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) (ii) Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Committee

(8 marks|7 minutes) (PYP, Nov 20)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 46. (i) National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) According to section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Central Government may, by notification, constitute the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) to provide for matters relating to accounting and auditing standards under this Act.

Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the NFRA shall—

(a) Make recommendations to the Central Government on the formulation and laying down of accounting and auditing policies and standards for adoption by companies or class of companies or their auditors, as the case may be;

(b) Monitor and enforce the compliance with accounting standards and auditing standards in such manner as may be prescribed;

(c) oversee the quality of service of the professions associated with ensuring compliance with such standards, and suggest measures required for improvement in quality of service and such other related matters as may be prescribed; and

(d) Perform such other functions relating to clauses (a), (b) and (c) as may be prescribed.

(ii) Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Committee:

According to section 135(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, every company having (1) net worth of rupees 500 crore or more, or

(2) Turnover of rupees 1000 crore or more or

(3) a net profit of rupees 5 crore or more during the immediately preceding financial year shall constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board consisting of three or more directors, out of which at least one director shall be an independent director. Provided that where a company is not required to appoint an independent director under subsection (4) of section 149, it shall have in its Corporate Social Responsibility Committee two or more directors.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 511 of 941

Duties of CSR Committee [Section 135(3)\]: The CSR Committee shall- (a) Formulate and recommend to the Board, a CSR Policy which shall indicate the activities to be undertaken by the company in areas or subject, specified in Schedule VII; (b) Recommend the amount of expenditure to be incurred on the activities referred to in clause (a); and (c) Monitor the CSR Policy of the company from time to time.

Therefore, the company did not filed its financial statements to the Registrar, Afterwards, on receipt of CAG comments on the accounts, the adjourned annual general meeting was held on 5th October, 2022 whereat the accounts were adopted. Thereafter, Moon Ltd. filed its financial statements relevant to the financial year 2021-22 with the Registrar of Companies on 25th October, 2022. According to second provision to section 137(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, financial statements adopted in the adjourned AGM shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the date of such adjourned AGM with such fees or such additional fees as may be prescribed.

th In the instant case, the accounts of Moon Ltd. were adopted at the adjourned AGM held on 5 October, 2022 and filing of financial statements with Registrar was done on 25th October, 2022 i.e. within 30 days of the date of adjourned AGM. However, Moon Ltd. has not filed its unadopted

financial statements within 30 days of the date of the Annual General Meeting held on 31st August 2022\.

Hence, Moon Ltd. has not complied with the statutory requirement regarding filing of unadopted accounts with the Registrar, but has certainly complied with the provisions by filing of adopted accounts within the due date with the Registrar.

Question 48. Define the term ‘Books of Account’ as per the Companies Act, 2013.

(3 marks | 3 minutes) (Study Material) (Easy | ICAI Fav)

Answer 48: As per Section 2(13) of the Companies Act, 2013 (no amendment to this definition till date), “Books of account” includes records maintained in respect of—

(a) All sums of money received and expended by the company and the matters in respect of which the receipt and expenditure take place;

(b) all sales and purchases of goods and services by the company;

(c) The assets and liabilities of the company; and

(d) The items of cost as may be prescribed under Section 148 in the case of a company which belongs to any class of companies specified under that section (i.e., companies required to maintain cost records as notified under Section 148).

Key Explanatory Points (for better understanding and exam presentation):  The definition is inclusive and not exhaustive — it covers all records necessary to give a true

and fair view of the state of affairs of the company.  It includes books like cash book, ledger, journal, sales register, purchase register, stock register,

fixed assets register, cost records (where applicable), vouchers, invoices, bank statements, etc.  Form of maintenance — As per Section 128, books of account and other relevant books and

papers may be kept in physical form or in electronic form or in any other form capable of being reproduced in physical/electronic form (Rule 3 of Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014).

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 513 of 941

 Place of maintenance — Normally at the registered office. If maintained at any other place in

India, the Board must decide by resolution and inform the Registrar within 7 days (Section 128(1)).  Preservation period — Books of account and other relevant papers must be preserved for a

minimum period of 8 financial years immediately preceding the current financial year (Section 128(5)).  In case of branch office — Proper books of account relating to the transactions effected at the

branch must also be maintained (Section 128(2)).  Conclusion: The definition under Section 2(13) ensures that all financial transactions and positions of the company are properly recorded, enabling accurate preparation of financial statements, statutory audit, and compliance with various provisions of the Companies Act, 2013

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize CSR Committee functions separately from composition.
2. State responsibilities of CSR Committee.
3. Mention Board's role thereafter.

Examiner Observations:

1. Functions and duties are frequently interchanged.

Question 49. Sanjana joined a company named as Designers Cloths Ltd. as an Independent Director. In order to know more about the company, she wanted to inspect the books of account and minutes books of the Board Meetings held during the previous three years. The company is keeping the books of account and other records at its Registered Office, which is at Mumbai whereas Sanjana resides in Kolkata. Therefore, through power of attorney, Sanjana Authorized her friend Avantika, who is a Chartered Accountant and does practice in Mumbai, to make an inspection of the books of accounts and minutes books of the meetings of the Board. Giving the relevant provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and its Rules made thereunder, examine, whether Avantika can make inspection on behalf of Sanjana.

(5 marks | 5 minutes) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 49: As per Section 128(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. The books of account and other books and papers maintained by the company within India shall be open for inspection at the registered office of the company or at such other place in India by any director during business hours, and in the case of financial information, if any, maintained outside the country, copies of such financial information shall be maintained and produced for inspection by any director subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

Provided that the inspection in respect of any subsidiary company of the company shall be done only by the person Authorized in this behalf by a resolution of the Board of Directors. Further, as per Rule 4(4) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 (as amended, including amendments up to 2022 and no further change thereafter):

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 514 of 941

The financial information required under sub-rules (2) and (3) [relating to financial information maintained outside India] shall be sought for by the director himself and not by or through his power of attorney holder or agent or representative.

Key Analysis:

 The right of inspection under Section 128(3) is granted personally to any director (including

an Independent Director).

 The books of account and other books and papers (which include minutes books of Board

Meetings, as they form part of the company's records and are relevant books/papers) are maintained within India (at the Registered Office in Mumbai).

 There is no express prohibition in Section 128(3) against inspection through an Authorized

agent or power of attorney holder for books maintained within India. However, judicial precedents under the corresponding Section 209 of the Companies Act, 1956 (and followed in interpretations of the 2013 Act) have held that a director may inspect personally or through an agent (such as an expert or professional), provided the agent undertakes not to disclose the information to anyone except the director (principal) and there is no reasonable objection to the agent chosen.

 However, the restriction in Rule 4(4) explicitly prohibits seeking financial information (for

cases involving records outside India) through a power of attorney holder, agent, or representative — this applies only to financial information maintained outside India.

In the given case:

 The records (books of account and minutes books of Board Meetings for the previous three

years) are maintained within India at the Registered Office in Mumbai.  Sanjana, as an Independent Director, has the statutory right to inspect them personally

during business hours.  The restriction under Rule 4(4) does not apply here, as no financial information is

maintained outside India.  Therefore, Sanjana can authorise Avantika (her friend, a practising Chartered Accountant in

Mumbai) to inspect on her behalf through a power of attorney, subject to Avantika giving an undertaking of confidentiality (i.e., not to disclose the information to any third party except Sanjana) and there being no reasonable objection from the company to the agent chosen.

Conclusion: Yes, Avantika can make the inspection on behalf of Sanjana. The company cannot refuse inspection merely on the ground that it is through an Authorized agent/power of attorney holder, as the prohibition under Rule 4(4) is limited to financial information maintained outside India. Sanjana should ensure that the power of attorney clearly specifies the purpose (inspection only) and Avantika provides the necessary confidentiality undertaking. If the company refuses, Sanjana may approach the appropriate authority (e.g., NCLT) for enforcement of her statutory right.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Write CSR spending formula first.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 515 of 941

2. Calculate average net profit of preceding 3 years.
3. Apply 8-year restriction.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students take current year profit instead of average of preceding three years.

Question 50. XYZ Ltd. uses an Accounting Software for recording its financial transactions. The statutory auditor of the company while auditing finds the following issues: Some journal entries were altered without creating edit logs for all such changes. The audit trail feature was disabled for certain modules (e.g., inventory adjustments, inter-company transactions). Keeping in view of the above issue, advise the company on the followings: (i) Audit trail and Edit Log requirements (ii) The back-up of books of accounts.

(6 marks | 5 minutes) (Question Bank) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 50: As per the second proviso to Section 128(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, every company may keep its books of account and other relevant papers in electronic mode in the manner prescribed under Rule 3 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014. Rule 3 provides the detailed manner for maintenance of books of account in electronic mode, including accessibility in India, proper systems for storage/retrieval, and specific compliances for companies using accounting software.

(i) Audit Trail and Edit Log Requirements As per the proviso to Rule 3(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 (inserted vide Companies (Accounts) Amendment Rules, 2021 dated 24.03.2021 and made effective from 1st April, 2023 after deferment): For the financial year commencing on or after the 1st day of April, 2023, every company which uses accounting software for maintaining its books of account shall use only such accounting software which has a feature of —

 Recording an audit trail of each and every transaction;  Creating an edit log of each change made in the books of account along with the date when

such changes were made; and  Ensuring that the audit trail cannot be disabled.

This requirement applies to all companies (including private, public, small, OPC, etc.) using accounting software for books of account maintenance. The purpose is to ensure tamper-proof recording of transactions and changes, enhancing transparency, preventing fraud, and aiding audits.

Additionally, under Rule 11(g) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, the statutory auditor is required to report in the audit report whether the company has used such software with the required audit trail feature, whether it was operational throughout the year for all transactions, and whether the audit trail has been preserved as per statutory requirements. In the given case:

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 516 of 941

 Journal entries were altered without creating edit logs for all changes.  The audit trail feature was disabled for certain modules (e.g., inventory adjustments, inter-

company transactions). Conclusion/Advice to XYZ Ltd.: XYZ Ltd. is not in compliance with the mandatory provisions of the proviso to Rule 3(1). The company must immediately switch to or configure its accounting software to ensure:

 Full activation of the audit trail feature across all modules and transactions.  Creation of edit logs for every change (including date, user, and details).  The audit trail feature is made non-disable able (permanently enabled and tamper-proof).

Non-compliance may lead to adverse audit qualifications, penalties under Section 128(6) (fine of ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh on responsible officers), and potential regulatory action. The company should also ensure preservation of audit trails for at least 8 years (as per Section 128(5) for books of account).

(ii) The Back-up of Books of Accounts As per the proviso to sub-rule (5) of Rule 3 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 (as amended vide Companies (Accounts) Fourth Amendment Rules, 2022 dated 05.08.2022, effective from the date of publication):

The back-up of the books of account and other books and papers of the company maintained in electronic mode (including at a place outside India, if any) shall be kept in servers physically located in India on a daily basis.

This is in addition to the general requirement under Rule 3(1) that electronic books remain accessible in India at all times.

In the given case: The statutory auditor has highlighted issues related to electronic maintenance (audit trail/edit log), implying the books are maintained electronically. The company must comply with this daily back-up mandate to ensure data integrity, disaster recovery, and compliance.

Conclusion/Advice to XYZ Ltd.: XYZ Ltd. must establish a proper system to take daily back-ups of all electronic books of account and relevant papers on servers physically located in India. This is mandatory even if primary storage is on cloud/servers outside India. Failure to do so may result in non-compliance findings in audit reports and penalties under Section 128(6). The company should document the back-up policy, frequency, and location for audit verification.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use heading "Unspent CSR Amount".
2. Determine whether project is ongoing or not.
3. Apply transfer requirements accordingly.

1. Students confuse ongoing project provisions with normal CSR expenditure.

Question 51. BBQ Ltd., with its registered office in Hyderabad, has two branch offices, one located in Delhi and the other in London. The accounting transactions of branches are recorded and all books of account are maintained in the branches. The branch accountant of the Delhi branch sent monthly and the branch accountant of London sent quarterly summarized trial balance, profits and loss account and balance sheet to the Hyderabad office. One of the assistants of the audit team, Mr. Naveen, raised the issue that BBQ Ltd. maintain its books and records at branches, so it defaults on not maintaining the proper books of account at the registered office. Mr. Naveen further objected to the fact that the London branch sent their summarised returns on a quarterly basis instead of a monthly basis. You are requested to analyse and decide the validity of both the objections of Mr. Naveen relating to the place of maintaining the books of account and sending summarised returns.

(6 marks | 5 minutes) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 51: As per Section 128(1) of the Companies Act, 2013: Every company shall prepare and keep at its registered office books of account and other relevant books and papers and financial statement for every financial year which give a true and fair view of the state of the affairs of the company, including that of its branch office or offices, if any, and explain the transactions effected both at the registered office and its branches and such books shall be kept on accrual basis and according to the double entry system of accounting.

Provided that all or any of the books of account aforesaid and other relevant papers may be kept at such other place in India as the Board of Directors may decide and where such a decision is taken, the company shall, within seven days thereof, file with the Registrar a notice in writing giving the full address of that other place (in Form AOC-5).

Provided further that the company may keep such books of account or other relevant papers in electronic mode in such manner as may be prescribed (under Rule 3 of Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014).

As per Section 128(2) of the Companies Act, 2013: Where a company has a branch office in India or outside India, it shall be deemed to have complied with the provisions of sub-section (1), if proper books of account relating to the transactions effected at the branch office are kept at that office and proper summarised returns periodically are sent by the branch office to the company at its registered office or the other place referred to in sub- section (1).

Further, as per Rule 4(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 (no material amendment to this provision as of January 2026):

The summarised returns of the books of account of the company kept and maintained outside India shall be sent to the registered office at quarterly intervals, which shall be kept and maintained at the registered office of the company and kept open to directors for inspection. Key Analysis:

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 518 of 941

 Place of Maintenance of Books of Account: The primary requirement under Section 128(1)

is to maintain books at the registered office. However, Section 128(2) provides a specific deeming provision for branches (whether in India or abroad), allowing the books relating to branch transactions to be maintained at the branch office itself, provided:

o They are proper books (i.e., compliant with accrual basis, double entry, and giving true & fair

view).

o Proper summarised returns (e.g., trial balance, P&L account, balance sheet) are sent

periodically to the registered office.

 The term "periodically" is not defined in the Act but implies regular intervals (e.g., monthly,

quarterly) based on business needs and practicality. For branches outside India, Rule 4(1) specifically mandates quarterly summarised returns. For Indian branches, no fixed frequency is prescribed, and monthly/quarterly is acceptable as long as it is regular.

 Recent amendments to the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 (e.g., vide notifications up to

2022-2023) focus on electronic maintenance, audit trails (effective from FY 2023-24), daily backups on Indian servers, and accessibility, but do not alter the core provisions on branch books or periodicity of returns.

In the given case:

 BBQ Ltd. maintains books at its branches (Delhi and London), with summarised returns sent

to the registered office (Hyderabad) – Delhi (monthly) and London (quarterly).  This setup complies with Section 128(2), as books are properly kept at branches, and

summarised returns are sent periodically (monthly for Delhi – which is periodic; quarterly for London – as mandated by Rule 4(1) for foreign branches).

(i) Validity of Objection on Place of Maintaining Books of Account: Mr. Naveen's objection that BBQ Ltd. is in default for not maintaining books at the registered office is invalid. Section 128(2) explicitly deems compliance if branch books are maintained at the branch with proper summarised returns sent to the registered office. No requirement exists to centralize all books at the registered office when branches are involved.

(ii) Validity of Objection on Frequency of Summarised Returns from London Branch: Mr. Naveen's objection that the London branch should send returns monthly (instead of quarterly) is invalid. For branches outside India, Rule 4(1) specifically requires summarised returns at quarterly intervals (not monthly). The London branch's quarterly submission is in full compliance. For the Delhi branch (in India), monthly returns are periodic and acceptable, though not mandatory (quarterly would also suffice).

Conclusion: Both objections raised by Mr. Naveen are not valid. BBQ Ltd. is compliant with the provisions of Section 128 and the relevant rules regarding maintenance of books of account and submission of summarised returns from branches. The statutory auditor should disregard these

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 519 of 941

objections and confirm compliance during the audit. If needed, the company can document the periodicity policy in its accounting manual for clarity.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Remember transfer timelines for unspent CSR amounts.
2. Identify applicable CSR fund/account.
3. Mention statutory time limit.

1. Timelines are often quoted incorrectly.

Question 52. Upkaar Nidhi Ltd., was about to hold an AGM on 25th August, 2022, for which the notice of AGM along with relevant documents, as prescribed, was sent to all its members including the following: A member individually holding shares with face value of ₹800 which amounted to 0.16% of the total paid-up share capital. Two members jointly holding shares with face value of ₹1,600 which amounted to 0.32% of the total paid-up share capital. Forty-two members each holding individually shares with face value of ₹600 which amounted to holding 0.12% of the total paid-up share capital for each such member. All the remaining members holding individually more than 1.2% of the total paid-up share capital of the company. In the AGM held on 25th August, 2022, members were not provided with the facility to vote by electronic means. In the context of aforesaid case-scenario, please answer whether Upkaar Nidhi Ltd. was required to send the notice of AGM along with relevant documents to all its members as aforesaid?

(6 marks | 5 minutes) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 52: Nidhi companies are governed by Section 406 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Nidhi Rules, 2014. As per Rule 18(1) of the Nidhi Rules, 2014 (no amendment to this provision as of January 2026):

The provisions of Section 136 (Right of member to copies of audited financial statement) of the Companies Act, 2013 shall apply to a Nidhi company subject to the following modification:

In the case of members who do not individually or jointly hold shares of more than one thousand rupees in face value or more than one per cent of the total paid-up share capital, whichever is less, it shall be sufficient compliance with the provisions of the section if an intimation is sent by public notice in a newspaper circulated in the district in which the registered office of the company is situated stating the date, time and venue of the AGM, and the financial statement with its enclosures can be inspected at the registered office of the company and the financial statement with enclosures are affixed on the notice board of the company and a member is entitled to vote either in person or through proxy.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 520 of 941

Key Interpretation:  The threshold for sending individual notice of AGM (along with financial statements,

explanatory statements, etc.) is higher than ₹1,000 face value or 1% of paid-up capital, whichever is less.  Members holding ₹1,000 or less in face value and1% or less of paid-up capital need only

newspaper intimation (public notice) — not individual notice.  Members holding more than ₹1,000 face value or more than 1% of paid-up capital (whichever is

less) must be sent individual notice of AGM with relevant documents.

Analysis of the given members (as on 2022 AGM):

1. Member holding ₹800 face value (0.16%) → Face value = ₹800 < ₹1,000 and % = 0.16% < 1% → Not entitled to individual notice → Newspaper intimation sufficient.
2. Two members jointly holding ₹1,600 face value (0.32%) → Joint holding = ₹1,600 > ₹1,000 even though % = 0.32% < 1% → Since face value exceeds ₹1,000, they qualify under “more than ₹1,000” → Required to be sent individual notice.
3. Forty-two members each holding ₹600 face value (0.12% each) → Face value = ₹600 < ₹1,000 and % = 0.12% < 1% → Not entitled to individual notice → Newspaper intimation sufficient.
4. All remaining members holding individually more than 1.2% → % > 1.2% > 1% (regardless of face value) → required to be sent individual notice.

Conclusion: Upkaar Nidhi Ltd. was not required to send the notice of AGM along with relevant documents to all its members.

It was required to send individual notices only to:  The two members jointly holding ₹1,600 face value (0.32%), and  All remaining members holding more than 1.2% of the paid-up share capital.

For the members mentioned at Sr. No. 1 (₹800, 0.16%) and Sr. No. 3 (₹600 each, 0.12% each), it was sufficient compliance to publish a public notice in a newspaper circulated in the district of the registered office, affix the financial statements on the notice board, and allow inspection at the registered office.

Additional Note: The fact that e-voting facility was not provided in the AGM is irrelevant to this question, as the query is only about the requirement to send notices (not about voting modes).

1. CSR expenditure outside India is generally not eligible.
2. Refer Schedule VII and CSR Rules.
3. Apply facts carefully.

Question 53. The Income Tax Authority (the statutory body) has gathered some information and is of the view that there has been a manipulation of accounts of FGH Ltd. reflecting an incorrect financial position of the company. The statutory body intends to get the accounts reopened to reflect correct financial position of the company. In light of the Companies Act, 2013 elucidate: (i) the statutory provisions governing the issue of re-opening of accounts by the Income Tax Authority. (ii) the voluntary revision of financial statements or board's report by the directors. (iii) For how many preceding financial years the board of directors may revise the financial statements?

(6 marks | 5 minutes) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 53: (i) Re-opening of Books of Account and Recasting of Financial Statements by Statutory Authorities As per Section 130 of the Companies Act, 2013 (no amendment to this provision till date):

A company shall not re-open its books of account and shall not recast its financial statements, unless an application in this behalf is made by:  The Central Government, or  The Income-tax authorities, or  The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), or  Any other statutory regulatory body or authority, or  Any person concerned,

And an order is made by a court of competent jurisdiction or the Tribunal (NCLT) to the effect that —

(a) The relevant earlier accounts were prepared in a fraudulent manner; or (b) the affairs of the company were mismanaged during the relevant period, casting a doubt on the reliability of the financial statements.

Important Limitation: No order shall be made in respect of re-opening of books of account and recasting of financial statements relating to a period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year.

Proviso: However, where the Central Government has issued a direction under the proviso to Section 128(5) for keeping of books of account for a period longer than eight years, the books may be ordered to be re-opened within such longer period.

In the given case: The Income Tax Authority is one of the specified statutory bodies empowered under Section 130 to make an application to the competent court or Tribunal for re-opening and recasting of accounts, provided it can establish fraud or mismanagement affecting reliability. The maximum period for such re-opening is 8 preceding financial years (unless extended by Central Government direction under Section 128(5)).

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 522 of 941

(ii) Voluntary Revision of Financial Statements or Board's Report by the Directors As per Section 131 of the Companies Act, 2013 (no amendment to this provision till date): If it appears to the directors of a company that — (a) The financial statements of the company do not comply with the provisions of Section 129 (preparation of financial statements), or (b) the Board’s report does not comply with the provisions of Section 134,

Then the directors may prepare revised financial statements or a revised Board’s report in respect of any of the three preceding financial years after obtaining the approval of the Tribunal (NCLT) on an application made by the company in this behalf.

Conditions:  Such revised financial statement or report shall not be prepared or filed more than once in a

financial year.  The revised statements shall be laid before the members in the general meeting and filed with

the Registrar in the prescribed manner (Form AOC-4 or AOC-4 revised).  The Tribunal may direct that the reason for revision be disclosed in the revised statements and

in the subsequent financial statements.

This is a voluntary power available to the Board (unlike Section 130 which is compulsory when ordered by court/Tribunal).

(iii) Period for which Board of Directors may revise Financial Statements As per Section 131(1) of the Companies Act, 2013: The Board of Directors may revise the financial statements or Board’s report in respect of any of the three preceding financial years (immediately preceding the current financial year).

Conclusion:  For compulsory re-opening/recasting (as sought by Income Tax Authority), Section 130 applies

– maximum 8 preceding financial years (subject to fraud/mismanagement proof and court/Tribunal order).  For voluntary revision by the directors themselves, Section 131 applies – limited to 3 preceding

financial years with Tribunal approval and not more than once in a financial year.

Question 54. Write down functions and duties of the National Financial Reporting Authority.

(4 marks|4 minutes) (Medium| ICAI Fav)

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 523 of 941

Answer 54: The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) is a statutory body constituted under Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013.

As per Section 132(2) read with Rule 4 and Rules 6 to 9 of the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules, 2018 (no material amendment to these provisions till date), the functions and duties of NFRA are as follows:

The NFRA shall protect the public interest and the interests of investors, creditors, and others associated with companies or bodies corporate by establishing and enforcing high quality standards of accounting and auditing and exercising effective oversight of accounting functions performed by companies/bodies corporate and auditing functions performed by auditors.

Without prejudice to the generality of the above, the NFRA shall, in particular, perform the following functions and duties:

(a) Maintain details of particulars of auditors appointed in the companies and bodies corporate governed by NFRA (i.e., maintain a database/register of auditors);

(b) Recommend accounting standards and auditing standards (including standards on auditing, cost auditing, and any other standards) for approval by the Central Government;

(c) Monitor and enforce compliance with accounting standards and auditing standards;

(d) Oversee the quality of service of the professions associated with ensuring compliance with such standards (including audit quality review) and suggest measures for improvement in the quality of service;

(e) Promote awareness in relation to the compliance of accounting standards and auditing standards;

(f) Co-operate with national and international organisations of independent audit regulators in establishing and overseeing adherence to accounting standards and auditing standards;

(g) Perform such other functions and duties as may be necessary or incidental to the aforesaid functions and duties.

Additional Important Functions (from NFRA Rules, 2018):

 Investigate professional or other misconduct committed by any member of the Institute of

Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) (Chartered Accountant) or firm of Chartered Accountants in respect of companies’/bodies corporate governed by NFRA.  Conduct disciplinary proceedings and impose penalties (including monetary penalties and

debarment from practice) for professional or other misconduct.

Conclusion: The primary objective of NFRA is to ensure high quality, transparent, and reliable financial reporting and auditing in India, particularly for listed companies, large unlisted companies,

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 524 of 941

banks, insurance companies, and other specified bodies corporate, thereby enhancing investor confidence and protecting public interest.

Question 55. Compute the minimum amount that Modern Furniture Limited is required to spend on account of Corporate Social Responsibility for the year 2022-2023. MFL was incorporated in August 2020. Net-profit made during the financial years 2020-2021 and 2021-2022 are ₹20 crores, and ₹38 crore respectively.

(3 marks | 3 minutes) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 55: As per Section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014 (as amended, including amendments up to 2025 – no change in the calculation formula for newly incorporated companies):

The Board of every company to which Section 135 applies shall ensure that the company spends, in every financial year, at least 2% of the average net profits of the company made during the three immediately preceding financial years.

Special provision for newly incorporated companies: Where the company has not completed the period of three financial years since its incorporation, the company shall spend, in every financial year, at least 2% of the average net profits of the company made during such immediately preceding financial years (i.e., the available completed financial years since incorporation).

In the given case:

 Modern Furniture Limited (MFL) was incorporated in August 2020.  For CSR obligation in FY 2022-23 (financial year commencing 1st April 2022), the

immediately preceding financial years are: o FY 2020-21 (completed, net profit = ₹20 crore), o FY 2021-22 (completed, net profit = ₹38 crore).  The company has completed only two financial years since incorporation (FY 2020-21 and FY

2021-22).  FY 2019-20 is not available (company not in existence).

Calculation: Average net profit = (₹20 crore + ₹38 crores) / 2 = ₹29 crore Minimum CSR expenditure required for FY 2022-23 = 2% of ₹29 crore = ₹0.58 crore or ₹58 lakhs. Conclusion: Modern Furniture Limited is required to spend a minimum of ₹58 lakhs on Corporate Social Responsibility activities during the financial year 2022-2023, in pursuance of its CSR Policy

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 525 of 941

(assuming it meets the applicability criteria under Section 135(1) in the immediately preceding financial year, i.e., FY 2021-22).

(Note: Net profit for CSR is computed as per Section 198 of the Companies Act, 2013. The question provides figures assumed to be as per Section 198. If the company does not meet the threshold criteria in FY 2021-22, CSR may not apply; however, the question implies computation based on given profits.)

Question 56. Quick Money Limited attracts the provisions of section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 and it has minimum average obligation to spend Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) amount of ₹15 crores during each of the preceding five years. In this connection, the Board of Directors of the company needs your expert views on the following matters: (i) What is the meaning of "impact assessment"? (ii) Whether impact assessment is required to be taken by all the companies? (iii) Who can conduct impact assessment?

(5 marks | 5 minutes) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 56. As per Rule 8(3) of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014 (as amended vide Companies (CSR Policy) Amendment Rules, 2021 dated 22.01.2021, and subsequent clarifications/amendments up to 2025 – no change in core provisions of impact assessment):

(i) Meaning of "Impact Assessment" Impact assessment means a systematic and objective evaluation (study) of the social, economic, and environmental effects/impacts created by the CSR projects/activities of the company on the intended beneficiaries, communities, and stakeholders.

It assesses whether the CSR projects have achieved the intended objectives, delivered measurable outcomes, brought about positive changes (e.g., improvement in quality of life, education levels, health indicators, environmental sustainability), and identifies areas for improvement. The purpose is to measure the actual impact (beyond mere expenditure), provide feedback for better planning, and enhance the effectiveness and accountability of CSR spending.

(ii) Whether impact assessment is required to be taken by all the companies? No, impact assessment is not mandatory for all companies. It is mandatory only for the following class of companies (as per Rule 8(3)(a)):

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 526 of 941

 Every company having an average CSR obligation of ₹10 crore or more in pursuance of Section

135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, in the three immediately preceding financial years.

Such companies shall undertake impact assessment, through an independent agency, of their CSR projects having outlays of ₹1 crore or more each, and which have been completed not less than one year before undertaking the impact study.

In the given case: Quick Money Limited has an average CSR obligation of ₹15 crores (which exceeds ₹10 crore) in each of the preceding five years (implying the three-year average is also ≥ ₹10 crore). Therefore, it is required to undertake impact assessment for qualifying projects (outlay ≥ ₹1 crore and completed ≥ 1 year prior).

Other companies (with average CSR obligation < ₹10 crore) are not required to conduct impact assessment, though they may do so voluntarily as good governance practice.

(iii) Who can conduct impact assessment? The impact assessment shall be conducted only through an independent agency (Rule 8(3)(a)). The company (or its internal team/CSR committee) cannot conduct the impact assessment itself (self-assessment is not permitted). The independent agency must be external, objective, and free from any conflict of interest.

Commonly, such assessments are conducted by reputed professional firms, NGOs with expertise, social audit firms, research organisations, or consultants specialised in impact evaluation (e.g., using frameworks like SROI – Social Return on Investment, or other recognised methodologies).

Additional Provisions:  The impact assessment report(s) shall be placed before the Board and annexed to the annual

report on CSR (Rule 8(3)(b)).  Expenditure on impact assessment can be booked as CSR expenditure in that financial year, but

shall not exceed the lower of 5% of the total CSR expenditure for that year or ₹50 lakh (Rule 8(3)(c) – limit as per original 2021 amendment; some sources indicate relaxation to 2% or ₹50 lakh higher in later amendments, but core requirement remains capped).

Conclusion: Quick Money Limited, having average CSR obligation of ₹15 crore (> ₹10 crore threshold), is mandatory required to conduct impact assessment through an independent agency for its large CSR projects (≥ ₹1 crore outlay, completed ≥ 1 year ago). This ensures objective evaluation of the social impact of its CSR initiatives.

1. Remember disclosure requirements in Board's Report.
2. Mention CSR policy disclosure.
3. Mention annual CSR reporting requirements.

Question 57. Mary Ltd is a listed company with a turnover of ₹1200 crores during the financial year 2024-25. The CSR Committee of the Board formulated and recommended a CSR project requiring a budget equivalent to 5% of the average net profits of the company for the last three financial years. The Board approved this project. With reference to the provisions of Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, and the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014, advise the company on the following:

1. Is the company permitted to spend more than the statutory minimum of 2%?
2. Can the excess 3% expenditure be "set off" against CSR obligations in subsequent financial years?
3. What are the specific conditions the company must fulfil to avail of this set-off? (4 Marks | 4 Minutes)

Answer 57. Statutory Provision: Under Section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 7(3) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014.

1. Legality of Excess Spending: There is no ceiling on CSR spending. A company can spend any

amount above the mandatory 2% of average net profits. In this case, Mary Ltd's decision to spend 5% is legally valid.

2. Provision for Set-off: If a company spends an amount in excess of the requirement (2%), such

company may set off such excess amount against the requirement to spend in the immediately succeeding three financial years.

3. Conditions for Set-off: To successfully set off the 3% excess, Mary Ltd must comply with the

following:

 Board Resolution: The Board of the company must pass a resolution to this effect.  Exclusion of Surplus: The excess amount available for set-off shall not include the surplus

arising out of the CSR activities (e.g., profit from a CSR project or interest on unspent funds).  Disclosure: The details of the set-off must be disclosed in the annual report on CSR.

Conclusion: Yes, Mary Ltd can count the excess 3% as a part of its CSR expenditure for the next three financial years, provided the Board passes a resolution and ensures the amount does not include any CSR surplus.

Question 58. The balances extracted from the financial statements of ABC Limited are as below: Sr. Particulars Balances as on 31.03.2020 as per Audited Balances as on 30.09.2020 No. Financial Statement (₹ in crore) (Provisional ₹ in crore)

1. Net Worth 100.00 100.00
2. Turnover 500.00 1000.00
3. Net Profit 1.00 5.00

Explaining the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, you are requested to examine whether ABC Limited is required to constitute 'Corporate Social Responsibility Committee' (CSR Committee) during the second half of the financial year 2020-21.

(5 marks | 5 minutes) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 58. As per section 135(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 (as it stood during FY 2020-21 and still applicable in January 2026, since the proposed amendments in the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 2025 to lower the thresholds have not been enacted yet), every company which —

 has a net worth of rupees five hundred crore or more, or  has a turnover of rupees one thousand crore or more, or  has a net profit of rupees five crore or more

During the immediately preceding financial year shall constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board consisting of three or more directors, out of which at least one director shall be an independent director.

Analysis of the given case:  For determining CSR applicability during the second half of FY 2020-21 (October 2020 – March

2021), the relevant immediately preceding financial year is FY 2019-20 (1.4.2019 to 31.3.2020).  As per the audited financial statements as on 31.03.2020:

o Net Worth = ₹100.00 crore (< ₹500 crore) o Turnover = ₹500.00 crore (< ₹1,000 crore) o Net Profit = ₹1.00 crore (< ₹5 crore)

ABC Limited does not satisfy any of the above three criteria in the immediately preceding financial year (FY 2019-20).

The provisional figures as on 30.09.2020 (relating to the current financial year FY 2020-21) are irrelevant for triggering CSR applicability in FY 2020-21, as the law specifically refers only to the immediately preceding financial year.

There is also no mention of any unspent CSR obligation from earlier years that could trigger committee formation under other provisions.

Conclusion: ABC Limited is not required to constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee during the second half of the financial year 2020-21 (or for the entire FY 2020-21).

Question 59. SKIP Limited (the Company) was incorporated on 01.04.2019. The balances extracted from its audited financial statements are as given below: Financial Year (FY) Net Profit before Net Profit after tax (Ignore Income Tax computation)

tax 2019-20 ₹ 5.00 crore ₹ 3.75 crore 2020-21 ₹ 7.00 crore ₹ 5.25 crore The Company proposes to allocate the minimum required amount for CSR Activities to be undertaken during FY 2021-22, if it is mandatory. You are requested to advise the Company in this regard and compute the minimum amount to be allocated, if required, taking into account relevant provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.

(5 marks | 5 minutes) (Question Bank) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 59. As per Section 135(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 (as applicable during FY 2021-22 and unchanged till January 2026, since the proposed amendments in the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 2025 to lower the thresholds have been introduced in Parliament in December 2025 but not yet passed into law), every company having —

 net worth of rupees five hundred crore or more, or  turnover of rupees one thousand crore or more, or  a net profit of rupees five crore or more

During the immediately preceding financial year shall constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board.

The net profit for the purpose of applicability under Section 135(1) is net profit after tax (PAT), as per the prevailing interpretation and practice (though some sources debate it, the threshold is generally applied on PAT as shown in the profit & loss account).

Further, as per Section 135(5), the Board shall ensure that the company spends, in every financial year, at least two per cent of the average net profits of the company made during the three immediately preceding financial years or, where the company has not completed the period of three financial years since its incorporation, during such immediately preceding financial years.

The net profit for computing the 2% CSR obligation is to be calculated in accordance with the provisions of Section 198 of the Companies Act, 2013, which is essentially profit before tax (PBT) with specified adjustments/exclusions (e.g., excluding income tax, certain capital items, etc.).

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 530 of 941

Analysis of the given case:

 The company was incorporated on 01.04.2019.  For determining CSR applicability and obligation in FY 2021-22, the immediately preceding

financial year is FY 2020-21.  In FY 2020-21:

o Net Profit before tax = ₹7.00 crore o Net Profit after tax = ₹5.25 crore (which exceeds ₹5 crore)

Thus, SKIP Limited satisfies the net profit criterion (₹5.25 crore > ₹5 crore) in the immediately preceding financial year (FY 2020-21) and is therefore required to comply with CSR provisions, including constituting a CSR Committee (if not already done) and spending on CSR activities during FY 2021-22.

Computation of minimum CSR amount for FY 2021-22: Since the company has not completed three financial years since incorporation (only two full financial years: 2019-20 and 2020-21), the average net profit shall be computed based on the two immediately preceding financial years (FY 2019-20 and FY 2020-21).

As the net profit for CSR spend (per Section 198) is profit before tax:

 FY 2019-20: ₹ 5.00 crore  FY 2020-21: ₹ 7.00 crore Average net profit = (₹5.00 crore + ₹7.00 crore) / 2 = ₹6.00 crore Minimum CSR contribution required = 2% of ₹6.00 crore = ₹0.12 crore (or ₹12 lakhs).

Conclusion: SKIP Limited is required to comply with CSR provisions during FY 2021-22. The minimum amount to be allocated/spent on CSR activities during FY 2021-22 is ₹12 lakhs.

(ii) Advise the company, how many members are eligible to be part of Committee and what is the criterion? Whether CSR committee formed was in compliance with the provisions of the Act and Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014? (iii) Whether activities proposed by company were in accordance with provisions of the Act and Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014?

(8 marks | 7 minutes) (Hard | Case Study Based)

Answer 60. (i) Basis for applicability of Section 135 As per Section 135(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 (unchanged as on January 2026, since the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 2025 introduced in December 2025 proposing lower thresholds has not been passed into law yet), every company having —

 net worth of rupees five hundred crore or more, or  turnover of rupees one thousand crore or more, or  a net profit of rupees five crore or more during the immediately preceding financial year

(here, FY 2022-23) shall constitute a CSR Committee.

“Net worth” is defined under Section 2(57) as the aggregate value of the paid-up share capital and all reserves created out of profits, securities premium account and debit or credit balance of the profit and loss account, after deducting the aggregate value of the accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off, as per the audited balance sheet, but does not include reserves created out of revaluation of assets, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation.

Net worth Calculation for FY 2022-23: Paid-up share capital: ₹ 200 Cr

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 532 of 941

 Free reserves created out of profits: ₹ 200 Cr  Securities Premium Account: ₹ 70 Cr  Credit balance of Profit & Loss account: ₹ 60 Cr – Miscellaneous expenditure not written off:

₹ 20 Cr = ₹510 Cr

Since the net worth exceeds ₹500 crore (even though turnover is ₹700 crore < ₹ 1,000 crore and net profit is ₹ 4 crore < ₹ 5 crore), the company attracts the provisions of Section 135. Vineet correctly concluded based on the net worth criterion.

(ii) Composition of CSR Committee As per Section 135(1) read with Rule 5 of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014 (as applicable in 2023 and unchanged till date), the CSR Committee shall consist of three or more directors, out of which at least one director shall be an independent director.

Since the company is a listed company, it is required to have independent directors under Section 149(1), and the CSR Committee must include at least one independent director. The Chief Compliance Officer (Vineet) is not a director and cannot be a member of the Committee.

The committee formed on 30.04.2023 comprises: CA. R.C Goel (Managing Director), Varun (executive director), Prabodh (executive director) and Vineet (Chief Compliance Officer).

It is not in compliance because:

 No independent director (e.g., Rudra Mittal or Pragya) is included.  Inclusion of Vineet (non-director) is invalid. The committee should have at least three directors with at least one independent director.

(iii) Eligibility of proposed activities As per Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014:

 (I) CSR projects for the benefit of employees of the company and their families only: No —

CSR activities must benefit the general public/community and not be exclusively for employees or their families (as they are considered normal business expenditure).

 (II) Contribution of ₹50,000 to a political party under Section 182: No — Contributions to

political parties are expressly prohibited as CSR expenditure.

 (III) Contribution to the PM CARES Fund (during Covid pandemic): Yes — As clarified by MCA

vide notification dated 26.05.2020 inserting PM CARES Fund in Schedule VII item (viii), contributions qualify as CSR expenditure (and remain eligible even after 2023 as per prevailing rules and clarifications).

 (IV) Local activities like promotion of child and women education: Yes — This falls under

item (ii) of Schedule VII (promotion of education, including special education and employment enhancing vocation skills).

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 533 of 941

Conclusion: The company attracts CSR provisions due to net worth > ₹500 crore. The formed CSR Committee is non-compliant due to absence of independent director and inclusion of non-director. Only activities (III) and (IV) are eligible for CSR spend.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. End every CSR answer with a clear conclusion.
2. Quote relevant provision.
3. Apply facts and conclude in one line.

1. Students lose marks by not giving a specific conclusion after legal discussion.

Question 61. PQR Private Limited operates as a manufacturing company, generating a turnover of ₹150 crore and holds an outstanding loan of ₹75 crore from a public financial institution solely in the previous financial year (with a total loan availed of ₹110 crore, but ₹35 crore were repaid during the same year). The company's Board has delegated the authority to CEO to designate an internal auditor to conduct internal audit. However, the CEO believes that the company is not legally obligated to have an internal auditor. Analyse the accuracy of the CEO's perspective by referring to the provisions outlined in the Companies Act, 2013. What would be your response if the Board of Directors wanted to appoint the Secretary of the company Mr. A as an internal auditor?

(5 marks | 5 minutes) (Medium | ICAI Fav)

Answer 61. As per Section 138 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 (as applicable in the relevant period and unchanged as on January 2026, since no amendments to the applicability thresholds for internal audit have been notified till date despite certain other amendments to audit-related rules in 2025), every private company which has —  turnover of rupees two hundred crore or more during the preceding financial year; or  outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding rupees

one hundred crore or more at any point of time during the preceding financial year

Shall be required to appoint an internal auditor, who shall either be a Chartered Accountant (whether in practice or not), a Cost Accountant (whether in practice or not), or such other professional as may be decided by the Board to conduct the internal audit of the functions and activities of the company.

Analysis of applicability:  Turnover during the preceding financial year = ₹150 crore (below ₹200 crore).  Outstanding loans/borrowings from public financial institution:

o Total availed during the year = ₹110 crore. o Repaid during the year = ₹35 crore. o Outstanding at year-end = ₹75 crore.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 534 of 941

o However, the threshold is triggered if the outstanding loans/borrowings exceeded ₹100

crore at any point during the preceding financial year.

Since the total loan availed was ₹110 crore (implying that at some point during the year, the outstanding balance exceeded ₹ 100 crore before repayments), the company satisfies the borrowing criterion.

Thus, PQR Private Limited is required to appoint an internal auditor. The CEO's belief that the company is not legally obligated is incorrect.

Eligibility of Mr. A (Company Secretary) as Internal Auditor: As per Section 138(1), the internal auditor may be a Chartered Accountant, a Cost Accountant, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board. The term "such other professional" is broad and includes professionals like a Company Secretary (CS), as there is no restriction prohibiting the appointment of a CS or an employee (such as the Company Secretary) as internal auditor. The internal auditor may or may not be an employee of the company.

Therefore, the Board of Directors may appoint Mr. A, the Secretary of the company (a qualified Company Secretary), as the internal auditor, subject to the Board's decision and terms of appointment.

Conclusion:

1. The CEO's perspective is not accurate; the company is required to appoint an internal auditor due to borrowings exceeding ₹100 crore at any point during the preceding financial year.
2. The Board can appoint Mr. A (Company Secretary) as the internal auditor.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Turnover ≥ ₹200 crore OR Outstanding loans/borrowings > ₹100 crore at any point of time during

preceding FY.

2. Internal Auditor may be a Chartered Accountant, Cost Accountant, or such other professional as

decided by the Board.

3. A Company Secretary can be appointed as Internal Auditor and may even be an employee of the

company

PART B Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Question 1. Modern Furniture Limited (MFL) is required to prepare the financial statement that comply with accounting standards and shall be in form specified in schedule III. But the financial statement prepared and presented are not in compliance with applicable accounting standards, therefore MFL required to disclose which of following: i. Deviation ii. Reason of deviation iii. Financial effects arise out of such deviation. (a) Only I (b) Only i and ii (c) Only i and iii (d) All of i, ii, and iii

(Practice question)

Answer: d) Reason: According to the Companies Act, 2013, if a company like Modern Furniture Limited (MFL) prepares its financial statements in a manner that does not comply with the applicable Accounting Standards (AS), it is required to disclose the following:

Deviation (i): MFL must disclose the deviation from the applicable accounting standards. This is a mandatory requirement to ensure transparency in financial reporting, especially if the company has made departures from the established norms.

Reason for Deviation (ii): MFL must also provide the reason for the deviation. This helps the users of financial statements understand why the company has not followed the standard practice.

Reasons could include practical challenges, a change in accounting policies, or unique circumstances affecting the company's financial reporting.

Financial Effects of Deviation (iii): The Company is also required to disclose the financial effects that arise from the deviation. This is crucial because the deviation from accounting standards may have a material impact on the financial statements, and stakeholders need to know the effect of such deviation on the company's financial position.

Therefore, as per the Companies Act, 2013, and Accounting Standards, MFL is required to disclose all of the above, which includes the deviation, the reason for the deviation, and the financial effects of the deviation. Thus, the correct answer is (d) All of i, ii, and iii.

During the half year ended September 2020, the board of directors (BOD) of Gold Leaf Limited has made an application to the Tribunal for revision in the accounts of the company for the financial year ended on March 2018. (c) The act of the BOD is invalid as the law provides for only one time application to be made in a financial year for revision of accounts and boards report. In this case, the application made by the BOD for the revision of accounts for the year March 2018 is not valid, as it is beyond the 2- year period from the end of the year 2020 (i.e., it should have been applied by March 2020). This may include companies that have not been active in business or whose operations are limited to maintenance work, like keeping the company active or preserving its corporate existence. When preparing financial statements for a dormant company, the following applies: Balance Sheet – A balance sheet is still required to show the assets and liabilities of the dormant company, even if no significant activity has taken place. Profit and Loss Account – Although there may be no profit or loss due to the company's inactivity, a dormant company is still required to prepare a Profit and Loss account. The account will typically show no activity or just minor administrative costs (such as legal or compliance expenses). Applicable Explanatory Note – A dormant company is required to include explanatory notes to explain the nature of its dormant status, as required by the Companies Act, 2013. However, Cash Flow Statement is not mandatory for a dormant company, as there are no significant transactions or cash flows to report. The cash flow statement is intended to show the inflows and outflows of cash during the financial year, which is unnecessary in the case of a dormant company. Therefore, the cash flow statement is not required for dormant companies under the Companies Act, 2013.

Question 24. The books of accounts of every company shall be maintained in order for (a) 3 years (b) 5 years (c) 8 years (d) 10 years

Answer: (c) 8 years Reason: As per Section 128(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, the books of account of every company (along with the relevant vouchers) relating to a period of not less than eight financial years immediately preceding a financial year shall be kept in good order. If the company has been in existence for less than eight years, it must preserve the books of account and vouchers for all the preceding years since incorporation. This is the standard statutory requirement in India for all companies (private, public, etc.). The Central Government may direct preservation for a longer period in case of any ongoing investigation under Chapter XIV of the Act. The other options (3, 5, or 10 years) do not match the provision under the Companies Act, 2013. Where such a decision is taken by the Board, the company shall, within seven days thereof, file with the Registrar a notice in writing giving the full address of that other place (filed in Form AOC-5 along with a certified copy of the Board resolution). Question 27. Ganesh Company Ltd, a public company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 has Mr. Jay - Director, Mr. Sagar - Independent Director, Mr. Abhishek - Nominee Director and Mr. Yash - Whole time director. You are required to state whether Mr. Abhishek is eligible to inspect the books of accounts of Ganesh Company Limited? (a) Yes, Mr. Abhishek can inspect the books of accounts of Shankar Company limited only on authorization of the public financial institution on whose behalf he has been so appointed in the board of the Ganesh Company Ltd. (b) No. Mr. Abhishek being a nominee director can only inspect the books of accounts of Ganesh Company Ltd and not its subsidiary company. (c) Yes, Mr. Abhishek can inspect the books of accounts of Shankar Company limited only on authorization by way of resolution of the board of directors. (d) Yes, Mr. Abhishek can inspect the books of accounts of Shankar Company limited only on authorization by way of resolution of the members holding not less than 25% of the paid-up share capital of the company.

Answer: (c) Yes, Mr. Abhishek can inspect the books of accounts of Shankar Company Limited only on authorization by way of resolution of the board of directors. Reason: As per Section 128(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, the books of account and other books and papers maintained by the company within India shall be open for inspection during business hours by any director of the company (including nominee, independent, whole-time, or other directors). However, there is an important proviso to this sub-section: "Provided that the inspection in respect of any subsidiary of the company shall be done only by the person Authorized in this behalf by a resolution of the Board of Directors." This meAnswer:  Mr. Abhishek, being a director (nominee director) of the holding company (Ganesh Company

Ltd.), has the right to inspect the books of accounts of the subsidiary (Shankar Company Limited).  But this inspection can only be carried out if he (or any person, who need not necessarily be a

director of the subsidiary) is specifically Authorized by a resolution passed by the Board of Directors of Ganesh Company Ltd. The status of Mr. Abhishek as a nominee director does not restrict or alter this right; the same proviso applies uniformly to all types of directors. The authorization must come from the Board resolution of the holding company, not from any public financial institution, members' resolution (e.g., 25% share capital), or other external body. Thus:  Option (a) is incorrect — No requirement for authorization from the public financial institution.  Option (b) is incorrect — A nominee director is not restricted to inspecting only the holding

company's books; the Board resolution proviso applies equally.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 550 of 941

 Option (d) is incorrect — No requirement for members' resolution or 25% paid-up capital

threshold. This provision ensures controlled access to subsidiary records while allowing directors of the holding company to fulfill their fiduciary duties.

Mr. Q, Mr. R and Mr. S (c) Mr. P. Mr. S, Mr. V and Mr. W (d) Mr. P. Mr. Q, Mr. R, Mr. S, Mr. V & Mr. W

 the Managing Director;  the whole-time director in charge of finance;  the Chief Financial Officer; or  any other person of the company who is charged by the Board with the duty of complying

with the provisions of this section. Such persons shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to five lakh rupees, or with both. In the given case:

 Mr. P is the Managing Director → Liable.  Mr. V is the Chief Financial Officer → Liable. The other persons are:

 Mr. Q and Mr. R → Ordinary Directors (not specified as in charge of finance or charged by

Board for this duty).  Mr. S → Nominee Director (same as above; no special charge mentioned).  Mr. W → Whole-time Company Secretary (not covered under Section 128(6) unless

specifically charged by the Board for books of account maintenance, which is not stated here). The liability under this section is not on all directors or all KMPs by default (unlike general "officer in default" under Section 2(60) for many other provisions). It is specific and limited to the Managing Director, finance-in-charge WTD/CFO, or the person expressly charged by the Board. Thus:

 Option (b), (c), and (d) incorrectly include ordinary directors, nominee director, or the

Company Secretary without basis.

 Only Mr. P (Managing Director) and Mr. V (CFO) are mandatorily liable as per the explicit

wording of Section 128(6). This is a targeted provision to fix responsibility on those directly accountable for financial records and compliance in this area.

Question 29. Which of the following company is mandatorily required to prepare cash flow statement? (a) OPC (b) Small company (c) Dormant company (d) Nidhi company

Answer (d) Nidhi Company Reason: As per Section 2(40) of the Companies Act, 2013, "financial statement" in relation to a company includes— (i) a balance sheet as at the end of the financial year; (ii) a profit and loss account (or income and expenditure account for non-profit companies); (iii) cash flow statement for the financial year; and (iv) any explanatory notes annexed thereto. However, the proviso to Section 2(40) explicitly states: "Provided that the financial statement, with respect to One Person Company, small company and dormant company, may not include the cash flow statement." This meAnswer:

 OPC (One Person Company), small company, and dormant company are exempt from

preparing and including a cash flow statement in their financial statements.  Nidhi company is not listed among the exempted categories under this proviso (or under any

specific exemption notification for Nidhi companies in relation to cash flow statement). Therefore, a Nidhi company (which is typically a public company registered under Section 406 of the Companies Act, 2013, and governed by Nidhi Rules) is mandatorily required to prepare a cash flow statement as part of its financial statements, in line with the general requirement under the Act and applicable Accounting Standards (AS 3 or Ind AS 7, as the case may be). Options (a), (b), and (c) are incorrect because OPC, small company, and dormant company enjoy the specific statutory exemption from including the cash flow statement. No such exemption applies to Nidhi companies. This provision promotes simplified compliance for smaller or inactive entities while ensuring full financial transparency for others, including Nidhi companies that deal with public deposits and have a larger stakeholder base.

Question 30. The financial statements of a One Person Company (OPC) include all of the following documents, except (a) Balance Sheet (b) Profit and Loss statement (c) Cash flow statement (d) Statement of changes in equity

Answer. (c) Cash flow statement Reason: As per the proviso to Section 2(40) of the Companies Act, 2013, the definition of "financial statement" includes:  Balance Sheet

 Profit and Loss Account (or Income and Expenditure Account, as applicable)  Cash Flow Statement  Statement of Changes in Equity (wherever applicable) However, the proviso explicitly states: "Provided that the financial statement, with respect to One Person Company, small company and dormant company, may not include the cash flow statement." This means a One Person Company (OPC) is exempt from the requirement to prepare and include the Cash Flow Statement as part of its financial statements. The other documents remain mandatory for an OPC:  Balance Sheet — Required  Profit and Loss Statement — Required  Statement of Changes in Equity — Required (to the extent applicable, generally for companies

following Ind AS or where there are changes in equity) Thus, the financial statements of an OPC include all the listed documents except the Cash Flow Statement. Options (a), (b), and (d) are incorrect because these are compulsory components for an OPC, while (c) is the one specifically exempted by law. Question 31. The financial statement in relation to a dormant company may not include: (a) Balance sheet (b) cash flow statement (c) Applicable explanatory note (d) profit and loss account

Answer. (b) cash flow statement Reason: As per Section 2(40) of the Companies Act, 2013, "financial statement" in relation to a company includes:  (i) a balance sheet as at the end of the financial year;  (ii) a profit and loss account (or income and expenditure account, as applicable) for the financial

year;  (iii) cash flow statement for the financial year;  (iv) a statement of changes in equity, if applicable; and  (v) any explanatory note annexed to, or forming part of, the above documents. However, the proviso to Section 2(40) explicitly states: "Provided that the financial statement, with respect to One Person Company, small company and dormant company, may not include the cash flow statement." This means a dormant company (like OPC and small company) is exempt from the requirement to prepare and include the cash flow statement in its financial statements. The other components remain mandatory:  Balance sheet — Required  Profit and loss account — Required  Applicable explanatory note — Required (as part of the financial statements) Thus, the financial statement of a dormant company may not include the cash flow statement, while the others listed in options (a), (c), and (d) are compulsory.

Question 32. Financial statements of a company are prepared as per (a) Schedule I (b) Schedule II (c) Schedule III (d) Schedule IV

Answer (c) Schedule III Reason: As per Section 129(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the financial statements of a company shall give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company, comply with the applicable Accounting Standards, and shall be prepared in the form prescribed in Schedule III to the Act. Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 lays down the detailed format, structure, and general instructions for the preparation and presentation of:  Balance Sheet  Statement of Profit and Loss  Cash Flow Statement (where applicable)  General Instructions for classification and disclosure of various items Key points about Schedule III:  It is divided into Division I (for companies following Indian Accounting Standards / traditional

format)  Division II (for companies following Ind AS)  Division III (for Non-Banking Financial Companies following Ind AS) This Schedule is mandatory for the preparation of financial statements of all companies (except where specific exemptions apply, e.g., for certain small companies, OPCs, etc., in limited aspects like cash flow statement). Other options are incorrect:  Schedule I — Does not exist in the Companies Act, 2013 (earlier Acts had different schedules).  Schedule II — Deals with useful lives to compute depreciation (useful life of assets).  Schedule IV — Contains the Code for Independent Directors (code of conduct, duties, etc.). Thus, financial statements are prepared as per Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013.

Question 33. On application of Central Government. Tribunal may order to re-open books of accounts of a company for maximum (a) 3 years (b) 5 years (c) 8 years (d) 10 year

Answer (c) 8 years Reason: As per Section 130(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, no order shall be made under sub- section (1) (i.e., by the court or the Tribunal) in respect of re-opening of books of account relating to a period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year. This means the Tribunal can order the re-opening of books of accounts for a maximum period of 8 financial years immediately preceding the current financial year, when an application is made

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 554 of 941

(including by the Central Government) on grounds such as fraudulent preparation of accounts or mismanagement casting doubt on the reliability of financial statements. Proviso to Section 130(3): However, where the Central Government has issued a direction under the proviso to Section 128(5) for keeping books of account for a period longer than eight years (e.g., due to ongoing investigation), the Tribunal may order re-opening for such longer period. In the standard/default case (without any extended preservation direction by the Central Government), the maximum limit is 8 years. Thus:  Options (a) 3 years, (b) 5 years, and (d) 10 years are incorrect.  The statutory cap aligns with the general preservation requirement under Section 128(5), which

mandates keeping books for at least 8 years, and Section 130 limits re-opening accordingly unless extended by government direction. This provision ensures finality of accounts while allowing corrective action in cases of fraud or mismanagement, but prevents indefinite re-opening of historical records.

Question 36. A company may apply to Tribunal for voluntary revision of accounts for a period not exceeding (a) 1 year (b) 2 years (c) 3 years (d) 8 years

(RTP NOV18)

Answer: (c) 3 years Reason: As per Section 131(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company may, with the prior approval of the Tribunal (NCLT), voluntarily revise or re-cast its financial statements or Board's report of any previous financial year(s) if it appears to the directors that the financial statements or report of the company do not comply with the requirements of the Act. However, such voluntary revision is permitted only for a period not exceeding three preceding financial years immediately preceding the current financial year. Key points of Section 131:  The application is made by the company itself (voluntary revision).  Prior approval of the Tribunal is mandatory.  The revision can cover a maximum of 3 financial years preceding the current one.  This is distinct from Section 130 (compulsory re-opening on application by regulatory

authorities like Central Govt., SEBI, Income Tax, etc., which allows up to 8 years in cases of fraud/mismanagement).  The voluntary revision under Section 131 is for genuine errors/omissions/non-compliance (not

involving fraud), and is time-bound to 3 years to balance correction with finality of accounts. Thus:  Options (a) 1 year and (b) 2 years are too short and incorrect.  Option (d) 8 years applies only to compulsory re-opening under Section 130 (not voluntary). The correct limit for voluntary revision by the company is 3 years.

Question 45. Compute the minimum amount the company (ABC Limited) is required to spend on account of Corporate Social Responsibility in financial year 2022-23, if during the financial years 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22 net profits are ₹30 Crores, ₹ 25 crores and ₹32 crores respectively (a) ₹ 87 lakhs (b) 1.45 crores (c) 1.64 crores (d) ₹ 58 lakhs

(MTP MAY 18)

Answer: (d) ₹58 lakhs Reason: Calculation as per Section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013: The company is required to spend at least 2% of the average net profits of the immediately preceding three financial years. For FY 2022-23, the relevant preceding three years are:

 2019-20: ₹30 crores  2020-21: ₹25 crores  2021-22: ₹32 crores Step 1: Total net profit of preceding 3 years = 30 + 25 + 32 = ₹87 crores Step 2: Average net profit = 87 crores ÷ 3 = ₹29 crores Step 3: Minimum CSR spend = 2% of ₹29 crores = 0.02 × 29,00,00,000 = ₹58,00,000 = ₹58 lakhs Therefore, the minimum amount ABC Limited is required to spend on CSR in FY 2022-23 is ₹58 lakhs. Analysis of options:

 (a) ₹87 lakhs → Incorrect (this is roughly 1% of total, not 2% of average)  (b) 1.45 crores → Incorrect  (c) 1.64 crores → Incorrect (common mistake: calculating 2% of total ₹87 crores ≈ ₹1.74

crores, but close variant)  (d) ₹58 lakhs → Correct The law requires 2% of the average, not 2% of the total sum of the three years.
