Question 17. What is the meaning and legal significance of the principle "generalia specialibus non derogant"? Explain with an example.

(4 marks|4 minutes)(RTP May 2025)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 762 of 941

Answer 17. The principle "generalia specialibus non derogant" means that when a general law and a specific law address the same subject matter, the specific law prevails. This ensures that specialized laws designed for particular situations are not overridden by broader, more general provisions. Example:

1. General Law: "All contracts must be in writing to be legally enforceable."
2. Specific Law: "An oral contract for the sale of goods under Rs 5000 is legally valid."

Here, the general rule states that all contracts must be in writing. However, the specific rule creates an exception for oral contracts involving goods under Rs5000. According to the principle of "generalia specialibus non derogant", the specific rule will revail in cases involving small-value goods, making oral agreements enforceable despite the broader general rule.

This principle helps maintain legal clarity by ensuring that specialized provisions are applied without being overridden by more general laws.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Explain the principle.
2. Illustrate with a general law vs special law example.
3. Remember: Special overrides General.

Examiner Observations:

1. Example-based explanation earns better marks.

Question 18. Ms. Mona employed in X-One Corporation, adopted a three-month-old baby applied for maternity leave under her company’s policy, which provided 26 weeks of paid maternity leave. However, her employer rejected the request, stating that maternity leave applies only to biological mothers as per the law. Mona approached the court against the company decision. In related to the above case, explain how the Rule of Beneficial Construction can be applied and interpreted as a welfare legislation?

(6 marks|5 minutes)(MTP May 2025)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 18. The Rule of Beneficial Construction is a judicial approach used to interpret statutes in a way that best serves their intended purpose, particularly when dealing with welfare legislation. This principle is applied when a legal provision can be understood in more than one way, allowing courts to choose the interpretation that ensures maximum benefit to the intended class of people.

In welfare laws, such as labour laws, social security laws, and laws protecting marginalized communities, this rule helps remove ambiguities and ensures that the law is applied in a just and equitable manner. One area where this rule has been significantly applied is in maternity leave benefits for adoptive mothers.

Maternity leave is an essential right granted to women to allow them time to recover from child birth and care for their new-borns. Laws in many countries, including India, grant paid maternity leave to working women.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 763 of 941

However, a strict interpretation of such laws often restricts these benefits only to biological mothers, creating an unfair disadvantage for adoptive mothers who also need time to bond with their adopted child.

The court will apply the Rule of Beneficial Construction, stating that:

1. Purpose Over Literal Meaning: The law's primary objective is child welfare and mother-child

bonding, not just post-delivery recovery. Therefore, maternity leave should not be denied based on a narrow interpretation.

2. No Discrimination between Biological and Adoptive Mothers: Excluding adoptive mothers would

create unjust discrimination against working women who adopt, violating the spirit of gender equality.

Hence the court can ruled in favour of the adoptive mother, directing the employer to grant her full maternity leave benefits.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Identify welfare legislation and beneficial interpretation.
2. Apply principle to adoptive mother's maternity leave claim.
3. Focus on Purpose of law + Application to facts

Examiner Observations:

1. Students lose marks by discussing theory without applying facts.

Question 19. At the time of interpreting a Statute what will be the effect of ‘Usage’ or ‘customs and Practices’?

(5 marks|5 minutes)(RTP Sep 2025)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 19. Effect of usage: Usage or practice developed under the statute is indicative of the meaning recognized to its words by contemporary opinion. A uniform notorious practice continued under an old statute and inaction of the Legislature to amend the same are important factors to show that the practice so followed was based on correct understanding of the law. When the usage or practice receives judicial or legislative approval it gains additional weight.

In this connection, we have to bear in mind two Latin maxims: (i) 'Optima Legum interpresest consuetude' (the custom is the best interpreter of the law); and (ii) ‘Contemporanea Expositioest optima et fortissinia in lege’ (the best way to interpret a document is to read it as it would have been read when made).

Therefore, the best interpretation/construction of a statute or any other document is that which has been made by the contemporary authority. Simply stated, old statutes and documents should be interpreted as they would have been at the time when they were enacted/written.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 764 of 941

Contemporary official statements throwing light on the construction of a statute and statutory instruments made under it have been used as contemporanea expositio to interpret not only ancient but even recent statutes in India.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Explain effect of long-standing usage.
2. Mention both Latin maxims.
3. Memorize the two maxims together.

Examiner Observations:

1. Examiners expect reference to judicial/legislative approval.

Question 20. What are the differences between interpretation and construction in the legal context, and how do these two concepts relate to each other as per Interpretation of Statute?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(PYP May’18)(Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 20. Difference and Relationship between Interpretation and Construction:- The two terms- 'Interpretation' and 'Construction', are used interchangeably to denote a process adopted by the courts to ascertain the meaning of the legislature from the words with which it is expressed, these two terms have different connotations.

Interpretation is the art of ascertaining the meaning of words and the true sense in which the author intended that they should be understood.

Thus, where the Court adheres to the plain meaning of the language used by the legislature, it would be 'interpretation' of the words, but where the meaning is not plain, the court has to decide whether the wording was meant to cover the situation before the court. Here, the court would be resorting to 'construction'. Conclusions drawn by means of construction are within the spirit though not necessarily within the letter of the law.

In practice construction includes interpretation and the terms are frequently used synonymously.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Define interpretation and construction separately.
2. Explain relationship between them.
3. Use a comparison table.

Examiner Observations:

1. Distinction must be clearly highlighted.

Question 21. Explain the principles of “Grammatical Interpretation” and “Logical Interpretation” of a Statute. What are the duties of a court in this regard?

(5 marks|4 minutes)(MTP Aug ’18)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 765 of 941

Answer 21. Principles of Grammatical Interpretation and Logical Interpretation: In order to ascertain the meaning of any law/statute the principles of Grammatical and Logical Interpretation is applied to conclude the real meaning of the law and the intention of the legislature behind enacting it. Meaning: Grammatical interpretation concerns itself exclusively with the verbal expression of law. It does not go beyond the letter of the law, whereas Logical interpretation on the other hand, seeks more satisfactory evidence of the true intention of the legislature.

Application of the principles in the court: In all ordinary cases, the grammatical interpretation is the sole form allowable. The court cannot delete or add to modify the letter of the law. However, where the letter of the law is logically defective on account of ambiguity, inconsistency or incompleteness, the court is under a duty to travel beyond the letter of law so as to determine the true intentions of the legislature. So that a statute is enforceable at law, however, unreasonable it may be. The duty of the court is to administer the law as it stands rather it is just or unreasonable.

However, if there are two possible constructions of a clause, the courts may prefer the logical construction which emerges from the setting in which the clause appears and the circumstances in which it came to be enacted and also the words used therein.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Define both interpretations.
2. Explain court’s duty when ambiguity exists.
3. Remember: Grammar first, Logic later if needed.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often omit the court’s role.

Question 22. Define Grammatical Interpretation. What are the exceptions to grammatical interpretation?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(PYP Nov’18)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 22. Grammatical Interpretation and its exceptions: 'Grammatical interpretation' concerns itself exclusively with the verbal expression of the law, it does not go beyond the letter of the law. In all ordinary cases, 'grammatical interpretation' is the sole form allowable. The Court cannot take from or add to modify the letter of the law.

This rule, however, is subject to some exceptions: (i) Where the letter of the law is logically defective on account of ambiguity, inconsistency or incompleteness. As regard the defect to ambiguity, the Court is under a duty to travel beyond the letter of the law so as to determine from the other sources the true intention of the legislature. In the case of the statutory expression being defective on account of inconsistency, the court must ascertain the spirit of the law.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 766 of 941

(ii) If the text leads to a result which is so unreasonable that it is self-evident that the legislature could not mean what it says, the court may resolve such impasse by inferring logically the intention of the legislature.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Define grammatical interpretation.
2. Discuss exceptions—ambiguity, inconsistency, absurdity.
3. Learn three keywords: Ambiguity, Inconsistency, Absurdity.

Examiner Observations:

1. Mere definition is insufficient for full marks.

Question 23. Explain how does 'natural and grammatical meaning' helps in the interpretation of a statute?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(RTP May’18)(Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 23. Natural and grammatical meaning: Statute are to be first understood in their natural, ordinary, or popular sense and must be construed according to their plain, literal and grammatical meaning. If there is an inconsistency with any express intention or declared purpose of the statute, or it involves any absurdity, repugnancy, inconsistency, the grammatical sense must then be modified, extended or abridged only to avoid such an inconvenience, but no further. [(State of HP v. Pawan Kumar (2005)]

Example: In a question before the court whether the sale of betel leaves was subject to sales tax. In this matter the Supreme Court held that betel leaves could not be given the dictionary, technical or botanical meaning when the ordinary and natural meaning is clear and unambiguous. Being the word of everyday use it must be understood in its popular sense by which people are conversant with it as also the meaning which the statute dealing with the matter would attribute to it. Therefore, the sale of betel leaves was liable to sale tax. (Ramavtar V. Assistant Sales Tax Officer, AIR 1961 SC 1325).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Explain ordinary and popular meaning rule.
2. Mention modification only to avoid absurdity.
3. Quote the betel leaves example briefly.

Examiner Observations:

1. Case law/example strengthens answer.

Question 24. Explain the rule which suggests that the 'Plain word requires no explanation' and 'Technical words be understood in technical sense only'.

(5 marks|4 minutes)(MTP Oct’19)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 767 of 941

Answer 24. Rule that suggests 'Plain Word requires no explanation' This Rule is called "Rule of Literal Construction". It is a cardinal rule of construction that a statute must be construed literally and grammatically giving the words their ordinary and natural meaning. Therefore, the language used in the statute must be construed in its grammatical sense. The correct course is to take the words themselves and arrive if possible, at their meaning without reference to cases, in the first instance.

If the phraseology of a statute is clear and unambiguous and capable of one and only one interpretation, then it would not be correct to extrapolate these words out of their natural and ordinary sense. When the language of a statute is plain and unambiguous it is not open to the courts to adopt any other hypothetical construction simply with a view to carrying out the supposed intention of the legislature.

This principle is contained in Latin maxim "absoluta sententia expositore non indiget" which literally means "absolute sentence or preposition needs not an expositor". In other words, plain words require no explanation.

Sometimes, occasions may arise when a choice has to be made between two interpretations— one narrower and the other wider or bolder. In such a situation, if the narrower interpretation would fail to achieve the manifest purpose of the legislation, one should rather adopt the wider one. Technical words are to be understood in a Technical sense only. This point of literal construction is that technical words are understood in the technical sense only.

In construing the word 'practice' in the Supreme Court Advocates Act, 1951, it was observed that practice of law generally involves the exercise of both the functions of acting and pleading on behalf of a litigant party. When legislature confers upon an advocate the right to practice in a court, it is legitimate to understand that expression as authorizing him to appear and plead as well as to act on behalf of suitors in that court. (Ashwini Kumar Ghose v. Arabinda Bose AIR 1952 SC 369).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Explain Literal Rule and Latin maxim.
2. Explain technical words in technical sense.
3. Remember maxim: Absoluta sententia expositore non indiget.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often explain only one part of the question.

Question 25. Explain the Latin term "Absoluta sententia expositore non indiget" and how would the same help in correctly interpreting a definition given in a legislation or statute?

(4 marks|3 minutes)(PYP Nov’19)(Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 25. “Absoluta Sententia Expositore Non Indiget”:- The first and primary rule of construction is that the intention of the legislature must be found in the words used by the legislature itself. Thus, if the words of a statute are capable of one construction only, then it would not be open to the

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 768 of 941

courts to adopt any hypothetical construction on the ground that such hypothetical construction is more consistent with the alleged object and policy of the Act.

It is a cardinal rule of construction that a statute must be construed literally and grammatically giving the words their ordinary and natural meaning. Therefore, the language used in the statute must be construed in its grammatical sense. The correct course is to take the words themselves and arrive if possible, at their meaning without reference to cases, in the first instance. If the phraseology of a statute is clear and unambiguous and capable of one and only one interpretation, then it would not be correct to extrapolate these words out of their natural and ordinary sense. When the language of a statute is plain and unambiguous it is not open to the courts to adopt any other hypothetical construction simply with a view to carrying out the supposed intention of the legislature.

Thus, it is the primary duty of the court to interpret the words used in legislation according to their ordinary grammatical meaning in the absence of any ambiguity or doubt. Normally, where the words of a statute are in themselves clear and unambiguous, then these words should be construed in their natural and ordinary sense and it is not open to the court to adopt any other hypothetical construction. This is called the rule of literal construction.

This principle is contained in the Latin maxim “absoluta sententia expositore non indiget” which literally means “an absolute sentence or preposition needs not an expositor”. In other words, plain words require no explanation.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. State meaning of the maxim.
2. Link it with Literal Rule of interpretation.
3. Focus on the phrase “Plain words need no explanation.”

Examiner Observations:

1. Mentioning connection with literal construction is essential.

Question 26. Sohel, a director of a Company, not being personally concerned or interested, financially or otherwise, in a matter of a proposed motion placed before the Board Meeting, did not disclose his interest although he has knowledge that his sister is interested in that proposal. He restrains from making any disclosure of his interest on the presumption that he is not required by law to disclose any interest as he is not personally interested or concerned in the proposal. He made his presumption relying on the 'Rule of Literal Construction'. Explaining the scope of interpretation under this rule in the given situation, decide whether the decision of Sohel is correct?

(6 marks|5 minutes)(MTP Jan 2025)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 26. Rule of Literal Construction:- Normally, where the words of a statute are in themselves clear and unambiguous, then these words should be construed in their natural and ordinary sense and it is not open to the court to adopt any other hypothetical construction. This is called the rule of literal construction.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 769 of 941

This principle is contained in the Latin maxim “absoluta sententia expositore non indeget” which literally means “an absolute sentence or preposition needs not an expositor”. In other words, plain words require no explanation.

Sometimes, occasions may arise when a choice has to be made between two interpretations – one narrower and the other wider or bolder. In such a situation, if the narrower interpretation would fail to achieve the manifest purpose of the legislation, one should rather adopt the wider one.

When we talk of disclosure of ‘nature of concern or interest, financial or otherwise’ of a director or manager of a company in the subject-matter of a proposed motion (as referred to in section 102 of the Companies Act), we have to interpret in its broader sense of referring to any concern or interest containing any information and facts that may enable members to understand the meaning, scope and implications of the items of business and to take decisions thereon. What is required is a full and frank disclosure without reservation or suppression, as, for instance where a son or daughter or father or mother or brother or sister is concerned in any contract or matter, the shareholders ought fairly to be informed of it and the material facts disclosed to them.

Here a restricted narrow interpretation would defeat the very purpose of the disclosure.

In the given question, Sohel (a director) did not disclose his interest in a matter placed before the Board Meeting (in which his sister has interest), as he is not personally interested or concerned in the proposal.

Here, he ought to have considered broader meaning of the provision of law; and therefore, even though he was personally not interested or concerned in the proposal, he should have disclosed the interest.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Explain literal rule and wider interpretation exception.
2. Apply facts and conclude disclosure was required.
3. Divide answer into Rule + Application + Conclusion.

Examiner Observations:

1. Fact application carries major marks in case studies.

Question 28. "No vehicles are allowed in the park." Comment on the statement, explaining the concept of 'Construction' in legal interpretation. Mention its significance in determining the legal interpretation.

(6 marks| 5 minutes)(MTP May 2025)(Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 28. In legal interpretation, ‘construction’ refers to the process of determining the true meaning and intent behind a statute or legal document. It extends beyond the literal words of the text and considers the broader legislative purpose, historical context, and other relevant factors. This method helps courts and legal professionals resolve ambiguities and apply laws in a just and reasonable manner.

As per the stated statement "No vehicles are allowed in the park" can have a strict literal interpretation which would mean that all types of vehicles, including bicycles, baby strollers, and even wheelchairs, are prohibited in the park. However, through legal construction, courts may consider the legislative intent behind the law. If the primary goal is to prevent pollution and ensure pedestrian safety, the restriction may only apply to motorized vehicles, while bicycles and strollers may still be allowed.

Significance of Construction in Legal Interpretation:

1. Clarifies Legislative Intent: Construction ensures that laws are interpreted in alignment with the

intention of the lawmakers rather than relying solely on the literal meaning of the words.

2. Resolves Ambiguities: Many legal texts contain vague or unclear language. Construction helps

eliminate confusion and ensures a consistent application of the law.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 771 of 941

3. Ensures Justice: By considering context and broader objectives, legal construction prevents unfair

or unintended consequences that could arise from rigid literal interpretations.

4. Adapts Laws to Changing Contexts: Societal norms and circumstances evolve over time.

Construction allows laws to be interpreted in a way that remains relevant and applicable to modern situations.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Explain concept of construction beyond literal meaning.
2. Apply it to “No vehicles are allowed in the park” and discuss significance.
3. Remember example: motor vehicles vs bicycles/wheelchairs.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students should explain both example and significance points for full marks.

Hence, option (d) is correct.

Question 2. If the used in a statute make it clear that a sense is intended, the rule of Ejusdem Generis shall not apply. (a) Specific words, narrow (b) Specific words, wider (c) General words, narrow (d) General words, wider

(MTP Oct ‘19)

Answer: (b) Specific words, wider Reason: Under the rule of Ejusdem Generis, general words following specific words are interpreted to include only things of the same kind as the specific ones. However, if the specific words used indicate a wider intention, then this rule does not apply, and the general words retain their broad meaning. So, when specific words show a wider sense is intended, Ejusdem Generis is excluded, making option (b) correct.

Answer: (d) All of the Above Reason: The Rule of Beneficial Construction is aimed at giving effect to the purpose and intent of the legislation, especially in remedial or welfare statutes. It is also known as:  Purposive construction – because it focuses on the purpose behind the law,  Mischief Rule – as it seeks to suppress the mischief the law intends to remedy, as laid down in

Heydon’s Case,  Heydon’s Rule – named after the landmark case establishing the principle. Hence, all options are correct, making (d) all of the above the right answer.

Question 26. When there is a conflict between two or more statues or two or more parts of a statute then which rule is applicable: (a) Welfare construction (b) Strict construction (c) Harmonious construction (d) Mischief Rule

Answer: (c) Harmonious construction Reason: This rule is specifically applied to resolve conflicts (repugnancy) between two provisions; it requires the court to interpret them in a way that reconciles the inconsistency, allowing both to remain effective rather than letting one destroy the other.

Question 27. If it is impossible to avoid inconsistency between two provisions of an Act, then (a) Provision enacted earlier in point of time must prevail (b) Provision enacted later in point of time must prevail (c) Both provisions will become repugnant (d) Provisions enacted later in Act will prevail even though it enacted earlier in point of time

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Provision enacted later in point of time must prevail Reason: If harmonization is impossible, the "Rule of Last Resort" applies, based on the maxim leges posteriores priores contrarias abrogant. This means the later provision (either appearing later in the statute or enacted later by amendment) prevails as it represents the latest will of the legislature.

Question 28. General words used in a statute will take their colour from the specific words. It is laid down by rule of (a) Harmonious construction (b) Ejusiem Generis (c) Exceptional construction (d) Reasonable construction

(RTP May 2022) Answer: (b) Ejusiem Generis Reason: The rule of Ejusdem Generis states that when general words follow a list of specific words of the same class, the general words are restricted to include only things of the same nature or kind as the specific words (e.g., "cows, goats, sheep and other animals" implies only farm animals).

Question 29. If the \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_used in a statute make it clear that a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ sense is intended, the rule of Ejusden Generis shall not apply. (a) Specific words, narrow (b) Specific words, wider (c) General words, narrow (d) General words, wider

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Specific words, wider

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 780 of 941

Reason: The rule of ejusdem generis (which restricts general words to the same class as the preceding specific words) does not apply when the specific words used in the statute clearly indicate that a wider sense (broader meaning) for the general words is intended by the legislature. In such cases, the general words are given their full, unrestricted meaning rather than being narrowed down.

Question 30. Associated words should be understood in common sense manner. This is laid down (a) Rule of Ejusdem Generis (b) Rule of Exceptional Construction (c) Noscitur a Sociis (d) Rule of Harmonious Construction

(RTP Nov 2019)

Answer: (c) Noscitur a Sociis Reason: The maxim Noscitur a Sociis translates to "it is known by its associates," meaning that the meaning of an ambiguous word should be determined by the context and "company" of the words surrounding it.

Question 31. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ means that when two or more words that are susceptible of analogous meaning, are coupled together they are understood to be used in their cognate sense. (a) Noscitur a Sociis (b) Contemporanea Expositio (c) prima facie (d) Absoluta sententia expositore non indigent

(PYQ June 2019)

Answer: (a) Noscitur a Sociis Reason: This legal maxim means "a word is known by the company it keeps," implying that when words with similar meanings are coupled together, they should be interpreted in their cognate (related) sense based on their shared context.

Question 32. In various rules of interpretation, what is the meaning of “Ejusden Generis?” (a) Of the same kind or species (b) To do purposive construction (c) Known by its associates (d) Of the different kind or species

(MTP April 2018) Answer: (a) Of the same kind or species Reason: The Latin phrase Ejusdem Generis literally means "of the same kind," and it dictates that general words following a list of specific items must be limited to the same category or "genus" as those specific items.

Question 33. The word ‘or’ is normally disjunctive and ‘and’ is normally conjunctive. However, at times they are read as vice versa to give effect the manifest intention of the legislature as disclosed from the context. This is as per (a) Noscitur A Sociis (b) Rule of Exceptional Construction (c) Rule of Literal Construction (d) Ejusdem Generis

(Study Material)

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 781 of 941

Answer: (b) Rule of Exceptional Construction Reason: Under the Rule of Exceptional Construction, courts may read "and" as "or" (and vice versa) to avoid absurdity and give effect to the true legislative intent when a literal reading would frustrate the purpose of the Act.

Question 34. A clause that begins with the words notwithstanding anything contained is called: (a) An obstacle clause (b) A non-obstante clause (c) An objectionable clause (d) A superior clause

(MTP Nov 2021)

Answer: (b) A non-obstante clause Reason: A "non-obstante" clause is used to give a particular provision overriding effect over other conflicting provisions in the same statute or other laws, essentially saying "despite anything to the contrary."

Question 35. Which of the following will override if there is conflict in interpretation of any point in Preamble and plain provision given in any statutory Act as per the General Clauses Act, 1897? (a) Preamble will override the plain provision of the Act (b) The plain provision of the Act will override the Preamble (c) The court will decide which of the above two will override (d) Provide summary of the entire Act

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) The plain provision of the Act will override the Preamble Reason: While the Preamble is a key to the mind of the legislature, it cannot qualify or limit the meaning of an enactment if the plain language of the provision is clear and unambiguous.

Question 36. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ expresses the scope, object and purpose of the Act (a) Preamble (b) Marginal Notes (c) Proviso (d) Usage

(MTP March 2022)

Answer: (a) Preamble Reason: The Preamble is an introductory statement that outlines the aims, objectives, and the philosophy behind the legislation, serving as a "key to open the mind of the makers" when the language of the Act is ambiguous.

Question 37. An internal aid that may be added to include something within the section or to exclude something from it, is (a) Proviso (b) Explanation

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 782 of 941

(c) Schedule (d) Illustration

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Explanation Reason: The primary purpose of an Explanation is to clarify the meaning of words used in a section, ensuring that a specific meaning is either included or excluded to remove any doubt or ambiguity.

Question 38.\_\_\_\_\_ expresses the scope and object of the Act more comprehensively than the \_\_\_ (a) Preamble, Short title (b) Short title, Long title (c) Long title, Preamble (d) Preamble, Long title

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) Preamble, Long title Reason: While the Long Title describes the general purpose of an Act (e.g., "An Act to consolidate and amend..."), the Preamble is a more detailed and comprehensive internal aid that expresses the underlying philosophy, spirit, and specific objectives the legislature intends to achieve.

Question 39. Which among the following cannot be considered as an internal aid for interpretation of a statue? (a) Illustrations (b) Previous Law (c) Explanations (d) Schedules

(RTP Nov 2022)

Answer: (b) Previous Law Reason: Internal aids are parts of the statute itself (like illustrations, explanations, and schedules), whereas Previous Law is an external aid because it exists outside the current document being interpreted.

Question 40. Which of the following is not an internal aid to interpretation? (a) Illustration (b) Dictionary (c) Explanation (d) Title

(PYQ Nov 2020)

Answer: (b) Dictionary Reason: A Dictionary is an external aid because it is a source found outside the statute itself, whereas illustrations, explanations, and titles are parts of the enactment and are considered internal aids.

The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999

PART A

Question 1. Mr. Sane, an Indian National desires to obtain Foreign Exchange for the following purposes:

(i) Remittance of US Dollar 50,000 out of winnings on a lottery ticket.

(ii) US Dollar 100,000 for sending a cultural troupe on a tour of U.S.A. Advise him whether he can get Foreign Exchange and if so, under what conditions?

(5 marks| 4 minutes)(Study Material)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam) Answer 1. Under provisions of section 5 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 certain Rules have been made for drawal of Foreign Exchange for Current Account transactions. As per these Rules, Foreign Exchange for some of the Current Account transactions is prohibited. As regards some other Current Account transactions, Foreign Exchange can be drawn with prior permission of the Central Government while in case of some Current Account transactions, prior permission of Reserve Bank of India is required.

(i) In respect of item No. (i), i.e., remittance out of lottery winnings, such remittance is prohibited and the same is included in First Schedule to the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000. Hence, Mr. Sane cannot withdraw Foreign Exchange for this purpose.

(ii) Foreign Exchange for meeting expenses of cultural tour can be withdrawn by any person after obtaining permission from Government of India, Ministry of Human Resources Development, (Department of Education and Culture) as prescribed in Second Schedule to the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000. Hence, in respect of item

(ii), Mr. Sane can withdraw the Foreign Exchange after obtaining such permission.

In all the cases, where remittance of Foreign Exchange is allowed, either by general or specific permission, the remitter has to obtain the Foreign Exchange from an Authorized Person as defined in Section 2(c) read with section 10 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Identify whether the transaction falls under prohibited, CG approval, or RBI approval category.
2. Apply Schedule I and Schedule II of FEMA Current Account Transaction Rules.
3. Remember: Lottery winnings = Prohibited; Cultural tour = Central Government approval.

(2 marks|2 minutes)(RTP Sep 2025)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 3. As per the fact, Ms. Pearl during her stayed in USA purchased a house in USA. As per the above provision and facts of the case, Ms. Pearl can purchase the new house in USA from her USA account.

Answer 4. According to the FEM (Acquisition and transfer of property in India) Regulations, 2018, a nonresident Indian, who is a person of Indian origin and resident outside India may acquire immovable property in India other than an agricultural property, plantation, or a farm house.

- Provided further that no payment for any transfer of immovable property shall be made either by

traveler’s cheque or by currency notes of any foreign country or any mode other than those specifically permitted by this clause.

can acquire the commercial premises in India and can transfer to person resident in India i.e., to the Company, Abhiman Ltd.

Question 11. Referring to the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, examine whether V, an exporter is bound to make declaration of a gift of Jewellery valued at Rs 20,000 exported from India to United Kingdom.

(4 marks|3 minutes)(Study Material)(Easy|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 11. In accordance with Section 7 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, every exporter of goods is generally required to furnish to the specified authority a declaration stating the true and correct material particulars, including the full export value. This declaration ensures that the exporter affirms the value for the purpose of ensuring the realization and repatriation of export proceeds to India as mandated by Section 8. However, this requirement is not absolute; Regulation 4 of the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015, specifically lists categories of exports that are exempt from furnishing this declaration. According to Regulation 4(i), the export of goods by way of a gift is exempt from the requirement of a declaration, provided that the value of such goods does not exceed ₹5,00,000 (Rupees Five Lakhs).

In the given scenario, Mr. V is exporting jewellery valued at ₹20,000 as a gift to the United Kingdom. Since this value is well within the prescribed exemption limit of ₹5 Lakhs, the transaction qualifies for the waiver. Therefore, referring to the provisions of FEMA, 1999, Mr. V is not bound to make a declaration to the specified authority for this specific export.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Determine amount retained.
2. Apply FEMA retention limit.
3. Remember: USD 2,000 may be retained.

Question 13. Mr. Suresh resided in India during the Financial Year 2023-24. He left India on 15th July, 2024, for Switzerland to pursue higher studies in Biotechnology for 2 years. What would be his residential status under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, during the Financial Years 2024-25 and 2025-26?

Mr. Suresh requires USD 25,000 towards tuition fees and USD 30,000 for incidental and stay expenses per year for studying abroad. Is it possible for Mr. Suresh to get the required Foreign Exchange and, if so, under what conditions?

(6 marks|5 minutes)(Study Material)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 13. Residential Status: According to Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, a person is considered a 'Person Resident in India' if they have resided in India for more than 182 days during the preceding financial year. However, this definition specifically excludes a person who has gone out of India for employment, for carrying on business or vocation outside India, or for any other purpose that indicates an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period.

In the case of students, while they may go abroad for a specific course duration, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) clarified in its AP (DIR Series) Circular No. 45 dated 8th December 2003 that students going abroad for higher studies are treated as ‘Person Resident outside India’ (Non-Resident). This is because students are considered to have gone abroad for an "uncertain period" as they often secure employment or extend their stay after completing their studies.

Therefore, for the Financial Year 2024-25, even though Mr. Suresh resided in India for more than 182 days in the preceding year (2023-24), he will be considered a Person Resident Outside India from the date of his departure (15th July, 2024). Furthermore, for the Financial Year 2025-26, he will

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 793 of 941

continue to be a Person Resident outside India because he did not reside in India for more than 182 days during the preceding financial year (2024-25).

Foreign Exchange for Studies Abroad: Regarding the request for foreign exchange, under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) governed by Schedule III of the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, resident individuals are allowed to remit up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year for permissible current or capital account transactions, including education.

In this case, Mr. Suresh requires USD 25,000 for tuition and USD 30,000 for incidental expenses, totaling USD 55,000 per academic year. Since this amount is well within the prescribed limit of USD 2,50,000, Mr. Suresh can obtain the required foreign exchange from an Authorized Dealer without any prior approval from the RBI. Even if the expenses were to exceed USD 2,50,000, he would still be permitted to remit the amount without RBI approval, provided the higher amount is supported by an estimate from the foreign university or institution.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Identify threshold transaction amount.
2. Apply designated business/profession provisions.
3. Remember threshold: ₹10 lakh cash transaction.

1. Linked transactions are often overlooked.

Question 21. What is an overseas direct investment? Differentiate between Automatic Route and Approval Route for direct investment?

(8 marks|6 minutes)(MTP March-21)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 21. Direct investment outside India/overseas direct investment means investments, either under the Automatic Route or the Approval Route, by way of:

(i) Contribution to the capital or subscription to the Memorandum of a foreign entity or

(ii) Purchase of existing shares of a foreign entity either by market purchase or private placement or through stock exchange, signifying a long-term interest in the foreign entity (JV or WOS).

Difference between Automatic Route and Approval Route for direct investment:- Automatic route for direct investment or financial commitment outside India: An Indian Party has been permitted to make investment/ undertake financial commitment in overseas Joint Ventures (JV)/ Wholly Owned Subsidiaries (WOS), as per the ceiling prescribed by the Reserve Bank. With effect from July 03, 2014, it has been decided that any financial commitment (FC) exceeding USD 1 (one) billion (or its equivalent) in a financial year would require prior approval of the Reserve Bank even when the total

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 800 of 941

FC of the Indian Party is within the eligible limit under the automatic route [i.e., within 400% of the net worth (Paid up capital + Free Reserves) as per the last audited balance sheet].

Approval route for direct investment or financial commitment outside India:

(i) Prior approval of the Reserve Bank would be required in all other cases of direct investment (or financial commitment) abroad.

(ii) Reserve Bank would, inter alia, take into account the following factors while considering such applications:

(a) Prima facie viability of the JV / WOS outside India;

(b) Contribution to external trade and other benefits which will accrue to India through such investment (or financial commitment);

(c) Financial position and business track record of the Indian Party and the foreign entity; and

(d) Expertise and experience of the Indian Party in the same or related line of activity as of the Therefore, under the val route (proposals not covered by the conditions under the automatic route) prior approval of the Reserve Bank would be required. For which a specific application in Form ODI with the documents to be made through the Authorized Dealer Category – I banks.

Question 23. Explain the meaning of “Capital Account Transactions” under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999. Examine whether an Investment by person resident in India in Foreign Securities is permissible or not under the above Act as Capital Account transactions.

(4 marks|4 minutes)(MTP March ‘18)(Medium|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 23. Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, a Capital Account Transaction is defined as any transaction that alters the assets or liabilities—including contingent liabilities—outside India of persons resident in India, or the assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India. This definition specifically covers transactions mentioned in Section 6 of the Act, which are designed to regulate the movement of capital across borders rather than routine trade or service payments. These transactions are governed by the Foreign Exchange Management (Permissible Capital Account Transactions) Regulations, which classify them into those permissible for residents (Schedule I), those permissible for non-residents (Schedule II), and those that are strictly prohibited, such as investing in chit funds or agricultural activities.

Regarding the permissibility of investments by a person resident in India in foreign securities, such transactions are explicitly categorized as permissible capital account transactions under Schedule I of the aforementioned regulations. While the Act generally allows these investments, they are subject to specific limits and conditions prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). For instance, resident individuals typically utilize the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), which sets an annual ceiling for such outflows, while Indian entities must follow the Overseas Investment (OI) Rules and Regulations. Therefore, as long as the resident complies with the procedural requirements and stays

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 802 of 941

within the financial limits set by the RBI, investing in foreign securities is fully permissible under the Act.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Define Capital Account Transaction.
2. Examine permissibility of investment in foreign securities.
3. Write statutory definition first.

Examiner Observations:

1. Students often omit Schedule I reference.

Question 24. Mr. Sugam resided in India during the Financial Year 2025-26. He left India on 15th July, 2026 for Australia for pursuing higher studies in Biotechnology for 2 years. What would be his residential status under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 during the Financial Years 2026-27?

Mr. Sugam requires every year USD 25,000 towards tuition fees and USD 30,000 for incidental and stay expenses for studying abroad. Is it possible for Mr. Sugam to get the required Foreign Exchange and, if so, under what conditions?

(6 marks|5 minutes)(MTP April 19, Old & New SM)(Easy|ICAI Fav|High chance for exam)

Answer 24. Residential Status: According to Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, ‘Person resident in India’ means a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the course of the preceding financial year [Section 2(v)(i)]. However, it does not include a person who has gone out of India or who stays outside India for employment or for any other purpose in such circumstances as would indicate his intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period.

Generally, a student goes out of India for a certain period. In this case, Mr. Sugam, who resided in India during the financial year 2025-26, left on 15-07-2026 for Australia to pursue higher studies in Biotechnology for 2 years. He will be considered a resident for 2026-27, as he has gone to stay outside India for a certain period.

Foreign Exchange for studies abroad: According to Para I of Schedule III to Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions), Amendment Rule, 2015 dated 26th May 2015, individuals can avail of foreign exchange facility for studies abroad within the limit of USD 2,50,000 only. Any remittance in excess of this limit requires prior approval of the RBI.

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 803 of 941

Further, provision to Para I of Schedule III states that individuals may be allowed remittances (without seeking prior approval of RBI) exceeding USD 2,50,000 based on the estimate received from the institution abroad.

In this case, the foreign exchange required is USD 55,000 per academic year (USD 25,000 tuition + USD 30,000 incidental/stay expenses) and hence approval of RBI is not required.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Determine residential status.
2. Apply study abroad remittance provisions.
3. Add tuition and stay expenses separately.

Question 26. Ice Slash (P) Ltd. had taken an INR denominated ECB of Rs 10 crore from HBSG Bank, a designated AD Category-I bank. It had last filed its Form ECB 2 Return on 5th April, 2019. The bank had send over 10 remainders vide emails during the past 9 quarters to the company to file Form ECB 2 for the month of April, 2019 and thereafter but there has been no response from either the entity or its directors till date. Also, the company had not submitted Statutory Auditor’s Certificate with respect to ECB transactions for F.Y. 2019-20 and F.Y. 2020-21, respectively. During the visit by the officials of the HBSG Bank at the registered office address of Ice Slash (P) Ltd., it was found inoperative. Accordingly, HBSG bank filed form

ECB 2 Return without certification from Ice Slash (P) Ltd. with ‘UNTRACEABLE ENTITY’ written in bold on top. The amount outstanding from the company at that time was Rs 2 crore.

In the context of aforesaid case-scenario, please answer to the following questions:-

(i) Whether HBSG Bank can be considered to have validly treated Ice Slash (P) Ltd. as an ‘untraceable entity’?

(ii) How the outstanding amount of Rs 2 crore shall be treated and what other actions would be taken in respect of Ice Slash (P) Ltd.?

(7 marks|6 minutes)(MTP Nov 21)(Medium|ICAI Fav)

Answer 26. (i) Under the ECB framework, any borrower who has raised ECB will be treated as ‘untraceable entity’, if entity/auditor(s)/director(s)/ promoter(s) of entity are not reachable/responsive/reply in negative over email/letters/phone for a period of not less than two quarters with documented communication/ reminders numbering 6 or more and it fulfills both of the following conditions:

(a) Entity not found to be operative at the registered office address as per records available with the AD Bank or not found to be operative during the visit by the officials of the AD Bank or any other agencies Authorized by the AD bank for the purpose;

(b) Entities have not submitted Statutory Auditor’s Certificate for last two years or more. Ice Slash (P) Ltd. or its directors have not responded to over 10 remainders made by HBSG Bank during the past 9 quarters for filing returns and had not submitted Statutory Auditor’s Certificate for F.Y. 2019- 20 and F.Y. 2020-21, respectively. Also, the company was found inoperative by the officials of the HBSG Bank.

Thus, HBSG Bank can be considered to have validly treated Ice Slash (P) Ltd. as an ‘untraceable entity’ as all the conditions with respect to the same had been satisfied in the case of it

CATESTSERIES.ORG Page 806 of 941

(ii) Under the ECB framework, in respect of ‘untraceable entities’, the outstanding amount will be treated as written-off from external debt liability of the country but may be retained by the lender in its books for recovery through judicial/ non-judicial means.

Thus, the outstanding amount of Rs 2 crore shall be written-off from the external debt liability of the country and it might be retained by the HBSG Bank for recovery. Other actions that would be taken in respect of Ice Slash (P) Ltd. are as follows:-

No fresh ECB application by Ice Slash (P) Ltd. should be examined/processed by the AD bank; Directorate of Enforcement should be informed about Ice Slash (P) Ltd. being designated as ‘UNTRACEABLE ENTITY’; and No inward remittance or debt servicing will be permitted under auto route for Ice Slash (P) Ltd.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

TDS as per Income Tax Act, 1961 40,000

- Amount is converted to USD from INR.

Answer 27. i. For a person who is resident but not permanently resident in India and-
